What is the most basic principle by which responsibilities are assigned in object-
oriented design? 
Solution: 
 
Assign a responsibility to the class that has the information necessary to fulfil the 
responsibility. 
 
Who, in the general case is responsible?

necessary to fulfil the responsibility.

Controller 
 
Problem: 
 
To assign responsibility for handling a system event? 
  
Solution: 
 
If a program receive events from external sources other than its graphical 
interface, add an event class to decouple the event source(s) from the objects that 
actually handle the events.  
Who handles a system event? 
Assign the responsibility for handling a system event message to a class representing 
one of these choices: 
1. The business or overall organization (a façade controller).  
2. The overall "system" (a façade controller).  
3. An animate thing in the domain that would perform the work (a role controller).  
4. An artificial class (Pure Fabrication) representing the use (a use case controller).

summary: A tutorial covering traditional and contemporary software processes through case studies and group discussions, relevant to COMP1821 coursework and group project planning.
text:
COMP1821 
Tutorial 3: Exercise – Software 
Methodologies 
 
 
Exercise 1: (20-30 min) 
Tutor lead Q&A session 
Name 3 traditional software processes and 3 contemporary ones and briefly 
discuss. Encourage students to focus on the self-study slides from lecture.  
 
Exercise 2: (20-25 min) 
Read the London Ambulance System case study provided on Moodle for this 
week 
Discuss within your tutorial group (tutor lead discussion with the whole group) 
and answer the following question: 
• From a Software engineering process point of view, what problems did 
the London Ambulance Computer-Aided Dispatch System might have 
encountered to contribute to its failure? 
 
Exercise 3: CW groups (4-5 students) to be finalized 
Tutors will form CW groups if they were not created already. Each CW group 
will be acting as a software house and the client will be your tutor. (You can 
give a name to your software house) 
 
Exercise 4: (20-30 min) – work in groups 
Read the Around London Book Stores case study provided on Moodle for this 
Discuss within your group the following: 
• Consider how you may advise Around London Book Stores as to which 
development process they should employ in developing their system. 
Within your answer compare at least two software development 
approaches of your choice. 
Present to the class your findings. 
 
 
Exercise 5: (The rest of the tutorial time) 
Within your software house (CW group) read and discuss the CW specification. 
Ask the client any clarifications that you may need. 
 
Unsupervised learning task: to be done by the next tutorial: 
Each member of a coursework group must attempt Deliverables 1) a) of the 
Coursework *. Before the next tutorial you should meet with your team, 
discuss your solutions p and decide a common solution. Please bring your 
team progress to the following tutorial for your client (Your tutor) to see.

summary: Explains Python's ternary operator as a compact alternative to if-else statements, with examples for odd number checks, grade passing status, and age categorization. Demonstrates syntax equivalence between traditional control flow and ternary expressions.
text:
COMP1811 
P a r a d i g ms  o f  P r o g r a mmi n g  
  
Control Flow Conditionals 
 
the ternary operator and alternative syntax 
 
Dr. Yasmine Arafa 
Ternary Operators 
•
Ternary operators allow the evaluation of a condition in a single line  
–
by replacing the multiline if-else statement,  
–
making the code compact. 
•
Alternative syntax:     
         <on_True> if <condition> else <on_False> 
•
Example: 
 
#get smallest of two values 
smallest = a if a < b else b  
• Check if odd number: 
 
– is the equivalent to: 
 
 
Examples 
is_odd = True if x%2 != 0 else False  
if x%2 != 0: 
   is_odd = True  
else:  
   is_odd = False  
• Check if grade is a pass: 
 
– is the equivalent to: 
 
 
Examples 
if grade >= 40: 
    pass_status = "pass" 
else: 
    pass_status = "fail" 
pass_status = "pass" if grade >= 40 else "fail" 
• Get age category: 
 
 
– is the equivalent to: 
 
 
Examples 
age_category = 'Child' if age < 13 else  
if age < 13: 
  age_category = 'Child'  
elif age < 18:  
  age_category = 'Teenager' 
else: 
  age_category = 'Adult' 
                    'Teenager' if age < 18 else 'Adult' 
• Get age category: 
 
 
– is the equivalent to: 
 
 
Examples 
age_category = 'Child' if age < 13 else  
if age < 13: 
  age_category = 'Child'  
elif age < 18:  
  age_category = 'Teenager' 
else: 
  age_category = 'Adult' 
                    'Teenager' if age < 18 else 'Adult' 
• Shares action: 
 
– is the equivalent to: 
 
 
Examples 
print('hold') if shares==0 else 
if shares == 0: 
   print('hold') 
elif shares < 0:  
   print('sell') 
else: 
   print('buy') 
print('sell') if shares<0 else print('buy') 
if shares != 0: 
    if shares < 0: 
        print('sell') 
    else: 
        print('buy') 
else: 
   print('hold') 
or 
Multiple Statements on a Single Line 
alternative syntax –legal in Python 
•
if x!=4: x+=y; print(x); print(y) 
–
Semi colons are used to delimit statements if multiple statements are put  
on the same line. 
–
If <condition> is True, all three statements are executed, otherwise, that 
block is skipped. 
•
The following is also legal in python: 
x=4; y=5; z=y*x; print(z) 
 
 
Further Reading  
•
w3school pages  
–
Ternary Operator

summary: This coursework logbook outlines requirements for a software engineering module, including a timed online quiz on topics like software process models, lifecycle phases, and ethical issues. It details submission guidelines and academic integrity policies.
text:
COMP1821  
Principles of Software 
Engineering 
Contribution: 40% of 
course 
Course Leader:  
Dr. Najma Taimoor 
Logbook 
Deadline Date: 19-11-2025 
 
This coursework should take an average student who is up to date with tutorial work 
approximately 10 hours  
 
Feedback and grades are normally made available within 15 working days of the 
coursework deadline 
Learning Outcomes:  
  
1. . Describe and compare different software process models and explain the 
merits and constraints of the various approaches (e.g. plan-based vs. agile-
based). 
2. 2. Describe the software lifecycle and the activities associated with each 
phase. 
3. 3. Critically evaluate and apply the choice of model for given real-world 
specifications and requirements and to justify and use appropriate tools and 
techniques for software development. 
4. 4. Demonstrate an understanding of Legal, Social, Ethical and Professional 
Issues and their practical implications for software engineering. 
 
Plagiarism is presenting somebody else's work as your own. It 
includes copying information directly from the Web or books without 
referencing the material; submitting joint coursework as an individual 
effort; copying another student's coursework; stealing coursework 
from another student and submitting it as your own work.  Suspected 
plagiarism will be investigated and if found to have occurred will be 
dealt with according to the procedures set down by the University. 
Please see your student handbook for further details of what is / isn't 
plagiarism.  
 
All material copied or amended from any source (e.g. internet, books) must 
be referenced correctly according to the reference style you are using.  
 
Your work will be submitted for plagiarism checking.  Any attempt to bypass 
our plagiarism detection systems will be treated as a severe Assessment 
Offence. 
 
Coursework Submission Requirements 
• An electronic copy of your work for this coursework must be fully 
uploaded on the Deadline Date using the link on the coursework 
Moodle page for COMP1821. 
• For this coursework you must submit a single PDF document.  In 
general, any text in the document must not be an image (i.e. must not 
be scanned) and would normally be generated from other documents 
(e.g. MS Office using "Save As ... PDF"). An exception to this is 
handwritten mathematical notation, but when scanning, ensure the 
file size is not excessive. 
• There are limits on the file size (see the relevant course Moodle 
page). 
• Make sure that any files you upload are virus-free and not protected 
by a password or corrupted otherwise they will be treated as null 
submissions. 
• Your work will not be printed in colour. Please ensure that any pages 
with colour are acceptable when printed in Black and White. 
• You must NOT submit a paper copy of this coursework. 
• All coursework must be submitted as above. Under no circumstances 
can they be accepted by academic staff 
The University website has details of the current Coursework Regulations, 
including details of penalties for late submission, procedures for 
Extenuating Circumstances, and penalties for Assessment

summary: This lecture explains Python's ternary operator syntax for conditional expressions, demonstrating how to replace multiline if-else statements with compact single-line logic through multiple code examples.
text:
COMP1811 
P a r a d i g ms  o f  P r o g r a mmi n g  
  
Control Flow Conditionals 
 
the ternary operator and alternative syntax 
 
Dr. Yasmine Arafa 
Ternary Operators 
•
Ternary operators allow the evaluation of a condition in a single line  
–
by replacing the multiline if-else statement,  
–
making the code compact. 
•
Alternative syntax:     
         <on_True> if <condition> else <on_False> 
•
Example: 
 
#get smallest of two values 
smallest = a if a < b else b  
• Check if odd number: 
 
– is the equivalent to: 
 
 
Examples 
is_odd = True if x%2 != 0 else False  
if x%2 != 0: 
   is_odd = True  
else:  
   is_odd = False  
• Check if grade is a pass: 
 
– is the equivalent to: 
 
 
Examples 
if grade >= 40: 
    pass_status = "pass" 
else: 
    pass_status = "fail" 
pass_status = "pass" if grade >= 40 else "fail" 
• Get age category: 
 
 
– is the equivalent to: 
 
 
Examples 
age_category = 'Child' if age < 13 else  
if age < 13: 
  age_category = 'Child'  
elif age < 18:  
  age_category = 'Teenager' 
else: 
  age_category = 'Adult' 
                    'Teenager' if age < 18 else 'Adult' 
• Get age category: 
 
 
– is the equivalent to: 
 
 
Examples 
age_category = 'Child' if age < 13 else  
if age < 13: 
  age_category = 'Child'  
elif age < 18:  
  age_category = 'Teenager' 
else: 
  age_category = 'Adult' 
                    'Teenager' if age < 18 else 'Adult' 
• Shares action: 
 
– is the equivalent to: 
 
 
Examples 
print('hold') if shares==0 else 
if shares == 0: 
   print('hold') 
elif shares < 0:  
   print('sell') 
else: 
   print('buy') 
print('sell') if shares<0 else print('buy') 
if shares != 0: 
    if shares < 0: 
        print('sell') 
    else: 
        print('buy') 
else: 
   print('hold') 
or 
Multiple Statements on a Single Line 
alternative syntax –legal in Python 
•
if x!=4: x+=y; print(x); print(y) 
–
Semi colons are used to delimit statements if multiple statements are put  
on the same line. 
–
If <condition> is True, all three statements are executed, otherwise, that 
block is skipped. 
•
The following is also legal in python: 
x=4; y=5; z=y*x; print(z) 
 
 
Further Reading  
•
w3school pages  
–
Ternary Operator

text:
Inheritance Tutorial 
 
Dr. Elena I Popa 
Exercise 1: Discussion (15 min) 
 
• 
What is the difference between the conceptual class diagram and design class diagram? 
• 
What is inheritance? 
• 
What are abstract classes and methods (functions) 
• 
What is polymorphism?    
 
Exercise 2: Design class diagram (20- 30 min) 
 
POST case study 
Your company has been hired to build a Point of Sales Terminal System (POST) for a small chain of 
specialised supermarkets operating in your area, called “CMS-Markets”. The brief is to design and 
build a system that, as soon as a customer comes to a till with a basket/trolley of goods, allows the 
checkout operator to process the items, calculate the total, process a payment and print a receipt. 
The system should be able to capture the sales, so that they can be used to determine stock levels 
and statistical information about customer preferences. 
A store has many tills and each till can be operated by operator.  The store has a product catalogue 
which hold the specifications of all their products. Each product has an UPC (unique product code) 
The first contact the sales team had with the company has given you the following information 
about them: 
At the moment they are using first generation tills that are not integrated between them or with the 
stock control system. Their stock control and pricing system is on a standalone database at each 
store. Their accounts and personnel systems are also not integrated, as there is a lot of manual re-
typing of data from system to system.  
The analysis diagrams and Object sequence diagrams were  already implemented. You are required 
to create the  design class diagram of the POST system 
.  
Inheritance Tutorial 
 
Dr. Elena I Popa

Dr. Elena I Popa

Dr. Elena I Popa

need to show a loop if you wish to buy mode items

Dr. Elena I Popa 
Exercise 3: Inheritance (20- 30 min) 
 
Life gets complicated- Case study:  
A person is created and enjoys life before it dies. Occasionally the person is answering questions 
The person has a pet.  The pet should be specified. Things about pets: 
 A pet can be a cat, a frog or a bird and they all have a name 
 Pets can move in different ways : 
 Walk, Hop, Swim, Fly.  Which one does which?  
 Regarding Frogs: tadpoles (young frogs) swim, but frogs can hop, as well hop 
 To be able to fly a bird needs to flap 
 All pets eat and sleep, and make a noise  
Produce a Class Diagram : 
 Identify the software classes .  Include the attributes from the domain model.  Include 
obvious methods 
1. Show the relationships for all classes, including inheritance.  
2. Show visibility for all members

summary: The document explains Python conditional statements, the use of the pass statement for stubbing code, and common indentation errors causing syntax and semantic issues in programming.
text:
COMP1811 
P a r a d i g ms  o f  P r o g r a mmi n g  
  
Professional Programming 2 
 
Python conditionals 
 
• You have to have at least one statement inside each branch but you can 
use the pass command while you’re still stubbing. 
  if x < 0: 
     pass  # Handle negative values  
Notes on Conditionals 
• The pass keyword indicates that nothing happens when it is executed. 
• Sometimes useful, e.g. during development: 
 
if a <= 40 and b <= 40: 
   print("Both marks are below 40. Try harder!") 
if a > 40 and b <= 40: 
   pass                  # figure out what to do later 
if a <= 40 and b > 40: 
   pass                  # figure out what to do later 
if a > 40 and b > 40: 
   pass                  # figure out what to do later 
 
The pass Statement 
"do nothing" 
• Wrong indentation could cause: 
– Syntax error: 
 
 
 
Common Errors 
reminder that indentation is important! 
# if x is even divide by 2, 
# otherwise, add 1 before dividing by 2. 
if x%2==0:  
   x /= 2  
print(x)  
else:  
   x = (x+1)/2  
   print(x)  
Wrong indentation on line 5 causes 
a syntax error on line 6 – unexpected 
keyword and colon. 
print(x) on line 5 should be indented 
at the same level as line 4. 
• Wrong indentation could cause: 
– Semantic/Logical error: 
 
 
 
Common Errors 
reminder that indentation is important!, Cntd. 
# if x is even divide by 2, 
# otherwise, add 1 before dividing by 2. 
if x%2==0:  
   x /= 2  
   print(x)  
else:  
   x = (x+1)/2  
print(x)  
Wrong indentation on line 8 causes 
a semantic error.  
If x is even, x/2 will be displayed twice. 
• Wrong indentation could cause: 
– Another syntax error: 
 
 
 
Common Errors 
reminder that indentation is important!, Cntd. 
# if x is even divide by 2, 
# otherwise, add 1 before dividing by 2. 
if x%2==0:  
   x /= 2  
   print(x)  
   else:  
     x = (x+1)/2  
     print(x)  
Wrong indentation on line 6. 
Indentation for else: should be 
aligned with "if". 
• Variable not always available: 
 
 
Common Errors 
variable existence depends on code flow 
# get grade classification. 
my_grade = 68 
if my_grade >= 70:  
   g_class = "first"  
print(g_class)  
Line 5 causes a run-time error, which is an error 
that happens when you try to run the code. 
g_class is not defined! Its existence depends  on 
the flow executed. 
Generally it's  a bad idea to refer to variables  
defined inside an if clause.

Your company has been hired to build a Point of Sales Terminal System (POST) for a small chain of 
specialised supermarkets operating in your area, called “CMS-Markets”. The brief is to design and build a 
system that, as soon as a customer comes to a till with a basket/trolley of goods, allows the checkout 
operator to process the items, calculate the total, process a payment and print a receipt. The system 
should be able to capture the sales, so that they can be used to determine stock levels and statistical 
information about customer preferences.
A store has many tills and each till can be operated by operator.  The store has a product catalogue which 
hold the specifications of all their products. Each product has an UPC (unique product code)
The first contact the sales team had with the company has given you the following information about 
them:
At the moment they are using first generation tills that are not integrated between them or with the 
stock control system. Their stock control and pricing system is on a standalone database at each store. 
Their accounts and personnel systems are also not integrated, as there is a lot of manual re-typing of 
data from system to system. 
All shops are run in a similar way, although it seems that there is very little communication between 
departments.
You are required to make a first attempt at the analysis and design of the POST system. 
After eliciting the initial requirements for the new system, you have agreed with the client to produce a 
preliminary design and build a prototype system using object-oriented methodologies (to allow for more 
flexible design/build iterations and re-use of design and code).

5:00pm 
This coursework should take an average student who is up to date with tutorial work 
approximately 40 hours  
 
Feedback and grades are normally made available within 15 working days of the 
coursework deadline 
Learning Outcomes:  
1. Describe and compare different software process models and explain the merits and 
constraints of the various approaches (e.g. plan-based vs. agile-based).

development.

practical implications for software engineering.

procedures set down by the University. Please see your student 
handbook for further details of what is / isn't plagiarism.  
 
All material copied or amended from any source (e.g., internet, books) must be 
referenced correctly according to the reference style you are using.  
 
Your work will be submitted for plagiarism checking.  Any attempt to bypass our 
plagiarism detection systems will be treated as a severe Assessment Offence.

not be scanned) and would normally be generated from other 
documents (e.g., MS Office using "Save As . PDF").

page). 
• Make sure that any files you upload are virus-free and not protected 
by a password or corrupted otherwise they will be treated as null 
submissions.

summary: Document covers requirements elicitation techniques, functional/non-functional requirements classification, and data modeling principles. Focuses on system requirements analysis and logical/physical data model creation.

UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
1
E. I. Teodorescu
Structured Analysis and Design
Principles of Software Engineering
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
2
E. I. Teodorescu
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
Structured Analysis and Design (SA/SD)
Structured Analysis:
is the activity of deriving a structured model of 
the requirements of a system including various 
stages like feasibility, requirement analysis, 
specification etc.,.
Structured design:
is the development of a blueprint of a computer 
system solution to a problem, having the same 
components and interrelationship as the original 
problem.
2
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
3
E. I. Teodorescu
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
Requirements Elicitation:
Tools and techniques
• Interviews, shadowing, questionnaires, JAD 
sessions, etc.
People involved
• Users, developers, management, consultants, 
analysists, etc.
3
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
4
E. I. Teodorescu
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
Functional / Non-functional
Requirements
Functional requirements are the actions that the 
system should do
• Data holding of a system
• Data transformations it performs
• Reports and outputs it can produce
Non-functional requirements describe the system
• Constraints
• Properties
• Control mechanisms
• Targets
4
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
5
E. I. Teodorescu
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
Functional Requirements: Examples
• The system should allow all registered users to 
log in.
• On the last day of each month, at 10am BST, 
the system should generate sales reports and 
store it in the cloud.
• The system should allow senior staff to view, 
change and delete products.
5
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
6
E. I. Teodorescu
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
Non-Functional Requirements: Examples 
Constraints, targets or control mechanisms: properties of the software product itself
•
Performance and speed requirements 
e.g. 20,000 transactions per day
•
Security and access requirements 
e.g meet auditors requirements, be available in both English and German language options
•
Technical constraints  (including interoperability, scalability and platform 
constraints)
e.g. run on existing hardware, or using existing networks. 
•
Project constraints 
e.g. require no new support posts, implemented within 6 months
•
Organisational constraints  (including cost and time to market)
 e.g. be teachable to new staff in 2 weeks
•
Usability and reliability issues
         e.g. must have a 100% uptime
6
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
7
E. I. Teodorescu
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
Data vs Information
Data = “raw material“ 
On its own - it is not very useful / not significant
It comes in many forms: numbers, words, symbols, and 
images. Characters. 
For example, John, 558, Greenwich,  London, 10, Kilometres
Information is data that has been processed in such a 
way as to be meaningful to the person who receives it.
It is not enough for data simply to be processed. It has to 
be of use to someone – otherwise, why bother?! 
For example, “John lives at house No. 558 in Greenwich, 
London.” “He can run 10 kilometres a day.”
7
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
8
E. I. Teodorescu
UNIVERSITY  of  GREENWICH
Data Modelling
Data modelling is the process of creating a visual 
representation of either a whole information system or parts 
of it to communicate connections between data points and 
structures. 
It involves a progression from a logical model to a physical 
schema. 
Logical Data Models 
to visualize data entities, attributes, keys, and relationships.
the basis for the creation of the physical data model.
Physical Data Model
to visualize the physical structure of databases and data files
represents an application and database-specific implementation 
of a logical data model.

The E-R model is a detailed, logical representation of the data for 
an organisation or business area
The model must be as ‘open’ as possible 
not tied to any technology

summary: This document outlines COMP1811's Python project coursework requirements, including learning outcomes, submission guidelines, and plagiarism policies. It emphasizes programming paradigms, simulation systems, and PyCharm integration for project implementation.
text:
COMP1811 Python Project Coursework Specification 
 
COMP1811 (2025/26) 
 
Paradigms of Programming 
 
Contribution: 40% of module 
Module Leader/Moderator 
Yasmine Arafa/Andy Wicks  
Practical Coursework 1: Python Project 
Deadline Date 
     Monday, 24/11/25 
This coursework should take an average student who is up-to-date with tutorial/lab work approximately 35 hours. 
Feedback and grades are normally made available within 21 days of the coursework deadline. 
Learning Outcomes:  
A. Understand the programming paradigms introduced and their applicability to practical problems. 
B. Apply appropriate programming constructs in each programming paradigm. 
C. Design, implement, and test small-scale applications in each programming paradigm. 
D. Use appropriate tools to design, edit, and debug programs for each paradigm. 
 
Plagiarism is presenting somebody else's work as your own. It includes copying information directly from 
the Web or books without citing the source, submitting joint coursework as your own, copying another 
student's coursework, or submitting it as your own. Suspected plagiarism will be investigated and, if found, 
dealt with in accordance with the University's procedures. Please see your student handbook for further 
details of what is/isn't plagiarism. 
All material copied or amended from any source (e.g. internet, books) must be referenced correctly 
according to the reference style you are using. Code snippets from open-source resources or YouTube 
and any code generated by generative AI (e.g. ChatGPT) must be acknowledged appropriately.  
Your work will be submitted for electronic plagiarism checking. Any attempt to bypass our 
plagiarism detection systems will be treated as a severe Assessment Offence. 
Coursework Submission Requirements 
• An electronic copy of your work for this coursework must be fully uploaded by 17:00 on Monday, 24/11/25. 
Submissions must be made using the Python Project Upload link under "Coursework Specification and 
Submission" on the Moodle page for COMP1811.  Your grade for the coursework will be capped at 40% if you 
fail to submit by the deadline, unless you have an accepted EC. 
• You must upload two SEPARATE files for this coursework: a) a zip file containing all the files needed to run 
your Python project in PyCharm and the screencast, AND b) a PDF version of your report. In general, 
any text in the document must not be an image (i.e. must not be scanned) and would normally be generated from 
other documents (e.g. MS Office using "Save As ... PDF"). A penalty will apply for the use of screenshots of 
code in place of code text, or if two separate files are not uploaded or named correctly. The maximum size for 
each upload is 2GB. It is your responsibility to make sure you are within the size limit. 
• Make sure that any files you upload are virus-free and not protected by a password or corrupted; otherwise, they 
will be treated as null submissions. Upload your screencast in a separate .zip if the file size is too large. 
• All coursework must be submitted as above. Under no circumstances can they be accepted by academic staff. 
 
The University website has details of the current Academic Regulations, including details of penalties for late 
submission, procedures for Extenuating Circumstances, and penalties for Assessment Offences. See 
https://gre.ac.uk/policies/undergraduate-and-postgraduate-taught 
 
Page 2 | 15 
Coursework Regulations 
• If you have been granted Extenuating Circumstances (ECs), you may submit your coursework up to 10 working 
days after the published deadline without penalty.  However, this is subject to your claim being accepted by the 
Faculty Extenuating Circumstances Panel. 
• Late submissions will be dealt with in accordance with University Regulations. 
• Coursework submitted more than two weeks late may be given feedback, but will be recorded as a non-
submission regardless of any extenuating circumstances. The only exception to this is where

summary: This report details the SafeCare Hospital Management System project, focusing on legal, social, ethical, and professional challenges in implementing digital safety protocols. It emphasizes GDPR compliance, accessibility issues, ethical AI use, and interoperability standards for healthcare systems.
text:
1
 
SafeCare Hospital Management System Implementation Report 
Overview 
The SafeCare Hospital Management System project aims to convert and digitalise 
safety protocols within a 700-bed facility. Automated access control, and digital 
emergency responses significantly improves patient safety and operational 
efficiency. It also reinforces the critical situation that Safecare currently finds itself in 
following Legal, Social, Ethical, and Professional (LSEPI) issues. This report then 
outlines the project methodology, strategic analysis, system requirements, and 
technical implementation required to deliver a compliant and robust solution. 
 
LEGAL ISSUES 
a. GDPR Compliance: The UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) 
states that personal data consists of any information pertaining to any person, 
on the other hand special category data needs additional protection due to its 
sensitivity. 
 
b. CCTV Rules: The use of CCTV must adhere to surveillance legislation like 
the Data Protection Act 2018 and the ICO CCTV Code of Practice. One of 
these rules includes the requirement to inform people when they are being 
recorded. 
 
c. Medical Device Regulations: Wearable sensors can be classed as medical 
devices under the UK Medical Devices Regulations 2002; as such, they must 
be examined, certified, and approved by regulatory authorities before they can 
be used. 
SOCIAL ISSUES 
a. Digital Ostracism: Digitalising hospital safety causes issues such as digital 
ostracism which is the gap between people who have the skills and 
confidence to use digital tools versus those who do not. This includes older 
adults (aged 75+), people with poor literacy skills, disabilities, or socio-
economic challenges. 
 
b. Access Barriers: If pre-registration via mobile app is expected, people who 
don’t own a device or understand may be ostracised or delayed. Additionally, 
the price of a device and other costs prevent people from accessing the app. 
 
 
 
 
2
 
c. Trust & Privacy Concerns: Not everyone trusts digital tools; there are 
concerns about how private data is being used or shared.  
 
d. Design Fairness: Digital tools must be functional, accessible, and fair by 
taking into account cultural diversities, languages, and cognitive abilities.  
ETHICAL ISSUES 
a. Lawful Basis: Under Article 6 of the UK GDPR, a lawful basis for processing 
sensitive health data must be identified, alongside Article 9 which states the 
requirements for processing procedures. 
 
b. Consent Validity: Demanding pre-registration raises the question of whether 
consent is independent and valid, especially for patients with language 
barriers or reduced capacity. Consent flows must be multidimensional (verbal 
support, translated text) with unambiguous opt-out choices. 
 
c. Surveillance vs. Dignity: Regular monitoring (high-definition cameras, 
biometric verification) increases safety but exposes patients to intrusive 
surveillance that erodes privacy and dignity unless justified. The ICO and UK 
Surveillance Camera Code of Practice set standards requiring monitoring to 
be proportionate to a valid aim. The General Medical Council (GMC) 
also highlights the doctor’s duty of confidentiality. 
 
d. AI & Bias: Any analytical tool or AI used to set up emergency alerts or predict 
deterioration via sensors can strengthen structural/historical biases. 
Healthcare providers must be able to explain AI recommendations to preserve 
accountability. To alleviate this, an Algorithmic Impact Assessment must be 
conducted to certify performance across demographic groups.  
 
PROFESSIONAL ISSUES 
a. Interoperability Standards: Clinical systems must transfer patients' booking 
data reliably using the UK/NHS recommended standard (HL7 Fast Healthcare 
Interoperability Resources or HL7 FHIR) for modern healthcare APIs. This 
decreases integration failures and guarantees secure data flow between the 
app, EMR, and monitoring systems. 
 
b. Code of Conduct: The British Computer So

summary: The document explains encapsulation principles in Python, focusing on data hiding through private variables, name mangling, and property decorators. It demonstrates class implementations with getter/setter methods and highlights Pythonic practices for encapsulation.
text:
C O M P 1 8 1 1
P a r a d i g m s  o f  P r o g r a m m i n g
Lecture 8 – Object-oriented Programming 1 - Classes and Objects
Dr. Ralph Barthel
Encapsulation
•
Encapsulation is the packing of data and functions operating on that data 
into a single object and restricting the access to some of the object’s 
attributes and methods.
•
Encapsulation is used for hiding information of the representation or 
state of an object to the outside world
•
In some programming languages such as Java specific keywords exist to 
make variables in objects private. In Python this is achieved by 
convention. Private variables receive a “__”   or “_” (convention)  prefix.
Encapsulation
class Car:
def __init__(self):
self.__update_software()
def drive(self):
print('driving')
def __update_software(self):
print('updating software')
redcar = Car()
redcar.__update_software()
# AttributeError: 'Car' object has no attribute '__update_software'
Encapsulation
•
In the previous example the private method __update_software is not 
accessible from the outside of the class
•
To access and manipulate the values of private variables “getter” and 
“setter” methods are normally being used in different programming 
languages
•
These are public methods of an object that access or alter the values of 
private variables
Encapsulation
class Car:
def __init__(self):
self.__maxspeed = 100
# getter method to get the value for __maxspeed
def get_speed(self):
return self.__maxspeed
# function to set value of __maxspeed
def set_speed(self, speed):
self.__maxspeed = speed
Getter and setter methods - Example 1
Encapsulation
porsche = Car()
print (porsche.get_speed())
porsche.set_speed(200)
print (porsche.get_speed())
# prints 
100
200
Getter and Setter methods – Example 1
Encapsulation
•
While the previous example with getter and setter method works 
fine it is not very “Pythonic” 
•
All attributes are public in Python. Variable names starting with “_” 
or “__” serve as warning that the attribute is an implementation 
detail that could change in the future. 
•
a single leading underscore “_” is a convention to signal to other 
developers that indicates that a variable is to be treated as private
•
a double leading underscore “__” is treated differently by the 
compiler and a process called name mangling is used
Encapsulation
• Name mangling in Python – a private variable __spam for example 
is textually replaced with _classname__spam, where classname is 
the current class name with leading underscore(s) stripped. 
• Name mangling is mainly used to avoid accidents not to achieve 
encapsulation
• The “Pythonic” way is using the property decorator
Decorators
Source: https://www.datacamp.com/community/tutorials/decorators-python
“A decorator is a design pattern in Python that allows a user to add 
new functionality to an existing object without modifying its 
structure. Decorators are usually called before the definition of a 
function you want to decorate.”
Encapsulation
class RaceCar:
def __init__(self, speed):
## initializing the attribute
self._maxspeed = speed
@property
def maxspeed(self):
return self._maxspeed
## the attribute name and the method name must be same which is used
## to set the value for the attribute
@maxspeed.setter
def maxspeed(self, speed):
if speed > self.maxspeed:
self._maxspeed = speed
Using the property decorator– Example 2
Encapsulation
ferrari=RaceCar(230)
print(ferrari.maxspeed)
ferrari.maxspeed=300
print(ferrari.maxspeed)
# prints
230
300
Using the property decorator– Example 2
Encapsulation
Advantages of using the property decorator
•
Identical syntax to standard attribute access so its easier to change the 
implementation
•
Typically used when the change of a variable is conditional 
•
Its also “cultural” and using property decorators is the common practice 
in the Python development community
•
Getters and setters are often used for testing
Decorators
•
Functions are first class objects in Python which means they can be 
passed around and used as

summary: Analyzes legal, social, and ethical challenges in digitalizing hospital safety systems, including GDPR compliance, NHS standards, digital inclusion issues, and sensitive data classification. Relevant to Bruno's AI server development for healthcare applications.
text:

Figure 3
CASE STUDY: SAFECARE HOSPITAL MANAGEMENT
Digitalising SafeCare Hospital safety and emergency management provides apparent benefits such as swift emergency responses, better access control and improved patient safety but it also reenforces crucial LSEP issues.
LEGAL ISSUES
GDPR Compliance: Under the EU/UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), personal data includes any information related to an identified person, while special category data requires extra protection due to its sensitivity.
Lawful Basis (Articles 6 & 9): Processing these data types requires a legal basis and definitive consent for sensitive data, as outlined in Articles 6 and 9 of the GDPR.
Data Rights & Security: The system must ensure data security (encryption, access control), data minimisation (Article 5), and uphold the right of access and right to be forgotten (Articles 15 and 17).
NHS Standards: NHS organisations must adhere to the Data Security and Protection Toolkit (a self-assessment against the National Data Guardian’s 10 standards) and the Health and Social Care Act 2012, which guarantees confidentiality and reliable use of patient data.
CCTV Regulations: The use of CCTV must follow surveillance laws such as the Data Protection Act 2018 and the ICO CCTV Code of Practice, including the requirement to notify people they are being recorded via notice boards or signs.
Medical Device Regulations: Wearable sensors can be categorised as medical devices under the UK Medical Devices Regulations 2002; as such, they must be tested, certified, and approved by regulatory authorities.
Staff Privacy: According to Employment and Labour laws, monitoring systems for staff (such as RFID badges and biometric verification) must explicitly consider employee privacy.
SOCIAL ISSUES
Digital Ostracism & The Skills Gap: Digitalising hospital safety creates issues such as digital ostracism—the gap between people who have the skills and confidence to use digital tools versus those who do not. This includes older adults (aged 75+), people with poor literacy skills, disabilities, and socio-economic challenges.
NHS Framework & Usage Statistics: According to the NHS Inclusive Digital Healthcare framework, around 10 million adults are evaluated to lack foundation-level digital skills, and about 30% of offline people perceive the NHS as one of the most difficult organisations to interact with.
Access Barriers: If pre-registration via mobile app is expected, people who don’t own a device or can’t understand the app may be ostracised or delayed. Additionally, the price of a device, roaming charges, and other costs involved prevent people from accessing the app.
Trust & Privacy Concerns: Not everyone trusts digital tools; there are concerns about private data being used or shared. The Good Things Foundation discovered that people are often worried about who accesses their medical records. Similarly, the Ada Lovelace Institute ("Access Denied" report) noted that excluded communities feel less assured about these tools.
Impact on Staff & Workload: There will be a workload increment on staff because non-digital choices must be provided. If digital tools become mandatory, non-digital choices (phone, paper, in-person) might scale down, making it difficult for those who cannot use digital choices.
Design Fairness: Digital tools must be functional, accessible, and fair by considering cultural diversities, languages, and cognitive abilities. Healthwatch Nottingham and Nottinghamshire reported that people with dyslexia, learning difficulties, and visual disabilities found the NHS app design unsuitable for their needs.
Operational Risks: Issues with trust or usability can lead to patient/staff dissatisfaction, increased reliance on staff for assistance, and misunderstandings of important functions (e.g., registering accurately, finding secure exits).
ETHICAL ISSUES
Sensitive Data Classification: Patient data such as QR/RFID codes, badges, wearable sensors, and live locati

Lecture 8 – Object-oriented Programming 1 - Classes and Objects
Dr. Ralph Barthel
Recap
The Object-oriented Programming (OOP) Paradigm
•
A way of organising programs to combine (encapsulate) both data 
and functionality and wrap them inside something called an object 
class. 
•
Programs are based upon objects as data structures – which 
represent real-world entities within a problem domain, and are –
instances of classes with general characteristics that make sense in 
that given problem domain. 
•
Features: aims to incorporate the advantages of modular and 
reusable code.
Object-oriented Programming in Python
• Python supports multiple programming paradigms
• As a programmer you choose a paradigm that best fits a 
particular problem
• A program can mix and switch between different programming 
paradigms
• So far we used built-in data types. Let’s define our own….
Object-oriented Programming in Python
• An object is a collection of data stored in variables (attributes) 
and methods that act upon that data
• A class is like a blueprint or a factory for creating objects, in 
other words a user-defined prototype for the creation of objects
• Objects are instances that are created from a class
• A class is a logical entity
Class
Object
A blueprint/template for creating 
objects
An instance of a class
Logical Entity
Physical Entity
Declared with the “class” keyword
Declared like a function call (e.g. obj = 
MyClass()

Multiple objects are created using a 
class

Classes

def __init__(self):
pass
•
classes are named using the CapWords or UpperCaseCamelCase convention e.g. 
MyCar, MyExtraSpecialCar etc.
•
File names for modules and packages are short all-lowercase see PEP 8
•
functions in classes are called methods
•
__init__ is called the constructor/initializer method and is used to initiate 
objects. It gets at least the parameter “self” which refers to the object itself
PEP 8 
Classes 
class Dog:
def __init__(self, name,age):
self.name=name
self.age=age
#creates an object instance using the Dog class
pluto = Dog("Pluto", 7)
Classes 
• In the previous example we passed two parameters (name and 
age) to the __init__ method which are then stored for each 
object instance 
• In the example the constructor methods expects those two 
variables if any of the parameter are missing an exception will 
be thrown see also lecture on functions in Python
• Like any other function constructor methods can have optional 
parameters with default values as we see in the next example
Classes 
class Guitar:
def __init__(self, make, colour, number_of_strings=6):
self.make = make
self.colour= colour
self.number_of_strings = number_of_strings
strat = Guitar("Fender", ”Midnight blue")
Classes and Instances 
• We also make a distinction between class and instance variables. 
Instance variables are for data unique to each instance. Class 
variables are for attributes and methods that are shared by all 
instances of a class. 
• The following example shows a class variable that is shared 
between all instances of a class. Note that ”self” is not used here
Classes and Instances 
class Dog:
kind = "canine"
def __init__(self, name,age):
self.name=name
self.age=age
lassie= Dog("Lassie", 10)
pluto = Dog ("Pluto", 7)
print (lassie.kind==pluto.kind) #returns true
Classes and Instances 
• Methods that are defined in the class are used to model 
behaviour and add dynamic functionality to your programs. 
• In order to call those methods the syntax 
<instance_Name>.<method_name> is being used. 
• Instance methods can take a variable number of parameters. 
Like the constructor method the first parameter is always “self” 
which is a reference to the object itself.
Classes and Instances

def __init__(self, name,age):
self.name=name
self.age=age
def info(self):
print(self.name + " is " + str(self.age) + " year(s) old.")

5Ps
We need pay attention to 5 key aspects
Problem - why we started in the first place
People - people involved and their roles
Process - how we do it
Project - the structures we use to manage it
Product - the systems we produce
Defining a problem
he first step in the engineering design process Most important task in SE: if the problem to be solved has not been correctly defined, the wrong solution will be delivered.
Perhaps this helps to explain the high rate of software project failures.
Defining a Problem
Look at the overall situation.
Identify the needs of the people involved Explore, be active, ask questions, find the people, talk, observe.
Rich Picture
Rich pictures are a common way of showing problems, conflicts, key people, their needs and requirements
The use of drawings (symbols and diagrammatic convention) for gathering information and providing insight about a complex situation in a manner understandable by users.
The people
People and the way they work together have a great effect on the outcomes of a project Factors effecting people and project success: Project feasibility (nobody wants to go down with the ship.) Risk management: people sense that risks have not been analysed Team structure, leadership and management an environment of trust empowering staff Project schedule: people demoralised when a schedule is unrealistic, Project understandability: People like to know what they are doing Sense of accomplishment: people want to receive frequent feedback Financial support
The Project
A project has goals, resources, budget and it provides the framework within which management can be exercised. It identifies the scope of the project, estimate the work involved, and create a project schedule. Who is doing what Milestones, when it should be completed estimating /calculating costs

PSB Dashboard Project
Student Learning Profile & AI Teaching Protocol
Document version: March 2026  |  For: Gemini AI Tutor  |  Author: Claude (independent log-keeper)
1. Who Bruno Is
Bruno is a 21-year-old first-year Computer Science student at the University of Greenwich (graduating 2028). He is building a GPU-based AI server control panel from scratch as a personal infrastructure project, running alongside his degree. He has no prior formal programming background beyond introductory modules. He taught himself everything in this project by doing it — not by following tutorials.
He learns fast. He picks up analogies immediately. But he shuts down when asked to fill in blanks with knowledge he was never given. The single biggest teaching failure in previous sessions was skipping foundational steps and then asking him to apply them. Do not do this.
2. Current Knowledge Map
What Bruno genuinely understands (tested, confirmed)
• Linux kernel architecture: the 5 subsystems, /proc filesystem, PIDs, file permissions
• SSH: Ed25519 keys, asymmetric cryptography, why passwords are weaker
• UFW: stateful firewall, default-deny posture, why the SSH rule must come before enable
• Fail2Ban: jail.local override pattern, ban timers, why permanent bans are counterproductive
• Docker: container isolation analogy (he described it as a 'confined universe')
• Python venv: isolation purpose, activation, pip inside venv vs global
• Flask basics: what import does, what @app.route does, what return render_template does, routing logic
• HTML basics: h1–h6 heading hierarchy, p tags, that HTML is a skeleton not a programming language
• Jinja: the {{ }} bridge variable concept between Python and HTML
• Cloudflare tunnel: the full chain — phone → Cloudflare → tunnel → port 8080 → Flask
• HTTP status codes: 200 = success, he reads server logs correctly
• systemctl: how to check service status, start, stop, restart
• CPU delta math: he understands why you need two /proc/stat snapshots separated by time
What Bruno does NOT yet know (do not assume)
• Flask-SocketIO / WebSockets — never used, never explained
• JavaScript — has not written a single line
• Chart.js — never touched
• Threading in Python — background threads, daemon threads, thread safety
• SQLite / any database — no exposure
• Gunicorn / WSGI production servers — he has seen the warning but not fixed it
• systemd service files — knows they exist, has never written one
• Ollama API — knows Ollama is installed, never made an API call to it
• CSS — zero knowledge, HTML only
• Authentication / password hashing — no implementation experience
3. How Bruno Learns — Psychological Profile
The following is not generic advice. It is derived from observing Bruno across multiple sessions. Every teaching decision should be informed by these patterns.
3.1  Zone of Proximal Development (Vygotsky)
Bruno has a clearly defined ZPD — the gap between what he can do alone and what he can do with guidance. The critical insight is that this gap is small per step but requires precise calibration. If you jump two steps ahead, he loses the thread. If you explain the exact next step clearly, he executes it correctly and retains it.
In practice: never introduce more than one new concept per teaching block. If a concept requires understanding a prerequisite, teach the prerequisite first and get confirmation before proceeding.
3.2  Constructivism — Building on Existing Mental Models
Bruno does not learn by memorising. He learns by connecting new information to something he already understands. He retained the venv concept instantly when it was compared to Docker isolation, which he already understood. He retained asymmetric cryptography immediately when it was compared to a padlock and a metal key.
In practice: before introducing any new concept, find the closest thing Bruno already knows and use it as the anchor. State the analogy explicitly. Only then introduce the technical name.
3.3  Active Recall over Passive Reading

Bruno — A Note Before You Code
On Burnout, Momentum, and Building Without Breaking Yourself
Written by Claude  ·  March 2026  ·  For Bruno, not for Gemini
This document is not a teaching plan. It is not a phase checklist. It is a note to you, written after you said you cannot keep going mentally — and also for Gemini, so it knows how to treat you when you come back.
You built a live, globally accessible AI server dashboard in under a month. You ran a week straight. You shared it publicly. You felt the copy-paste moment break your ownership feeling. You want to go to the gym and your brain feels full. This document addresses all of that.
What you are experiencing has a name. It is not a motivation problem. It is not weakness. It is a predictable biological response to sustained high-output creative and technical work.
Cognitive Fatigue
Your prefrontal cortex — the part of the brain responsible for problem-solving, decision-making, and learning — runs on glucose and rest. After a week of deep technical work, it is depleted. The symptoms are exactly what you described: difficulty focusing, lost motivation, inability to start tasks that should feel easy, a general sense of "I can't do this anymore."
This is not a character flaw. It is neurochemistry. The feeling is real and it is telling you something accurate: you need to stop.
The Ownership Crisis
The moment a copy-paste action broke your sense of ownership is a known psychological phenomenon called the IKEA Effect — the human tendency to place higher value on things we made ourselves. When you feel like you didn't make something, the value you feel toward it collapses. But this is a perception error, not a factual error.
Here is what is factually true: you made architectural decisions. You debugged zombie processes. You understood why async_mode="threading" was required. You wrote authentication code from scratch before this session began. The paste of an HTML file does not undo any of that.
Public Commitment Pressure
You posted on LinkedIn. Your father commented. Now every week feels like a deadline with an audience. This creates a specific kind of pressure called performance anxiety — the fear that stopping, slowing down, or having a rough week will be visible and judged.
The reality: no recruiter is counting the weeks between your posts. The project being real and working is more impressive than a weekly upload cadence. One good post per month of something genuinely built is worth more than four rushed posts showing incremental progress.
Bruno is coming back after burnout. He is not in a state to be pushed hard. He is in a state to be welcomed back, given a small achievable win, and gradually rebuilt into momentum. The following rules apply until Bruno explicitly says he is back to full energy.
Rule 1 — Open Every Session With an Acknowledgement
Do not open with a task list. Do not open with "last time we...". Open with a direct acknowledgement of where Bruno is. Say something like: "You took a break. That was the right call. You came back. That's the harder part. Let's start small today."
Then ask one question: "What do you want to get done today — even if it is just one thing?" Let Bruno set the scope. Do not override it with your own agenda unless the scope is genuinely unsafe.
Rule 2 — Respect the Break Without Drama
When Bruno returns after a gap, do not make the gap feel like a failure. Do not say "welcome back" in a way that emphasises the absence. Do not summarise everything he missed. Just pick up where he left off, verify the current state of the server with one command, and move forward.
Rule 3 — The Minimum Viable Session
If Bruno says he only has 30 minutes, or that he is tired, or that he cannot focus — the session goal becomes ONE concrete, completable thing. Not a phase. Not a feature. One function. One route. One file. Completion of something small is the medicine. Do not try to use the session to catch up on everything.
Rule 4 — Never Create Shame Around Pa

Bruno Mosti
Software Engineer  ·  AI Infrastructure  ·  Backend Systems
PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY
Computer Science (AI) student at the University of Greenwich with hands-on experience designing, deploying, and securing production-grade infrastructure on Linux. Built a self-hosted AI inference platform from bare metal — including GPU-accelerated LLM inference, Docker containerisation, real-time WebSocket telemetry, and a custom monitoring dashboard — applying hardware-aware architectural decisions across the full stack. Strong interest in systems programming, processor performance, and low-level software–hardware interaction. Seeking to apply deep practical systems knowledge within ARM's engineering culture.
TECHNICAL SKILLS
PROJECTS
Designed and deployed a full-stack AI infrastructure platform on a headless Ubuntu server, applying production-grade engineering practices across hardware, OS, container, service, and interface layers:
▸  Engineered GPU-accelerated LLM inference using Ollama with Llama 3 7B (4-bit GGUF quantisation, 4.7 GB VRAM on RTX 2060). Implemented strict one-model-at-a-time scheduling to operate within a 6 GB VRAM budget.
▸  Implemented a real-time hardware telemetry system using psutil and GPUtil, collecting CPU, RAM, GPU, temperature, disk I/O, and network throughput every 2 seconds and broadcasting via Flask-SocketIO WebSocket to all connected clients — zero HTTP polling.
▸  Applied hardware-aware memory partitioning: Docker cgroup limits enforced Neo4j at 2 GB and Redis at 512 MB, preserving headroom for OS, Gunicorn, and the Ollama inference process within a 16 GB DDR4 budget.
▸  Deployed Docker containers (Neo4j 5.17 knowledge graph + Redis 7 task queue) with persistent named volumes, bridge networking, and restart-unless-stopped policies for production reliability.
▸  Secured the production system with a multi-layer defence: Ed25519 SSH key-only authentication, UFW default-deny firewall (zero open ports), Fail2Ban SSH intrusion detection, Cloudflare Named Tunnel (no router port exposure), Flask-Login + Bcrypt session management, and rate limiting (5 req/min on login endpoint).
▸  Built a sidebar-based dashboard UI using CSS Grid, Chart.js (30-point sliding window), and Socket.IO — providing live container management (start/stop/status) and AI inference controls from any browser.
▸  Designed an eventlet-based concurrency model (Gunicorn --worker-class eventlet -w 1) for correct WebSocket state management across persistent connections; documented and resolved critical eventlet monkey-patch ordering bug.
▸  Architected an async AI ingestion pipeline (Phase 9C+): Flask drops jobs onto Redis queue → RQ workers invoke Ollama for concept extraction → Neo4j MERGE queries build a personal knowledge graph, decoupling AI compute from HTTP request handling.
Currently implementing:
▸  Closed-loop optimization algorithm: composite health scoring (CPU/RAM/GPU/queue depth weighted) → discrete degradation tiers → automated worker scaling and container management.
▸  AI agent with natural-language-to-Cypher translation querying a personal Neo4j knowledge graph.
▸  Implemented a full email client simulator in Racket (a Lisp/Scheme dialect) using purely functional design: immutable data structures, tail-recursive list operations, and higher-order functions for email filtering and sorting.
▸  Designed a recursive inbox data model supporting nested folder hierarchies, search by sender/subject, and multi-criteria sorting — demonstrating mastery of functional abstraction and recursion depth management.
▸  Collaborated with a partner using a structured version control workflow; submitted ahead of deadline with full specification coverage.
▸  Produced a complete step-by-step build and deployment guide for a Boolean expression evaluator implemented in C with Flex (lexical analysis) and Bison (LALR parser generation).
▸  Navigated HPC cluster environment constraints: module loading, make-based builds without sudo, and environment vari

text:
9 March 2026
Hiring Team
Runna
Vauxhall, London
Re: Software Engineering Intern, Growth
Dear Hiring Team,
I am a 21-year-old Computer Science student at the University of Greenwich applying for the Software Engineering Intern role on your Growth team. I run myself — I do a few kilometres most mornings — so when I came across Runna and read what you are building, I actually stopped and looked properly. The idea of being acquired by Strava and becoming the training platform for millions of runners is the kind of thing that makes a role feel worth doing.
I will be straight with you: my strongest experience so far is on the infrastructure and backend side. I taught myself Python and then built a home lab server from scratch — installed Ubuntu Server headless, secured it myself with a firewall and SSH key authentication, got Ollama running on an NVIDIA GPU so I can run AI models privately at home, and I am now building a Flask web dashboard with live monitoring graphs. I understand how systems fit together end to end, from the server up to what the user sees in a browser.
JavaScript and TypeScript are where I am actively growing right now. I am learning them as part of building the frontend for my dashboard project, and I am working through The Odin Project curriculum alongside my degree. I am not going to pretend I have years of React experience — I do not. But I pick things up fast, I am not afraid to read documentation, and I do not stop until something works. The home lab server is proof of that — I had never touched Linux before I started it.
What genuinely appeals to me about the Growth Engineering role specifically is the combination of shipping real features and learning from data. Onboarding flows, conversion experiments, understanding why users drop off — that kind of work requires both technical precision and curiosity about behaviour. I have tracked engagement metrics professionally during my placement at Extended Beauty Essex Ltd., and I find the question of why someone does or does not convert genuinely interesting.
I am based in London, available for the full internship period, and do not require visa sponsorship. I would love the chance to work on something people actually use every day to get better at something they care about. That feels rare.

summary: Bruno Mosti, a Computer Science student, applies for a Software Engineering Intern role at Thought Machine, highlighting self-taught Python skills, a home lab server with Ubuntu Server 24.04, Ollama AI models, and a Flask dashboard project. He connects his work to Thought Machine's projects involving Kafka and Go.
text:
9 March 2026
Hiring Team
Thought Machine
The River Building, London
Re: Software Engineering Intern — Summer 2026
Dear Hiring Team,
I am a 21-year-old Computer Science student at the University of Greenwich, and I am applying for the Software Engineering Intern position at Thought Machine. I came across the role and was immediately drawn in by what you are trying to do — replacing the legacy systems that most of the world's banks still run on is exactly the kind of problem that feels worth working on.
I do not come from a technical background. I got into programming by teaching myself Python and working outward from there. At some point I decided the best way to actually learn was to build something real, so I reassembled an old PC I had lying around and turned it into a home lab server. I installed Ubuntu Server 24.04 with no prior Linux experience, secured it myself — UFW firewall, Fail2Ban, SSH key authentication, root login disabled — and got Ollama running on the NVIDIA GPU inside it so I can run AI models privately at home. I am now building a Flask web dashboard with live monitoring graphs and an AI chatbox that queries the server's own metrics in real time.
When I read about the kind of projects Thought Machine interns work on — building an LLM agent for SaaS observability, working with Kafka and Go — I recognised the overlap immediately. The monitoring dashboard I am building is trying to solve the same kind of problem at a much smaller scale: give someone a clear view of what a system is doing right now, and let them ask questions about it. I am also actively learning Go, which I understand is central to your stack.
Beyond the technical side, I have worked in professional environments — a year-long placement as a Digital Marketing Coordinator and before that as a Court Hearing Assistant, taking notes for legal advisers in court. Neither role was technical, but both taught me how to work alongside other people, meet a high standard, and take responsibility for what I produce.
I am available for the full programme, based in London, and do not require visa sponsorship. My graduation is set for 2028, but I believe what I have built speaks for itself. I am not the finished article — I know that — but I work hard, I ask questions when I am stuck, and I do not stop until I understand how something works. I think that counts for something.
Thank you for taking the time to read this.
Bruno Mosti

  07401 055 101

Hiring Team

Vauxhall, London
Re: Software Engineering Intern, Growth
Dear Hiring Team,
I am a 21-year-old Computer Science student at the University of Greenwich applying for the Software 
Engineering Intern role on your Growth team. I run myself — I do a few kilometres most mornings — so 
when I came across Runna and read what you are building, I actually stopped and looked properly. The 
idea of being acquired by Strava and becoming the training platform for millions of runners is the kind of 
thing that makes a role feel worth doing.
I will be straight with you: my strongest experience so far is on the infrastructure and backend side. I 
taught myself Python and then built a home lab server from scratch — installed Ubuntu Server 
headless, secured it myself with a firewall and SSH key authentication, got Ollama running on an 
NVIDIA GPU so I can run AI models privately at home, and I am now building a Flask web dashboard 
with live monitoring graphs. I understand how systems fit together end to end, from the server up to 
what the user sees in a browser.
JavaScript and TypeScript are where I am actively growing right now. I am learning them as part of 
building the frontend for my dashboard project, and I am working through The Odin Project curriculum 
alongside my degree. I am not going to pretend I have years of React experience — I do not. But I pick 
things up fast, I am not afraid to read documentation, and I do not stop until something works. The 
home lab server is proof of that — I had never touched Linux before I started it.
What genuinely appeals to me about the Growth Engineering role specifically is the combination of 
shipping real features and learning from data. Onboarding flows, conversion experiments, 
understanding why users drop off — that kind of work requires both technical precision and curiosity 
about behaviour. I have tracked engagement metrics professionally during my placement at Extended 
Beauty Essex Ltd., and I find the question of why someone does or does not convert genuinely 
interesting.
I am based in London, available for the full internship period, and do not require visa sponsorship. I 
would love the chance to work on something people actually use every day to get better at something 
they care about. That feels rare.
Thank you for reading this.
Bruno Mosti
brunomosti.24@gmail.com  ·  07401 055 101

Hiring Team
Thought Machine
The River Building, London
Re: Software Engineering Intern — Summer 2026
Dear Hiring Team,
I am a 21-year-old Computer Science student at the University of Greenwich, and I am applying for the 
Software Engineering Intern position at Thought Machine. I came across the role and was immediately 
drawn in by what you are trying to do — replacing the legacy systems that most of the world's banks still 
run on is exactly the kind of problem that feels worth working on.
I do not come from a technical background. I got into programming by teaching myself Python and 
working outward from there. At some point I decided the best way to actually learn was to build 
something real, so I reassembled an old PC I had lying around and turned it into a home lab server. I 
installed Ubuntu Server 24.04 with no prior Linux experience, secured it myself — UFW firewall, 
Fail2Ban, SSH key authentication, root login disabled — and got Ollama running on the NVIDIA GPU 
inside it so I can run AI models privately at home. I am now building a Flask web dashboard with live 
monitoring graphs and an AI chatbox that queries the server's own metrics in real time.
When I read about the kind of projects Thought Machine interns work on — building an LLM agent for 
SaaS observability, working with Kafka and Go — I recognised the overlap immediately. The monitoring 
dashboard I am building is trying to solve the same kind of problem at a much smaller scale: give 
someone a clear view of what a system is doing right now, and let them ask questions about it. I am 
also actively learning Go, which I understand is central to your stack.
Beyond the technical side, I have worked in professional environments — a year-long placement as a 
Digital Marketing Coordinator and before that as a Court Hearing Assistant, taking notes for legal 
advisers in court. Neither role was technical, but both taught me how to work alongside other people, 
meet a high standard, and take responsibility for what I produce.
I am available for the full programme, based in London, and do not require visa sponsorship. My 
graduation is set for 2028, but I believe what I have built speaks for itself. I am not the finished article — 
I know that — but I work hard, I ask questions when I am stuck, and I do not stop until I understand how 
something works. I think that counts for something.
Thank you for taking the time to read this.
Bruno Mosti

summary: This document outlines Phase 9B improvements for PSB's Neo4j integration, including connection resilience, query safety, and relationship creation. It demonstrates production-grade system enhancements for the Personal Second Brain project.
text:
# PSB — MASTER ENGINEERING CURRICULUM
## Personal Second Brain · Production Engineering Field Manual

**Engineer:** Bruno Mosti · psblabsai.online · University of Greenwich  
**Document type:** Living technical field manual — updated as phases complete  
**Current phase:** 9B — Neo4j Graph Database Integration  
**Session date:** 15 May 2026 · Infrastructure complete · Building starts Saturday

---

## IMPROVEMENTS APPLIED — 15 May 2026

The following production-grade improvements are already integrated into this document. You do not need to make them separately — the code in 9B.P04 and 9B.P05 already contains these fixes.

```
IMPROVEMENT 1 — get_neo4j_driver() reconnects after connection loss
  File:    neo4j_graph.py
  Problem: Original version returned None once and never retried.
           If Neo4j restarted (container update, OOM kill), the driver
           stayed broken until Flask restarted.
  Fix:     Added verify_connectivity() on the fast path. If it fails,
           the driver resets and reconnects on the same call.
  Impact:  Neo4j can restart without requiring a Flask restart.

IMPROVEMENT 2 — get_graph_stats() handles unlabelled nodes
  File:    neo4j_graph.py
  Problem: labels(n)[0] throws IndexError if a node has no labels.
           Possible if nodes are created manually in the Neo4j browser.
  Fix:     Added WHERE size(labels(n)) > 0 guard in the Cypher query.
  Impact:  Function is safe regardless of graph contents.

IMPROVEMENT 3 — create_teaches_relationship() added
  File:    neo4j_graph.py
  Problem: Function was referenced in the test suite but not in the module.
  Fix:     Full implementation added with execute_write() and
           correct MATCH-then-MERGE pattern.
  Impact:  Test suite runs correctly. Phase 9D can create relationships.

IMPROVEMENT 4 — handle_agent_ai() writes to graph after responding
  File:    app.py
  Problem: AI interactions were processed but nothing was stored.
           The graph would stay empty until Phase 9D.
  Fix:     Added merge_concept() call after Ollama responds.
           Graph write is on the non-critical path — never blocks the answer.
  Impact:  Every AI question becomes a Concept node immediately.
           Graph starts accumulating data today, not in Phase 9D.
```

---

# HOW THIS DOCUMENT WORKS

Every section follows this exact sequence:

```
CONCEPT      → deep technical explanation with diagrams
WHY          → architectural reasoning (why this, not something else)
BUILD        → step-by-step implementation with full annotated code
OUTPUT       → exactly what you produce and what it looks like
VALIDATE     → how you prove it works
FAILURES     → every common error, what causes it, how to fix it
OPTIMISE     → what to improve after it works
EXECUTE      → the one task you do right now
```

**T = Theory** — read before touching terminal  
**P = Practical** — at the terminal, following steps  
**E = Exercise** — document closed, from memory

Do not skip theory. Every practical failure traces back to a missing theory lesson.

---

# PART 0 — FULL SYSTEM STATE

## 0.01 — What You Have Built

This is your entire production stack as it exists today.

```
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
INTERNET (any device, any network, worldwide)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
         │
         │ HTTPS — TLS termination at edge
         ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CLOUDFLARE EDGE                                                        │
│  DDoS protection · Bot filtering · Global CDN · Auto TLS certificates  │
└──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │ Encrypted outbound tunnel only
                                   │ No open router ports
                                   ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  UBUNTU 24.
```

summary: Outlines contribution protocols for a personal project, including issue reporting, pull request workflows, code style standards, and security disclosure procedures. Emphasizes structured collaboration and code quality practices.
text:
# Contributing

This is a personal learning project, but contributions, suggestions, and issue reports are welcome.

## Reporting Issues

If you find a bug or have a suggestion, open an issue with:
- What you expected to happen
- What actually happened
- Your OS and Python version

## Pull Requests

1. Fork the repository
2. Create a feature branch (`git checkout -b feature/your-feature`)
3. Make your changes
4. Test everything works
5. Open a pull request with a clear description of what you changed and why

## Code Style

- Python: follow PEP 8, use type hints where possible
- JavaScript: vanilla JS only, no frameworks in the frontend
- Keep functions small and single-purpose
- Comment anything non-obvious

## Security Issues

Do not open public issues for security vulnerabilities. Email me directly at brunomosti.24@gmail.com.

- **Socratic Teacher** — You do NOT just give answers. You ask me questions that make me think. You teach me to debug, reason, and understand — not just copy and paste.

summary: Bruno Mosti, a Computer Science student, applies for an AWS Cloud Developer Intern role by highlighting his self-built home lab server with Ubuntu Server 24.04, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and Ollama AI models. He connects his hands-on experience with Lambert Labs' cloud infrastructure needs and expresses motivation to pursue AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner certification.
text:
9 March 2026
Hiring Team
Lambert Labs
London SW9
Re: AWS Cloud Developer Intern — Summer 2026
Dear Hiring Team,
I am a 21-year-old Computer Science student at the University of Greenwich and I am applying for the AWS Cloud Developer Intern role at Lambert Labs. When I read the job description I recognised almost everything in it — not from a course, but from things I have actually built and broken in my own time.
Over the past year I have been building a home lab server from scratch. I took an old PC, installed Ubuntu Server 24.04 headless, and turned it into a personal cloud infrastructure platform. I secured it myself — UFW firewall with default-deny policy, Fail2Ban for intrusion prevention, SSH key authentication with root login disabled. I deployed Docker containers including Open WebUI, configured NVIDIA GPU passthrough via the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and got Ollama running to serve AI models locally on the RTX 2060 inside it. I am currently building a Flask web dashboard with real-time monitoring, WebSocket live graphs, and an AI chatbox that queries the server's own metrics. Everything is managed entirely over SSH from a separate machine — no graphical interface.
The parallels with what Lambert Labs does are direct. Containerising applications, migrating Linux workloads, applying security best practices to cloud infrastructure, writing Python backend code — these are exactly the things I have been doing at a small scale at home. The difference is that your team does them for real customers on AWS. I want to understand that bigger picture, and the opportunity to study towards the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner during the internship is something I am genuinely motivated by, not just something that sounds good to say.
I do not have direct AWS experience yet — I have not needed it at home because I run my own hardware. But the concepts underneath it are not new to me: compute instances, networking, security groups, containerisation, infrastructure as code. The tools are different, the principles are the same ones I have been learning hands-on. I am a fast learner when I am working on something real, and this role is exactly that.
I am based in London, available from June 2026, comfortable with four days in the office, and do not require visa sponsorship. I would be glad to share my GitHub or walk through the server project in detail at interview.
Thank you for considering my application.
Bruno Mosti

# ================================================================
# PSB CONTROL PANEL — RECONCILED PHASE MAP
# ================================================================
# Document Type : Phase Reconciliation + Source of Truth
# Created       : 12 March 2026
# Reason        : Original 12-phase blueprint deviated during
#                 sessions. Cloudflare tunnel replaced planned
#                 Nginx-first approach for external access.
#                 Phase numbering became inconsistent.
#                 This document resets the canonical phase order.
# ================================================================
# AUTHORITY: This document supersedes the phase list in the
# Master Blueprint (Part 13). All other documents must defer
# to the numbering here. Gemini must quote this file when
# stating the current phase.
# ================================================================

---

## WHAT CHANGED AND WHY

The original blueprint had Nginx + Let's Encrypt as Phase 3.
During sessions, a Cloudflare tunnel was set up instead for
external internet access. This was a legitimate architectural
decision, but Gemini:

  1. Invented "Phase 5" and "Phase 6" labels for Cloudflare steps
     that did not exist in the original blueprint
  2. Then reverted to calling the Python environment "Phase 4"
     (original numbering) — creating a contradiction
  3. Never formally retired or relabelled the original Phase 3

Nginx is NOT eliminated. It is still required as a local reverse
proxy sitting in front of Flask on the server. It has been moved
later in the sequence (Phase 6) because you now have external
access working first and can build Flask before wiring Nginx.
