summary: README.md describes a self-hosted AI server control panel with real-time monitoring, security features, and phase-based development progress. It details the tech stack and hardware specifications for Bruno's PSB project.
text:
# PSB Control Panel

A secure, browser-accessible server control panel for monitoring, managing, and protecting a GPU-based AI server running Ollama and Docker. Built from scratch on bare metal — no cloud, no subscriptions, full ownership.

> **Status:** 🔧 Active Development — Phase 2 of 12 in progress

---

## What This Is

PSB Control Panel is a self-hosted web dashboard that runs on my home lab server (`psb`). It gives me a real-time view of everything happening on the machine — CPU, RAM, GPU, Docker containers, AI models — accessible securely from anywhere in the world via HTTPS.

The project is built entirely by hand, phase by phase, with the goal of understanding every layer of what gets built rather than just copying code.

---

## Hardware

| Component | Spec |
|-----------|------|
| CPU | Intel Core i5-9400F (6 cores) |
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 (6 GB VRAM) |
| RAM | 16 GB DDR4 (XPG) |
| Storage | Intel Optane NVMe SSD |
| PSU | Antec 750W |
| OS | Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (headless) |

The server runs headless — no monitor, no keyboard. Everything is managed remotely over SSH from a separate Windows PC.

---

## Stack

| Layer | Technology |
|-------|-----------|
| Backend | Python · Flask · Flask-SocketIO · Gunicorn |
| Frontend | HTML · CSS · JavaScript · Chart.js · xterm.js |
| Database | SQLite (WAL mode) |
| Reverse Proxy | Nginx |
| Security | UFW · Fail2Ban · SSH key auth · Let's Encrypt |
| AI Engine | Ollama (Llama 3 / Gemma 2) |
| Containers | Docker · NVIDIA Container Toolkit |
| Real-time | WebSockets |

---

## Features (planned across 12 phases)

- 📊 **Live monitoring** — CPU per core, RAM, disk I/O, network traffic, updating every 2 seconds
- 🎮 **GPU dashboard** — RTX 2060 temperature, VRAM usage, utilisation, power draw
- 🤖 **AI service manager** — Ollama model controls, VRAM tracking, built-in AI chatbox with live server context
- 🐳 **Docker manager** — Container start/stop/restart, live log streaming
- 🖥️ **Web terminal** — Full PTY terminal in the browser, audit-logged, idle timeout
- 🚨 **Alert engine** — Threshold rules, anomaly detection, Telegram notifications
- 🔒 **Security dashboard** — Fail2Ban events, active SSH sessions, UFW status
- 📈 **Historical charts** — 30-day metric history stored in SQLite
- 🌐 **Remote access** — HTTPS with Let's Encrypt, accessible from anywhere

---

## Project Structure

```
psb-control-panel/
├── backend/
│   ├── app/
│   │   ├── api/          # REST endpoints (system, gpu, docker, ollama, security...)
│   │   ├── auth/         # Login, logout, session management
│   │   ├── services/     # Background collectors, alert engine, GPU service
│   │   ├── sockets/      # WebSocket handlers for real-time data

AI Server Control Panel README.md describes a self-hosted AI server control panel with real-time monitoring, security features, and phase-based development progress. It details the tech stack and hardware specifications for Bruno's PSB project. # PSB Control Panel

A secure, browser-accessible server control panel for monitoring, managing, and protecting a GPU-based AI server running Ollama and Docker. Built from scratch on bare metal — no cloud, no subscriptions, full ownership.

> **Status:** 🔧 Active Development — Phase 2 of 12 in progress

---

## What This Is

PSB Control Panel is a self-hosted web dashboard that runs on my home lab server (`psb`). It gives me a real-time view of everything happening on the machine — CPU, RAM, GPU, Docker containers, AI models — accessible securely from anywhere in the world via HTTPS.

The project is built entirely by hand, phase by phase, with the goal of understanding every layer of what gets built rather than just copying code.

---

## Hardware

| Component | Spec |
|-----------|------|
| CPU | Intel Core i5-9400F (6 cores) |
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 (6 GB VRAM) |
| RAM | 16 GB DDR4 (XPG) |
| Storage | Intel Optane NVMe SSD |
| PSU | Antec 750W |
| OS | Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (headless) |

The server runs headless — no monitor, no keyboard. Everything is managed remotely over SSH from a separate Windows PC.

---

## Stack

| Layer | Technology |
|-------|-----------|
| Backend | Python · Flask · Flask-SocketIO · Gunicorn |
| Frontend | HTML · CSS · JavaScript · Chart.js · xterm.js |
| Database | SQLite (WAL mode) |
| Reverse Proxy | Nginx |
| Security | UFW · Fail2Ban · SSH key auth · Let's Encrypt |
| AI Engine | Ollama (Llama 3 / Gemma 2) |
| Containers | Docker · NVIDIA Container Toolkit |
| Real-time | WebSockets |

---

## Features (planned across 12 phases)

- 📊 **Live monitoring** — CPU per core, RAM, disk I/O, network traffic, updating every 2 seconds
- 🎮 **GPU dashboard** — RTX 2060 temperature, VRAM usage, utilisation, power draw
- 🤖 **AI service manager** — Ollama model controls, VRAM tracking, built-in AI chatbox with live server context
- 🐳 **Docker manager** — Container start/stop/restart, live log streaming
- 🖥️ **Web terminal** — Full PTY terminal in the browser, audit-logged, idle timeout
- 🚨 **Alert engine** — Threshold rules, anomaly detection, Telegram notifications
- 🔒 **Security dashboard** — Fail2Ban events, active SSH sessions, UFW status
- 📈 **Historical charts** — 30-day metric history stored in SQLite
- 🌐 **Remote access** — HTTPS with Let's Encrypt, accessible from anywhere

text:
# Security Policy

## Supported Versions

This project is under active development. Only the latest version on `main` is supported.

## Reporting a Vulnerability

If you discover a security vulnerability, please do **not** open a public GitHub issue.

Email: brunomosti.24@gmail.com

Include:
- Description of the vulnerability
- Steps to reproduce
- Potential impact

I will respond within 72 hours and work to fix confirmed issues promptly.

## Security Design Decisions

This project makes the following security choices by design:

- **SSH only via key authentication** — password authentication is disabled
- **Firewall default-deny** — only ports 22 and 443 are open
- **No raw tokens stored** — API tokens are bcrypt-hashed before storage
- **Audit log is append-only** — no update or delete operations are permitted on audit records
- **Rate limiting on all auth endpoints** — prevents brute force attacks on the dashboard login
- **HTTPS enforced** — HTTP requests are redirected to HTTPS at the Nginx layer
- **Session expiry** — dashboard sessions expire after inactivity
- **Web terminal idle timeout** — terminal sessions disconnect after 5 minutes idle

ACTIVE BLOCKERS:

⚠️ CRITICAL INCIDENT — Session 2 — SEQUENCING ERROR BY GEMINI
  Gemini taught "sudo systemctl restart ssh" BEFORE teaching "sudo sshd -t".
  Bruno had already executed the restart before the safety test was introduced.
  He was lucky — his config had no typos so no lockout occurred.
  This is documented as a real error. The correct order is ALWAYS:
    1. Edit file
    2. sudo sshd -t  (test — no output = safe)
    3. sudo systemctl restart ssh  (only after test passes)

  GEMINI INSTRUCTION FOR ALL FUTURE SSH CONFIG CHANGES:
  You MUST follow this order without exception.
  Never give the restart command before the test command.
  This is non-negotiable. It was documented in PSB_RISK_AND_ERROR_MANAGEMENT.md
  as an IRREVERSIBLE ACTION requiring confirmation before execution.

⚠️ CRITICAL INCIDENT — Session 3 — MISSING "ufw allow ssh" BY GEMINI
  Gemini's UFW command block in Session 2 was missing "sudo ufw allow ssh".
  The block given was: default deny incoming → default allow outgoing → ufw enable.
  "ufw allow ssh" was completely absent from the instructions.
  Bruno followed the instructions exactly and ran ufw enable without the SSH rule.
  Bruno remained connected only because UFW does not kill existing sessions.
  Had he closed his terminal before this was caught, he would have been
  permanently locked out over the network. Fixed at start of Session 3:
    sudo ufw allow ssh → Rule added / Rule added (v6) → confirmed in ufw status.
  This is Bruno's fault: ZERO. Gemini's fault: COMPLETE.

RESOLVED:
  [Session 1] UFW not yet configured → RESOLVED Session 2 (UFW active)
  [Session 3] Missing ufw allow ssh → RESOLVED Session 3 (rule confirmed active)

# PSB — Project Roadmap
**Personal Second Brain · psblabsai.online**
Bruno Mosti · BSc Computer Science AI · University of Greenwich

---

## Current State — Phase 9E (Complete with v2 UI)

### What is deployed and working
- Flask + Flask-SocketIO dashboard, Gunicorn/eventlet, systemd service
- Cloudflare Zero Trust tunnel, UFW default-deny, Fail2Ban, Ed25519 SSH-only auth
- Docker: Neo4j (bolt://localhost:7687) + Redis (localhost:6379), 127.0.0.1 port binding only
- Ollama: qwen3:8b, GPU-accelerated (RTX 2060 6GB VRAM)
- RQ task queue: `psb_tasks` worker, non-blocking AI and ingest
- Knowledge Graph: ~794 nodes, 1004+ edges, vis-network 9.1.9 (local static)
- Document ingestion pipeline: PDF/DOCX/MD/TXT/JSON → Ollama parse → Neo4j nodes + routing
- Document routing: filename patterns connect to Module/Phase/Project/Identity hub nodes
- Graph UI: draggable float panel, node search with neighbourhood focus, batch progress bar, minimap, fullscreen, inspector

### Known bugs to fix before moving on
- `initGraph` hardcodes `gvGraphApiUrl('all')` — view buttons (PSB/University/Career/AI) broken
  Fix: change to `gvGraphApiUrl(gvCurrentView)`
- `gvApplyFilters` is a stub — node type toggle filtering removed with left rail
  Fix: either add toggles back to float panel or remove dead calls

---

## Immediate Actions (Do before anything else)

| Priority | Task | Command / Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fix view bug in index.html | `gvGraphApiUrl(gvCurrentView)` |
| 2 | Deploy index.html to server | `cp index.html ~/psb-dashboard/templates/index.html` |
| 3 | Deploy app.py to server | Contains `/api/neo4j/search` and `/api/neo4j/neighborhood` endpoints |
| 4 | Restart service | `sudo systemctl restart psb-dashboard` |
| 5 | Run backfill | `python3 -c "from tasks import backfill_document_routing; print(backfill_document_routing(dry_run=False))"` |
| 6 | Gate checkpoint Phase 9E | Verify 10 items below |
| 7 | Push Phase 9E to GitHub | After checkpoint passes |
| **URGENT** | **LEC AI application** | **talent@lecai.ai — deadline 31 May 2026 — fit score 10/10** |

### Phase 9E Gate Checkpoint (10 items)
1. Graph loads and shows nodes in the canvas
2. View buttons (PSB / University / Career / AI) load different subgraphs
3. Full graph toggle loads all 794 nodes (status bar shows "794 in Neo4j")
4. Search finds a node by name (type "Flask" — should return results)
5. Clicking a search result jumps to the node or loads neighbourhood
6. Node inspector shows name, type, summary, key insight on click
7. Minimap renders and click-to-pan works
8. Fullscreen opens, ESC closes
9. Drop a file in the bottom bar — ingestion pipeline completes (green ✓)
10. Status bar shows correct count after ingest: "N nodes · M in Neo4j"

---

## Phase 10 — Ensemble Chat Box

**What it is:** Fan out a question to multiple AI models simultaneously, display their individual responses, then have Ollama synthesise a final answer.

**Architecture:**
```
User question
    ├─ Claude API    (documentation, analysis)
    ├─ Gemini API    (reasoning, research)
    ├─ GPT-4o API    (general)
    └─ Ollama/qwen3  (local, always available)
            ↓
    Ollama reads all 4 responses
    Synthesises: "The consensus is... Claude added... Gemini disagreed on..."
            ↓
    Dashboard displays: 4 panels + synthesis
```

**Why it matters for PSB:**
- Ollama already runs on your GPU — always on, zero cost per call
- Claude and Gemini are your primary tools already — putting them in the dashboard removes context-switching
- Synthesis panel is novel portfolio material: "my system queries 4 AIs and reconciles them"

**Implementation approach:**
- New SocketIO event: `ensemble_ask` with the question
- `tasks.py`: `ask_ensemble(question, system_prompt)` — fires 4 parallel RQ jobs
- Flask polls all 4 job IDs, emits partial results as each arrives
- UI: 2x2 grid of response panels + synthesis panel below
- Synthesis prompt: "You have 4 AI responses to the same question. Identify agreem

# you asked

message time: 2026-05-22 22:41:32

chat gpt is the first time asking you use all my avaible token to make the bst in depth overview about me

---

# chatgpt response

You’re in a very specific phase of life: the point where raw curiosity is turning into technical identity.

Right now you’re not just “learning tech.” You’re building the mental infrastructure of someone who wants to understand systems deeply — AI, cybersecurity, infrastructure, databases, hardware, performance tuning, knowledge architecture, learning systems, even human psychology and communication. Most beginners stay at the surface. You instinctively push downward toward foundations.

That changes everything.

---

# Core Personality Structure

You’re highly pattern-driven.

You don’t naturally learn by memorizing isolated facts. Your brain tries to connect everything into systems:
- graphs
- structures
- relationships
- layers
- flows
- dependencies
- architectures

That’s why you’re attracted to:
- knowledge graphs
- Neo4j/Cypher
- AI infrastructure
- malware detection systems
- optimisation
- CPU tuning
- deep tutorials
- educational frameworks

You don’t want “what.”
You want:
- why it exists
- how it interacts
- what breaks it
- what controls it
- how to scale it
- how to rebuild it from scratch

You repeatedly ask for:
- beginner-friendly explanations
- visual structures
- progressive mastery
- one concept at a time
- deep understanding instead of broad shallow learning

That combination is extremely important.

Because it means your issue is NOT lack of intelligence.

Your issue is:
> cognitive overload from abstraction density.

You understand best when:
1. complexity is decomposed
2. systems are hierarchical
3. learning is sequential
4. concepts are operationalized immediately

You essentially need:
> “infrastructure-style learning.”

Which ironically matches the exact fields you are drawn toward.

---

# Your Learning Psychology

You have an unusually strong “mastery impulse.”

You dislike fake competence.

You can feel when:
- you’re copying without understanding
- information is disconnected
- tutorials skip reasoning
- explanations assume hidden knowledge

That frustrates you heavily.

Which is why you constantly ask for:
- beginner breakdowns
- deeper explanations
- structured progression
- rewritten systems
- educational redesigns

You are trying to build:
> internal mental models.

Not just finish tasks.

That is a massive difference between:
- future engineers
vs
- people who only consume tutorials.

---

# Your Biggest Strength

Your biggest strength is probably this:

> You naturally think in architectures before you think in outputs.

Most beginners ask:
“How do I do X?”

You ask:
“How does the whole system work?”

That’s rare.

Even your prompts reveal this.

You repeatedly attempt to:
- redesign learning systems
- create frameworks
- create reusable structures
- create scalable educational pipelines
- optimise cognitive flow
- integrate visual + operational learning

That is engineering thinking.

Not just coding.

---

# Your Biggest Weakness

Your brain tries to jump too many abstraction layers at once.

Example pattern:
- beginner Cypher
→ knowledge graphs
→ AI systems
→ multi-agent architecture
→ database design
→ infrastructure logic
→ optimisation
→ educational framework engineering

All within very short time spans.

This creates a dangerous illusion:
> “I understand the direction, therefore I understand the layer.”

But understanding direction ≠ mastering foundations.

And you’ve already started realizing this yourself.

That’s why recently you said things like:
- “maybe I need to start extremely with one thing”
- “master create first”
- “one command at a time”

That realization is one of the healthiest developments you’ve had.

Because your natural ambition is FAR ahead of your current operational fluency.

That’s normal.

The danger is not ambition.

La tua idea ha senso. È un sistema molto più stabile rispetto a “mi presti soldi” continuamente, perché trasforma le spese familiari in una divisione chiara e prevedibile.

Il modo corretto per farlo è questo:

1. Calcolare quanto spendete mediamente al mese.
2. Dividere le spese comuni in percentuale al reddito di ogni persona.
3. Stabilire una quota fissa mensile per ciascuno.

Esempio semplice:

- Persona A guadagna £3000
- Persona B guadagna £2000
- Persona C guadagna £1000
- Persona D guadagna £0

Percentuali:
- A = 50%
- B = 33.3%
- C = 16.7%
- D = 0%

Se la famiglia spende £2400 al mese:
- A paga £1200
- B paga ~£800
- C paga ~£400
- D paga £0

Così:
- chi guadagna di più contribuisce di più;
- nessuno sente di “mantenere” gli altri senza criterio;
- spariscono molte discussioni casuali sui soldi.

Le spese da includere dovrebbero essere:
- affitto/mutuo;
- bollette;
- internet;
- spesa alimentare;
- benzina comune;
- abbonamenti condivisi;
- eventuali spese familiari ricorrenti.

Non includete:
- acquisti personali;
- vestiti personali;
- hobby;
- uscite individuali.

La parte importante è fare una media reale:
- prendete gli ultimi 3–6 mesi;
- sommate tutte le spese familiari;
- dividete per il numero di mesi.

Poi potete:
- aprire un conto comune;
oppure
- fare un bonifico fisso ogni mese a chi gestisce le spese.

Vi consiglio anche di creare:
- un fondo emergenze piccolo;
- un limite massimo di spesa senza avvisare gli altri.

Per esempio:
“Se una spesa familiare supera £100 bisogna dirlo prima.”

Questo evita tensioni.

summary: This document explains knowledge graph concepts, graph data modeling, and API integration for PSB. It details how relationships between nodes create a unified knowledge structure and demonstrates the Flask backend's graph endpoints.
text:
# PSB Phase 9E — Full Teaching Lesson

---

## Part 1: The Big Picture

Before any code, you need to understand what you actually built and why it matters.

### What is a knowledge graph?

Forget the technical name. A knowledge graph is just a way of storing information where the **connections between things** are as important as the things themselves.

A normal database stores rows. You have a `documents` table, a `concepts` table, a `modules` table. Each table is independent. If you want to know which concepts appear in which module, you need a JOIN — a manual bridge you write in SQL.

A graph database inverts this. The relationships **are** the data. You do not JOIN tables — you traverse edges. A Document node has a `MENTIONS` edge pointing to a Concept node. A Module node has a `HAS_DOCUMENT` edge pointing to that same Document. The graph *is* the schema.

This is why your graph is powerful: when you ask "what concepts does COMP1765 mention?", you do not query two tables — you follow edges. Two hops:

```
Module → HAS_DOCUMENT → Document → MENTIONS → Concept
```

### What was broken before Phase 9E?

You had the ingestion pipeline working (Phase 9D). Files were being uploaded, parsed by Ollama, and written to Neo4j as Document + Concept + Insight nodes. But those nodes were **floating**. Disconnected islands. The graph looked like a star field with no constellations.

Why? Because nothing connected `COMP1765_lecture.pdf` to the `COMP1765` Module node that already existed in your schema. The ingest worker created the document but never asked: *"where does this document belong in the existing hierarchy?"*

Phase 9E is two things:

1. The **routing fix** — connects documents to the hierarchy
2. The **UI** — lets you see the result visually

---

## Part 2: The Graph Data Model

Your Neo4j graph has two kinds of things: **nodes** and **relationships**.

### Nodes

Nodes are labelled. The label tells you what kind of thing a node is:

```
:Module    { code: "COMP1765", name: "Computer and Communication Systems" }
:Document  { name: "COMP1765_lecture.pdf", summary: "...", topic: "..." }
:Concept   { name: "Boolean Algebra", mention_count: 5 }
:Insight   { name: "Mastering logic gates is essential for..." }
:Phase     { name: "Phase_9D", title: "Document Ingestion Pipeline" }
:Identity  { name: "Stolid", full_name: "Bruno Mosti" }
```

### Relationships

Relationships are directed edges with a type:

```
(m:Module)   -[:HAS_DOCUMENT]-> (d:Document)
(d:Document) -[:MENTIONS]->     (c:Concept)
(d:Document) -[:PRODUCED]->     (i:Insight)
(d:Document) -[:PRODUCED_BY]->  (a:AIAgent)
(s:Identity) -[:AUTHORED]->     (d:Document)
(p:Phase)    -[:HAS_DOCUMENT]-> (d:Document)
```

The arrow direction matters in Cypher but not for traversal — you can always ask "what connects to this node in either direction."

### Why this structure?

The Module node for COMP1765 already existed in your schema from Phase 9B. It just had no documents attached. Every lecture, lab sheet, and coursework you upload should create a `HAS_DOCUMENT` edge from that Module node to the new Document node. When you click COMP1765 in the graph you see all its documents, their concepts, their insights — one click away.

This is the brain structure you wanted. Concepts that appear in both your uni modules AND your PSB engineering sessions become **bridge nodes** — they have edges pointing to them from both hemispheres. `Flask-SocketIO` is mentioned in PSB session logs and will eventually appear in coursework. One Concept node, multiple incoming edges from different Document nodes, connecting different hub nodes. That is the brain shape forming.

---

## Part 3: The API Layer

Your Flask backend has two graph endpoints. Understand these before the frontend — the frontend is just a consumer of what these return.

### GET /api/neo4j/health

Asks Neo4j: "are you alive, and how many nodes of each type do you have?"

```python
stats = get_graph_stats()
# Returns: { "Phase": 19,

## 15 drills. End goal: 8 nodes built from scratch.

---

The pattern you are drilling:

```
CREATE (variable:Label {key: "value", key: value})
RETURN variable
```

Every drill is this pattern. Something changes each time.

---

### Drill 1 of 15 — The bare minimum

No label. No properties. Just a node.

```cypher
CREATE (n)
RETURN n
```

Run it. See the grey dot.
That is a node. The emptiest one possible.

Delete it:
```cypher
MATCH (n) WHERE size(labels(n)) = 0 DETACH DELETE n
```

---

### Drill 2 of 15 — Add a label

Same as Drill 1. One change: add a label.

```cypher
CREATE (n:TestNode)
RETURN n
```

The dot has a colour now. Labels give nodes a category.
Labels always start with a capital letter.

Delete it:
```cypher
MATCH (n:TestNode) DETACH DELETE n
```

---

### Drill 3 of 15 — Add a text property

Same as Drill 2. One change: add one property. Text value.

```cypher
CREATE (n:TestNode {name: "first"})
RETURN n
```

Click the node. See `name: first` in the panel.
Text values always need quotes.

Delete it:
```cypher
MATCH (n:TestNode) DETACH DELETE n
```

---

### Drill 4 of 15 — Add a number property

Same as Drill 3. One change: the value is a number, not text.

```cypher
CREATE (n:TestNode {count: 1})
RETURN n
```

No quotes around 1. Numbers never get quotes.
`"1"` is text. `1` is a number. They are not the same.

Delete it:
```cypher
MATCH (n:TestNode) DETACH DELETE n
```

---

### Drill 5 of 15 — Add a boolean property

Same pattern. One change: the value is true or false.

```cypher
CREATE (n:TestNode {active: true})
RETURN n
```

No quotes. Lowercase. `true` not `True` not `TRUE`.

Delete it:
```cypher
MATCH (n:TestNode) DETACH DELETE n
```

---

### Drill 6 of 15 — All three value types in one node

Same pattern. One change: three properties, one of each type.

```cypher
CREATE (n:TestNode {
    name:   "all types",
    count:  3,
    active: true
})
RETURN n
```

Note the commas after each property except the last one.

Delete it:
```cypher
MATCH (n:TestNode) DETACH DELETE n
```

---

### Drill 7 of 15 — Find the mistake and fix it

Do not run this yet. Read it. Find the error. Fix it. Then run the fixed version.

```cypher
CREATE (n:TestNode {name: "broken" active: true})
RETURN n
```

What is wrong?

```
Missing comma between name and active.
Fixed:
CREATE (n:TestNode {name: "broken", active: true})
RETURN n
```

Run the fixed version. Delete after:
```cypher
MATCH (n:TestNode) DETACH DELETE n
```

---

### Drill 8 of 15 — Find the mistake and fix it

Read. Find. Fix. Then run.

```cypher
CREATE n:TestNode {name: "broken", active: true}
RETURN n
```

What is wrong?

```
Missing parentheses around the node.
Fixed:
CREATE (n:T

Capisco benissimo il tuo "Brooo what????". È del tutto normale essere scioccati da una notizia del genere! Ma fai benissimo ad avere paura e ad ascoltare il tuo istinto. Analizziamo i fatti con razionalità:

Alfa spa, impresa industriale che opera nel settore della meccanica di precisione, offre prodotti in grado

commerciali con la clientela.

il rafforzamento patrimoniale;

summary: This document contains spoiler-free survival mechanics and interface tips for Kenshi, focusing on combat progression, economy management, and early-game strategies. It provides actionable advice for surviving the game's brutal sandbox environment.
text:
# psb_server_interface_chat
Exported on: 29/05/2026, 16:18:52

---

**You:**
teach me no spolier just small tips Kenshi

**Gemini:**
If you thought the early-wipe scramble in Rust was unforgiving, Kenshi is going to test your survival instincts on a completely different level. It is a brilliant, brutal sandbox, but it explains almost nothing to you.

Here are some essential, completely spoiler-free mechanics and mindset shifts to keep you alive in the early game:

### The Golden Rule

* **You are not the main character:** You start at the absolute bottom of the food chain. You are not a hero; you are a target. Even a starving bandit with a rusty stick is a lethal threat to you right now.

### Combat & Progression

* **Getting beaten up is how you level up:** This is the most counter-intuitive mechanic in the game. You gain the "Toughness" stat by taking damage, and "Melee Defense" by getting swung at. As long as you don't actually die, losing fights is a necessary part of getting stronger.
* **Use a designated survivor:** If you have more than one squad member, keep one of them hiding far away from the combat. When your main fighters inevitably get knocked out, wait for the enemies to wander off, then send your hidden character in to bandage everyone before they bleed out.

### Economy & Survival

* **Athletics is your greatest weapon:** Running away is how you survive your first ten hours. Keep your inventory light and avoid heavy armor so your run speed stays high. If you can outrun your enemies, you control your fate.
* **Scavenge from the guards:** Hang out near the gates of your starting town. Bandits will frequently attack the heavily armed town guards. Let the guards do all the dirty work, then swoop in to loot the unconscious bandits and sell their rusty gear for easy starting cash.
* **Never leave town without medical supplies:** Bleeding out slowly in the dirt is the most common end to a playthrough. Always have basic bandages in your inventory.

### Interface Tips

* **Hold the 'ALT' key:** This is a lifesaver. It highlights items lying on the ground, making it incredibly easy to spot dropped weapons or loose loot after a chaotic brawl.
* **Watch your encumbrance:** Carrying too much weight severely tanks your combat stats and your movement speed. Don't be a hoarder when traveling between safe zones.

What kind of starting scenario did you choose, or are you just getting ready to launch the game for the first time?

---

**You:**
im at the waystation

**Gemini:**
Waystations are perfect early-game sanctuaries. They are scattered around the map and act as safe havens when you are out in the middle of nowhere.

Here is how to maximize your time there without spoiling what lies beyond:

* **Rent a Bed:** If you are banged up from a fight, talk to the bartender and rent a bed (usually for around 100-200 Cats). Sleeping in a real bed gives you a massive multiplier to your healing rate. It is the fastest way to recover from critical injuries and get your Toughness back into the fight.
* **The "Bar Brawl" Lure:** Waystations are guarded by tough NPCs (usually Tech Hunters or Mercenaries). If you spot a group of starving bandits roaming nearby, aggro them and sprint straight into the waystation bar. The guards will obliterate them, leaving you free to loot the weapons and sell them right back to the bartender.
* **Hire Expendable Muscle:** You will often find groups of Mercenaries hanging out at the tables. If you have scraped together some Cats, you can hire them as bodyguards for a day or two. They are incredibly useful if you need an escort to a major city or want to safely mine resources nearby without getting jumped.
* **Check for Drifters:** Waystation bars are great places to find your first recruit. Having a second character is a game-changer because they can patch you up when you inevitably get knocked unconscious.
* **Buy Maps:** The travel gear merchants or bartenders often sell maps. Reading them will unlock loc

## What's next — in order

**Immediate (9B) — Connect Python to Neo4j**
The Neo4j container is running but nothing talks to it yet. This is the smallest possible next step:
```bash
pip install neo4j
```
Then add a driver connection in `app.py` and run your first `MERGE` query to create a concept node. One afternoon of work.

**9C — Redis + RQ task queue**
Right now `handle_agent_ai` blocks Flask while Ollama thinks (up to 60s). Add RQ so questions go into a Redis queue, an RQ worker calls Ollama in the background, and the result comes back via WebSocket. The dashboard stays responsive.

**9D — Ingestion pipeline**
POST a transcript/notes to PSB → Ollama extracts concepts/entities → stored as nodes + edges in Neo4j. This is where the system starts building a personal knowledge graph.

**9E — Graph visualisation panel**
Render the Neo4j graph in the dashboard with D3.js or Neovis.js. Same pattern as your Docker panel — a new section, same WebSocket + Flask backend style.

**10 — systemd unit file**
Convert your manual `tmux` Gunicorn start into a proper systemd service so the server auto-restarts on reboot. Mostly config, maybe 20 lines.

**11 — Web terminal panel**
xterm.js on the frontend + paramiko/WebSocket shell on the backend. A browser terminal inside your dashboard.

**12 — Security hardening to 9.5/10**
Cloudflare Zero Trust email OTP gate, Fail2Ban watching Flask login logs, structured security logging.

**13 — Alerts panel**
CPU/RAM thresholds, container-down events, Fail2Ban bans — all pushed to the dashboard in real time via the WebSocket infrastructure you already have.

**14 — AI agent memory (the big one)**
PSB-Agent queries its own Neo4j graph. Natural language → Cypher. Llama 3 answers from *your* personal knowledge base. Everything else has been building toward this.

---

**Where to start right now:** 9B — `pip install neo4j`, one driver connection, one MERGE query. Want me to write the exact code to drop into your `app.py`?

ITALIANO

Il relativismo, la maschera, l'umorismo e il teatro nel teatro
� BIOGRAFIA
Luigi Pirandello
Agrigento, 28 giugno 1867 — Roma, 10 dicembre 1936
Narratore, drammaturgo e poeta italiano, tra i massimi esponenti del Novecento europeo.
Nacque ad Agrigento (allora Girgenti) in una famiglia borghese. Si laureò in Filologia romanza
a Bonn nel 1891 con una tesi sul dialetto agrigentino. Tornato in Italia, iniziò l'insegnamento e
la carriera letteraria. La moglie Antonietta Portulano, che sposò nel 1894, sviluppò una grave
malattia mentale che influenzò profondamente la visione pirandelliana dell'identità e della follia.
Nel 1934 ricevette il Premio Nobel per la Letteratura "per il suo audace e ingegnoso
rinnovamento dell'arte drammatica e scenica". Fondò nel 1925 il Teatro d'Arte di Roma. Morì a
Roma nel 1936.
� TEORIA ESSENZIALE
Il relativismo gnoseologico. Per Pirandello non esiste una verità assoluta: la realtà cambia a seconda del
punto di vista di chi la osserva. Ogni individuo percepisce il mondo in modo soggettivo, e quindi non è
possibile una conoscenza oggettiva e definitiva del reale.
Vita e Forma. La vita è un flusso continuo, caotico e irriducibile. La forma è ciò che la società impone
all'individuo: un ruolo sociale fisso, una maschera che cristallizza la persona in un'identità rigida. L'individuo è
intrappolato nella forma e soffre perché sente che essa non corrisponde alla sua vera essenza vitale.
L'Umorismo (1908). Nel saggio teorico "L'Umorismo", Pirandello distingue il comico dall'umoristico. Il comico
è l'avvertimento del contrario (ridiamo di qualcosa). L'umorismo è il sentimento del contrario: dopo la prima
reazione comica, riflettiamo e scopriamo il dramma nascosto (compatiamo). Es.: la vecchia signora truccata
da giovane.
Il Fu Mattia Pascal (1904). Mattia Pascal scappa dalla propria vita e, creduto morto, tenta di vivere con una
falsa identità (Adriano Meis). Scopre però che senza identità legale non può esistere socialmente. Ritornato
a se stesso, è ormai un "fu": né morto né vivo.
Uno, nessuno e centomila (1926). Vitangelo Moscarda scopre di essere percepito in modo diverso da ogni
persona che lo conosce: è contemporaneamente uno (per sé), nessuno (nella realtà oggettiva) e centomila
(nelle proiezioni altrui). Approda a una liberatoria dissoluzione dell'io.

Il relativismo, la maschera, l'umorismo e il teatro nel teatro
� BIOGRAFIA
Luigi Pirandello
Agrigento, 28 giugno 1867 — Roma, 10 dicembre 1936
Narratore, drammaturgo e poeta italiano, tra i massimi esponenti del Novecento europeo.
Nacque ad Agrigento (allora Girgenti) in una famiglia borghese. Si laureò in Filologia romanza
a Bonn nel 1891 con una tesi sul dialetto agrigentino. Tornato in Italia, iniziò l'insegnamento e
la carriera letteraria. La moglie Antonietta Portulano, che sposò nel 1894, sviluppò una grave
malattia mentale che influenzò profondamente la visione pirandelliana dell'identità e della follia.
Nel 1934 ricevette il Premio Nobel per la Letteratura "per il suo audace e ingegnoso
rinnovamento dell'arte drammatica e scenica". Fondò nel 1925 il Teatro d'Arte di Roma. Morì a
Roma nel 1936.
� TEORIA ESSENZIALE
Il relativismo gnoseologico. Per Pirandello non esiste una verità assoluta: la realtà cambia a seconda del
punto di vista di chi la osserva. Ogni individuo percepisce il mondo in modo soggettivo, e quindi non è
possibile una conoscenza oggettiva e definitiva del reale.
Vita e Forma. La vita è un flusso continuo, caotico e irriducibile. La forma è ciò che la società impone
all'individuo: un ruolo sociale fisso, una maschera che cristallizza la persona in un'identità rigida. L'individuo è
intrappolato nella forma e soffre perché sente che essa non corrisponde alla sua vera essenza vitale.
L'Umorismo (1908). Nel saggio teorico "L'Umorismo", Pirandello distingue il comico dall'umoristico. Il comico
è l'avvertimento del contrario (ridiamo di qualcosa). L'umorismo è il sentimento del contrario: dopo la prima
reazione comica, riflettiamo e scopriamo il dramma nascosto (compatiamo). Es.: la vecchia signora truccata
da giovane.
Il Fu Mattia Pascal (1904). Mattia Pascal scappa dalla propria vita e, creduto morto, tenta di vivere con una
falsa identità (Adriano Meis). Scopre però che senza identità legale non può esistere socialmente. Ritornato
a se stesso, è ormai un "fu": né morto né vivo.
Uno, nessuno e centomila (1926). Vitangelo Moscarda scopre di essere percepito in modo diverso da ogni
persona che lo conosce: è contemporaneamente uno (per sé), nessuno (nella realtà oggettiva) e centomila
(nelle proiezioni altrui). Approda a una liberatoria dissoluzione dell'io.

PSB — Personal Second Brain
Complete Master Learning Document — Full Edition
Bruno Mosti · BSc Computer Science AI · University of Greenwich psblabsai.online · May 2026

This document covers every file, every phase, every decision, and every future direction of PSB. It is written so that after reading it, you can explain any part of the system to an interviewer, a teammate, or yourself at 2am when something breaks. Read it linearly the first time. After that, use the headers to jump to any section you need.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
FILE DIRECTORY — WHAT EVERY FILE DOES
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
Before diving into any details, here is the complete map of every file in the project and why it exists. Understanding what each file is responsible for prevents confusion when you are debugging.

psb-dashboard/
│
├── app.py                    ← The Flask application. All HTTP routes, WebSocket events,
│                               hardware detection, Docker control. The entry point.
│
├── tasks.py                  ← RQ background jobs. Document ingest pipeline, Ollama calls,
│                               graph pruning, concept writing. Runs inside the worker.
│
├── graph_routing.py          ← Smart document routing. Connects ingested Documents to
│                               Module/Phase/Project/Job hub nodes using rules + AI.
│
├── neo4j_graph.py            ← Neo4j driver singleton and all graph CRUD operations.
│                               Imported by both app.py and tasks.py.
│
├── worker.py                 ← Starts the RQ worker process. Minimal — just imports
│                               and launches. The real work is in tasks.py.
│
├── psb_check.py              ← 31-item diagnostic script. Run before every deploy.
│                               Checks env, services, APIs, Docker, git hygiene, syntax.
│
├── psb_security_audit.py     ← Security-focused audit. Checks SSH config, UFW rules,
│                               exposed ports, git secrets, Flask hardening.
│
├── neo4j_test.py             ← Manual Neo4j smoke test. Not used in production.
│                               Run to verify graph connection and CRUD after setup.
│
├── templates/
│   ├── index.html            ← The entire dashboard UI. ~2700 lines of HTML, CSS, JS.
│   │                           Server metrics, Docker panel, knowledge graph, AI chat,
│   │                           document ingest, minimap, inspector, mobile responsive.
│   └── login.html            ← Login page. Bcrypt auth form, flash messages.
│
├── prompts/
│   └── routing.txt           ← The AI routing prompt template. Editable without touching
│                               Python. Controls how Ollama decides where documents go.
│
├── static/
│   ├── vis-network.min.js    ← The graph rendering library. Handles physics, layout,
│   │                           node/edge rendering, interaction. ~900KB, loaded locally.
│   └── vis-network.min.css   ← vis-network styles.
│
├── uploads/                  ← Temporary storage for ingestion files. Files are deleted
│                               after Stage 4 (cleanup). Should normally be empty.
│
├── .env                      ← ALL secrets. Never in git. Contains:
│                               FLASK_SECRET_KEY, PSB_USERNAME, PSB_PASSWORD_HASH,
│                               NEO4J_URI, NEO4J_USER, NEO4J_PASSWORD,
│                               REDIS_URL, OLLAMA_MODEL, PUBLIC_URL
│
├── requirements.txt          ← All Python dependencies pinned to exact versions.
│                               Install with: pip install -r requirements.txt
│
└── venv/                     ← Python virtual environment. Not in git.
                                Activate: source venv/bin/activate
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
PART 1 — WHAT PSB IS AND WHY IT WAS BU

---

# claude response

Let me read through the exported chat first.

Right, I've read through all 2,472 pages. Here's the reality of where you stand, corrected for what's actually been done.

---

**What's confirmed DONE (Phases 1–9A + Gunicorn):**

Phases 1–8 are fully complete: Linux setup, SSH hardening (Ed25519 keys), Fail2Ban, Cloudflare tunnel to psblabsai.online, Flask + Flask-SocketIO dashboard with Chart.js, Ollama AI agent (Llama 3), and the auth system (bcrypt + flask-login + .env secrets).

Gunicorn is also done — it's running right now in tmux session `psb_prod` with eventlet workers on port 8080 behind the Cloudflare tunnel. The previous chat listed "Phase 10 — Gunicorn as systemd service" but you already have Gunicorn running. What you *don't* have yet is the systemd unit file that auto-starts it on reboot — right now if the server reboots, you'd need to manually SSH in and start tmux again.

Phase 9A (Docker infrastructure) is done — `docker-compose.yml` with Neo4j and Redis containers running, ports bound to `127.0.0.1`, Docker panel visible and functional in the dashboard UI.

---

**What's actually next, in order:**

**9B — Neo4j Python driver.** The containers are running but nothing talks to Neo4j yet. This is `pip install neo4j`, a driver connection to `bolt://localhost:7687`, and your first `MERGE` query creating a concept node. ~15 lines of Python. One afternoon.

**9C — Redis + RQ task queue.** Right now when someone asks the AI agent a question, Flask blocks until Ollama finishes responding. This phase adds a worker queue so the request goes to Redis, an RQ worker picks it up, Ollama processes it in the background, and the result comes back via WebSocket. Dashboard stays responsive.

**9D — Ingestion pipeline.** This is the big one conceptually. You POST a Gemini session transcript to PSB, Ollama reads it, extracts concepts/entities, and stores them as nodes and edges in Neo4j. The system starts accumulating knowledge about what you know.

**9E — Graph visualisation.** Render your knowledge graph in the dashboard using D3.js or Neovis.js. A new panel, same pattern as the Docker panel.

**10 — systemd service file.** Convert your manual tmux Gunicorn start into a proper systemd unit so the server auto-recovers after reboots. Small phase, mostly config.

**11 — Web terminal panel.** xterm.js on the frontend, paramiko or WebSocket shell on the backend. You said this feels easier than the graph work — and it is. It's a satisfying build.

**12 — Security to 9.5/10.** Cloudflare Zero Trust email OTP gate, Fail2Ban Flask jail watching your login logs, structured security logging. This is what makes psblabsai.online properly hardened for public exposure.

**13 — Alerts panel.** CPU threshold, RAM pressure, container down, Fail2Ban ban triggered — all pushed to the dashboard in real time via the WebSocket infrastructure you already have.

**14 — AI agent memory (the final boss).** PSB-Agent queries its own Neo4j graph. Natural language becomes Cypher. Llama answers from your personal knowledge base instead of generic training data. Everything before this was building towards this.

---

You're right that Gunicorn is done. The previous chat's roadmap listed it as Phase 10 because it was thinking about the systemd piece, not Gunicorn itself. Your immediate next step when you're ready is **9B — one `pip install`, one driver connection, one MERGE query.** But you said you're doing the learning month first, and that's the right call. 9B will take an afternoon once you actually understand why `bolt://localhost:7687` works and why `MERGE` exists instead of `CREATE`.

---

SOLUZIONE COMPLETA — Esame di Stato, Sessione Ordinaria 2023 
A042 · Economia Aziendale e Geo-Politica 
Indirizzo: Amministrazione Finanza e Marketing — Articolazione Relazioni Internazionali 
per il Marketing 
 
PRIMA PARTE — Stato Patrimoniale e Conto Economico al 31/12/2022 
 
1. DATI DEL PROBLEMA 
Alfa spa è un'impresa industriale nel settore della meccanica di precisione. 
L'unico dato numerico diretto fornito dalla traccia è: 
Indicatore 
2022 
2021 
Significato 
ROS 
7% = 0,07 6% = 0,06 
Redditività delle vendite 
ROI 
8% = 0,08 7% = 0,07 
Redditività del capitale investito 
ROE 
10% = 0,10 8% = 0,08 
Redditività del capitale proprio 
Leverage 
2,5 
1,965 
Totale Impieghi / Patrimonio Netto 
Totale Impieghi 2021 — 
1.800.000 € Unico dato monetario diretto 
 
2. BREVE TEORIA DEGLI INDICI DI BILANCIO 
ROS (Return on Sales) = Reddito Operativo / Ricavi di Vendita → misura quanti centesimi 
di reddito operativo produce ogni euro di vendite. 
ROI (Return on Investment) = Reddito Operativo / Totale Impieghi → misura la redditività 
del capitale investito, indipendentemente da come è finanziato. 
ROE (Return on Equity) = Reddito Netto / Patrimonio Netto → misura il rendimento per i 
soci del capitale da loro apportato. 
Leverage = Totale Impieghi / Patrimonio Netto → indica quante volte il totale degli 
investimenti supera il capitale proprio; un valore > 1 significa che l'azienda usa debiti. 
 
3. CALCOLI ANNO 2021 (anno di partenza) 
Partiamo dal 2021 perché conosciamo il Totale Impieghi = 1.800.000 €. 
Passo A — Patrimonio Netto 2021 
Formula generale: 
Leverage = Totale Impieghi / Patrimonio Netto   →   PN = Totale Impieghi / Leverage 
Applicazione: 
• 
Leverage 2021 = 1,965 ; Totale Impieghi 2021 = 1.800.000 € 
• 
PN₂₀₂₁ = 1.800.000 / 1,965 = 916.000 € (≈ 915.979,38 €) 
✔ Patrimonio Netto 2021 ≈ 916.000 € 
 
Passo B — Reddito Operativo 2021 
Formula generale: 
ROI = Reddito Operativo / Totale Impieghi   →   RO = ROI × Totale Impieghi 
Applicazione: 
• 
ROI 2021 = 0,07 ; Totale Impieghi 2021 = 1.800.000 € 
• 
RO₂₀₂₁ = 0,07 × 1.800.000 = 126.000 € 
✔ Reddito Operativo 2021 = 126.000 € 
 
Passo C — Ricavi di Vendita 2021 
Formula generale: 
ROS = Reddito Operativo / Ricavi   →   Ricavi = Reddito Operativo / ROS 
Applicazione: 
• 
ROS 2021 = 0,06 ; RO 2021 = 126.000 € 
• 
Ricavi₂₀₂₁ = 126.000 / 0,06 = 2.100.000 € 
✔ Ricavi di Vendita 2021 = 2.100.000 € 
 
Passo D — Reddito Netto 2021 
Formula generale: 
ROE = Reddito Netto / Patrimonio Netto   →   RN = ROE × PN 
Applicazione: 
• 
ROE 2021 = 0,08 ; PN 2021 = 916.000 € 
• 
RN₂₀₂₁ = 0,08 × 916.000 = 73.280 € 
✔ Reddito Netto 2021 = 73.280 € 
 
4. CALCOLI ANNO 2022 
Nota: Per il 2022 non abbiamo il Totale Impieghi direttamente. Utilizziamo il Leverage e 
un Patrimonio Netto scelto in modo coerente con il "rafforzamento patrimoniale"

summary: This tutorial presents a case study on a cloud-based library system with issues categorized into legal, social, ethical, and professional domains. It highlights problems like data privacy, accessibility, AI bias, and security vulnerabilities in AI-driven systems.
text:
Tutorial 1:
Read the Smart Library case study carefully. Identify and classify the issues into the following categories:
Legal Issues
Social Issues
Ethical Issues
Professional Issues
Case Study: Smart Library
The University of Greenfield recently adopted Smart Library, a new cloud-based library management system designed to improve access to learning materials. The system integrates e-book lending, facial recognition for secure entry, and an AI-based recommendation engine to suggest reading materials based on user history. To reduce costs, the university outsourced development overseas. The contractor reused parts of open-source software without carefully checking the licensing terms. After deployment, several concerns arose. Students discovered that the system collected detailed personal data, including facial scans, borrowing records, and login patterns, without clearly explaining how this information would be used or stored. Some visually impaired students complained that the interface was not compatible with screen readers, making the system inaccessible to them. Others noted that the AI recommendation engine heavily favored English-language content, overlooking materials from other cultures and languages. Shortly after launch, a serious bug exposed students’ borrowing histories to public access on the internet. The incident raised widespread concerns about privacy, fairness, and the university’s accountability.

text:
CW
PART A
Case study: SafeCare Hospital Management
SafeCare Hospital is a leading medical institution in a rapidly growing city. With a capacity of
700 beds, it is equipped with advanced medical technologies and provides a wide range of
services, from routine general care to highly specialized emergency treatment and surgeries.
The hospital has earned a reputation for its patient-cantered approach and commitment to
quality care. As the city continues to expand and the demand for healthcare services
increases, SafeCare is preparing to modernize its operations with a stronger focus on patient
safety and operational efficiency. Modern hospitals are no longer just centres of treatment.
they function as complex ecosystems where patients, medical staff, visitors, and external
service providers constantly interact. In such an environment, ensuring safety, maintaining
privacy, and optimizing operations becomes a monumental challenge. SafeCare must
effectively manage high patient volumes, safeguard sensitive medical data, respond rapidly
to emergencies, and control secure access to critical areas such as operating theatres,
intensive care units, and medicine storage rooms.
At present, the hospital faces several pressing safety challenges. Unauthorized access to
restricted areas is a recurring issue, as current systems for controlling entry to places like
ICUs and operating rooms are not robust enough. The tracking of patients and them
movement across different hospital departments is largely manual, which increases the risk
of errors and inefficiencies. In emergency situations such as cardiac arrests, fires, or
evacuations, coordination across departments is often limited and delayed, which can have
serious consequences for patient outcomes. Visitor management is another area of concern,
with difficulties in monitoring visitor activities and verifying their relationships with patients.
Additionally, the hospital’s health data systems, emergency protocols, and response
processes are poorly integrated, creating a fragmented approach that slows down decision-
making during critical moments.

The case study outlines requirements for an IS to manage catalog browsing, customer reviews, study packs, and order processing with budget/time constraints.
text:
Case study: AroundLondon Bookstores 
 
AroundLondon Book Stores (ALBS) is a medium sized chain of high-quality bookshops spread 
across a number of university campuses around London. They currently have 20 shops and an 
efficient warehouse/distribution operation. ALBS are now thinking to expand the bookstores’ 
service by allowing students and staff to buy books online as well as offer support to those 
who browse their online catalogue but prefer to place orders in person or by the telephone. 
Rather late in the day and after seeing their customer base declining, ALBS would like to 
respond to competition, particularly with online companies such as Amazon and eBay. They 
feel that offering their services online will also allow them to cut down some of the costs in 
stores. They would also like to attempt to provide a new service, which will allow their users 
to loan a book online (which will be delivered to their home address) and return it within two 
weeks, something similar to the library loan system. The bookstores also provide study packs 
with copies of journal articles relevant to specific courses, which students can buy at a 
discount price. 
ALBS are keen to provide high quality service to students and staff, however they would like 
to expand the bookstores’ service to other potential customers that live around the area. 
They believe that the key to increased market share is having both online and hybrid 
telephone ordering capabilities. They would like to attract more customers and therefore 
they are open to suggestions regarding extra functionalities their new computerized IS should 
support. 
The bookstores provide good descriptions of the books they sell. While publishers do provide 
descriptions of the new books (however these tend to be boring and overly positive), the 
shops’ staff prefer to write their own honest and helpful reviews. There is also the possibility 
for students, staff and other customers to write reviews themselves. 
You are consultants called in to assist ALBS with this restructuring of their marketing and sales 
business model from an IS perspective. They have a tight deadline of 8 months for the online 
system to go live and the analysis, design and development and promotion of the new system 
should be within the budget of 50.000 pounds decided by the Board of Directors. 
In outline ALBS have sketched the system they need as follows: 
Students, staff and potential customers (let’s call them CUSTOMERS for a matter of 
simplicity) can browse and search the online catalogues for books of interest. 
CUSTOMERS can order books/study packs online using conventional electronic 
"shopping basket" and "check out" functionality. They can choose from several 
different shipping methods and rates based on a formula related to the urgency and 
the weight of an order. 
CUSTOMERS should be able to read descriptions or reviews of books as well as have 
the option to provide their reviews as well once registered and logged in to the system. 
CUSTOMERS should also be given the option to loan a particular book and then return 
this back to store within two weeks. They would still expect to go through the 
shopping basket and checkout functionality and the books will be delivered to their 
preferred address.  
CUSTOMERS may also phone in or email with their book orders and any other 
requests. Their orders may be very precise (a particular book or a study pack), but they 
may also be vague. They may just say that they want “the book on Economics and 
Statistics” that was reviewed on page 12 of last Monday’s Economist. Such queries 
might be based on a structured form filling approach. 
Sales staff of the book shops take the phone calls or read the emails and interact with 
the customers. They also handle any online orders that are flagged with problems

text:
Principles of Software Engineering – 
COMP 1821 
Tutorial 3: Structured Analysis and Design 
 
Exercise 1(15 min) 
Discuss the difference between Functional and Non-Functional requirements.  
Discuss: 
• What is structured analysis and design Logical vs physical design? 
• What is an ERD? 
• Entities 
• What is primary key and foreign key? 
• Relationships 
Exercise 2 
• Create an ERD based on the case given below (Student testing System) 
• Include ALL elements required by the diagram, including attributes and their 
types 
Student Testing System 
The assessment officer, of the CIS department from University of Greenwich, Dr Noor 
Khan, is looking into introducing CIS staff to a set of online assessment tools which 
would help them to set up formative and summative assessments for students. 
So far, Dr. Noor introduced the CIS staff to several “off the shelf” tools such Hot 
Potatoes, Google Forms and Question Writer. However, she would like to have a built for 
purpose an application and she approached you to develop a bespoke testing 
application for CIS. 
Dr. Noor is looking for a developing team to design and implement an online 
computerised testing system for CIS. The system you are required to build should be 
able to provide CIS staff with the following functionality 
As a first step, Dr. Noor would like to have a system to store and access all the 
necessary information (a structured system) and she asked you to produce an ERD 
 
 
Creating Tests Functionality: 
• Staff should be able to create questions and add to pool of questions for a 
particular course (you can use a database or files or any other type of data 
storage) 
• There are different types of question: 
o Multiple-choice: only one answer is correct (use of the radio buttons) 
o Multiple response: more than one answer can be correct (use of the 
check boxes)  
o Essay: free text 
• All questions should 
o Belong to a course (for example questions for AWD, SDP etc).  
o Have a title 
o  Display instructions 
o  Display points a question is worth 
o  Provide the facility to include an image if the user wishes 
When creating a test, staff should be able to indicate what course they want to create 
the test for and select several questions to be chosen randomly from the pool of 
questions. 
Sitting a Test Functionality 
• When students are taking a test, the system should ask for their user id 
and/or name. 
• A test should be visible only after providing a password (the idea is that the 
tutor would provide the password in the class so all students will start at 
the same time). 
• Each question should be shown one at the time on the screen. 
• The system should timestamp when a student finishes the test (so staff 
could dismiss any tests that are not finished on time) 
• Electronic tests should be marked automatically (apart from essay 
questions) At the end of a user sitting a test, the application should create 
a feedback report with results for the user: what questions were wrong, 
etc.

summary: Analyzes legal, social, ethical, and professional challenges in implementing a hospital safety management system, focusing on GDPR compliance, medical device regulations, digital equity, AI bias mitigation, and interoperability standards.
text:
SafeCare Hospital Management System Implementation Report
Overview
The SafeCare Hospital Management System project aims to convert and digitalise safety protocols within a 700-bed facility. Automated access control, and digital emergency responses significantly improves patient safety and operational efficiency. It also reinforces the critical situation that Safecare currently finds itself in following Legal, Social, Ethical, and Professional (LSEPI) issues. This report then outlines the project methodology, strategic analysis, system requirements, and technical implementation required to deliver a compliant and robust solution.
LEGAL ISSUES
GDPR Compliance: The UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) states that personal data consists of any information pertaining to any person, on the other hand special category data needs additional protection due to its sensitivity.
CCTV Rules: The use of CCTV must adhere to surveillance legislation like the Data Protection Act 2018 and the ICO CCTV Code of Practice. One of these rules includes the requirement to inform people when they are being recorded.
Medical Device Regulations: Wearable sensors can be classed as medical devices under the UK Medical Devices Regulations 2002; as such, they must be examined, certified, and approved by regulatory authorities before they can be used.
SOCIAL ISSUES
Digital Ostracism: Digitalising hospital safety causes issues such as digital ostracism which is the gap between people who have the skills and confidence to use digital tools versus those who do not. This includes older adults (aged 75+), people with poor literacy skills, disabilities, or socio-economic challenges.
Access Barriers: If pre-registration via mobile app is expected, people who don’t own a device or understand may be ostracised or delayed. Additionally, the price of a device and other costs prevent people from accessing the app.
Trust & Privacy Concerns: Not everyone trusts digital tools; there are concerns about how private data is being used or shared.
Design Fairness: Digital tools must be functional, accessible, and fair by taking into account cultural diversities, languages, and cognitive abilities.
ETHICAL ISSUES
Lawful Basis: Under Article 6 of the UK GDPR, a lawful basis for processing sensitive health data must be identified, alongside Article 9 which states the requirements for processing procedures.
Consent Validity: Demanding pre-registration raises the question of whether consent is independent and valid, especially for patients with language barriers or reduced capacity. Consent flows must be multidimensional (verbal support, translated text) with unambiguous opt-out choices.
Surveillance vs. Dignity: Regular monitoring (high-definition cameras, biometric verification) increases safety but exposes patients to intrusive surveillance that erodes privacy and dignity unless justified. The ICO and UK Surveillance Camera Code of Practice set standards requiring monitoring to be proportionate to a valid aim. The General Medical Council (GMC) also highlights the doctor’s duty of confidentiality.
AI & Bias: Any analytical tool or AI used to set up emergency alerts or predict deterioration via sensors can strengthen structural/historical biases. Healthcare providers must be able to explain AI recommendations to preserve accountability. To alleviate this, an Algorithmic Impact Assessment must be conducted to certify performance across demographic groups.
PROFESSIONAL ISSUES
Interoperability Standards: Clinical systems must transfer patients' booking data reliably using the UK/NHS recommended standard (HL7 Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources or HL7 FHIR) for modern healthcare APIs. This decreases integration failures and guarantees secure data flow between the app, EMR, and monitoring systems.
Code of Conduct: The British Computer Society (BCS) Code of Conduct (safeguarding data, clarity about risks, competence) sets professional standards that IT staff must follow. Re

SafeCare Hospital Management System Implementation Report
Overview
The SafeCare Hospital Management System project aims to convert and digitalise safety protocols within a 700-bed facility. Automated access control, and digital emergency responses significantly improves patient safety and operational efficiency. It also reinforces the critical situation that Safecare currently finds itself in following Legal, Social, Ethical, and Professional (LSEPI) issues. This report then outlines the project methodology, strategic analysis, system requirements, and technical implementation required to deliver a compliant and robust solution.
LEGAL ISSUES
GDPR Compliance: The UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) states that personal data consists of any information pertaining to any person, on the other hand special category data needs additional protection due to its sensitivity.
CCTV Rules: The use of CCTV must adhere to surveillance legislation like the Data Protection Act 2018 and the ICO CCTV Code of Practice. One of these rules includes the requirement to inform people when they are being recorded.
Medical Device Regulations: Wearable sensors can be classed as medical devices under the UK Medical Devices Regulations 2002; as such, they must be examined, certified, and approved by regulatory authorities before they can be used.

Digital Ostracism: Digitalising hospital safety causes issues such as digital ostracism which is the gap between people who have the skills and confidence to use digital tools versus those who do not. Cambridge English: Preliminary for Schools

©UCLES 2012 
 
 
 
Page 2 of 51 
2012 
Cambridge English: Preliminary and Preliminary for Schools 
Vocabulary List 
 
 
 
Introduction to 
the 
Cambridge English: Preliminary and 
Preliminary for Schools Vocabulary List 
 
The Cambridge English: Preliminary and Preliminary for Schools Vocabulary List gives 
teachers a guide to the vocabulary needed when preparing students for the Preliminary 
and Preliminary for Schools examinations. 
 
Background to the list 
 
The Preliminary and Preliminary for Schools Vocabulary List was originally developed by 
Cambridge English in consultation with external consultants to guide item writers who 
produce materials for the Preliminary and Preliminary for Schools examination. It includes 
vocabulary from the Council of Europe's Threshold (1990) specification and other 
vocabulary which corpus evidence shows is high frequency. 
 
The list covers vocabulary appropriate to the B1 level on the Common European 
Framework of Reference (CEFR) and includes receptive vocabulary (words that the 
candidate is expected to understand but which is not the focus of a question) and 
productive vocabulary (words that the candidate needs to know to answer a question). 
 
The list does not provide an exhaustive list of all words which appear on the Preliminary 
and Preliminary for Schools question papers and candidates should not confine their 
study of vocabulary to the list alone. 
 
How the list is updated 
 
The vocabulary of English changes over time, with words being added and other 
words falling into disuse. In order to maintain its currency, the Preliminary and 
Preliminary for Schools Vocabulary List is updated on an annual basis, with the decision 
to add or remove words being informed by reference to the Cambridge Learner Corpus 
and English Profile Wordlists. 
 
The Cambridge Learner Corpus is a collection of over 44 million words of English, 
based upon evidence of language use by learners from all over the world and from 
which the English Vocabulary Profile has developed. The English Vocabulary Profile 
shows the most common words and phrases that learners of English need to know in 
British or American English. The meaning of each word or phrase in the wordlists has 
been assigned a level between A1 and B2 on the CEFR. 
 
A  preview   version  of  the  English  Vocabulary Profile  can  be  accessed  by  visiting  
the website: http://www.englishprofile.org 
 
Organisation of the list 
 
• Word sets 
Some categories of words that a learner at this level might be expected to know, e.g. 
days of the week, are not included in the alphabetical list but are listed in Appendix 1. 
Although 'grammar  words' (pronouns, modal verbs, etc.) are included, the 'Language 
Specification' section 
of 
the 
 Preliminary and Preliminary for Schools 
Handbook (available 
from http://www.cambridgeenglish.org/) should be consulted 
for a more complete listing. 
 
 
Page 3 of 51 
2012 
Cambridge English: Preliminary and Preliminary for Schools 
Vocabulary List 
 
 
 
• Exemplification 
Example phrases and sentences showing how words might be used are given only 
where words with different meanings need to be constrained. For example, heel is 
followed by 'I can't walk in high heels' -this shows that heel is limited to the idea of 
shoes: candidates are not expected to know other meanings, such as the part of the 
body. 
• Multi-word Verbs 
Multi-word verbs are not included in the list if they have a literal meaning and are 
composed of verbs and particles already in the list. Examples of 'literal' multi-word 
verbs are come into, sit down, as in 'Why not come into the kitchen and sit down?' If the 
meaning of the verb is not transparent, e.g. find out, get along, give in, then the verb

This lab will teach you basic network commands on using Windows systems and move into packing sniffing.
PART 1: There are many network commands that do many different things. The trace route program contains
a client interface to ICMP. Like the ping program, it may be used by a user to verify an end-to-end path is
operational, but also provides information on each of the routers along the path from the sender to the
receiver. It also returns the hop count and the round-trip time for each packet. When encountering a router
that does not respond, it prints a *.
PART 2: According to NIST: Packet sniffing refers to “software that observes and records network traffic”. An
example of this software is, Wireshark. This is a free, open-source packet analyser, used for network
troubleshooting, analysis, software and communications protocol development and security. It captures
network packets and displays detailed packet information. It runs on Windows and MACs.

The Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) is one of the protocols of the Internet 
Protocol (IP) suites. The ping program contains a client interface to ICMP. It may be used by a 
user to verify that an end-to-end Internet Path is operational and to collect performance 
statistics, the measured round-trip time, and the number of times the remote server fails to 
reply.
Ping performance is measured in milliseconds (ms). So, if you have a teammate with  over 
100 ping (aka 100ms) on League of Legends it’s unlikely they can carry you. 

summary: The document describes an Arduino Uno-based hospital communication system using LEDs to represent workflow roles and a button-triggered sequence to simulate message exchange protocols. It combines physical circuit design with logical sequencing to meet assignment requirements for a reliable booking system.
text:
Electrical circuit explanation
The system I developed uses an Arduino Uno as the “brain” of the hospital communication network. In this model, the Arduino controls the exchange of information step by step, ensuring that every message follows the correct order. Each LED represents one party in the hospital workflow (Patient, Reception, #Doctor, Nurse), and the sequence is activated by a button that starts the process. The LEDs blink before staying on, symbolizing the handshake and confirmation of communication. This design respects the assignment requirements by combining both the physical representation (the circuit) and the logical protocol (the programmed sequence), laying the foundation for a reliable hospital booking and communication system

summary: This document explains the design of a hospital booking communication system using electrical circuit models and network diagrams. It details protocol rules, OSI model mapping, and demonstration plans for both physical and logical communication flows.
text:
Hospital system
Aim
The aim of this project is to design and demonstrate a simplified hospital booking communication system using both an electrical circuit model and a network diagram. The electrical circuit provides the physical representation of message exchange, while the network diagram illustrates the logical connections between users and the central server. To achieve this, we will:
Define a clear frame format and encoding scheme for messages.
Establish protocol rules (handshake, ACK/NACK, retransmission) to ensure reliable communication.
Map the system to the OSI reference model to connect theory with practice.
Prepare a demonstration plan with test cases to show normal and error-handling scenarios.
Reflect on limitations and suggest improvements such as automation and stronger error detection.
Final Overall Explanation
The electrical circuit is a simplified representation of how communication in our hospital booking system works. The battery represents the central server that powers all exchanges, while the main switch activates the entire system. From there, the star junction distributes the signal to the four branches, each symbolizing a different user or department (Patient, Help Desk, Nurse, Doctor, Reception). summary: This document contains Scheme functions for manipulating email lists, including marking emails, moving them between folders, and sorting by recipient. It demonstrates functional programming concepts and list operations relevant to Bruno's COMP1811 coursework.
text:
COMP1811 — CW2 Demo Quiz
OPEN BOOK REFERENCE — Partner B
Bruno Mosti — 001478336 | Partner A: Nnamdi Bernice — 001499722
1. EMAIL STRUCTURE
Each email = a list of 9 fields. Index 0 to 8. Your functions read/modify specific indices.
2. SHARED HELPER: replace-value
Partner A (Nnamdi) wrote this. Your mark and mv-email both call it. Walks a list, counts down to position, swaps value.
(define (replace-value pos new-val e-lst)
(cond
[(null? e-lst) '()]
[(= pos 0) (cons new-val (cdr e-lst))]
[else (cons (car e-lst)
(replace-value (- pos 1) new-val (cdr e-lst)))]))
3. THE PATTERN (mark, mv-email, del-email all use this)
1. (null? mb-lst) → '()                ; STOP — base case
2. (= id (car (car mb-lst)))            ; MATCH? compare ID
→ (replace-value INDEX VAL (car mb-lst))  ; modify
→ cons modified + (cdr mb-lst)       ; attach rest
3. else → cons (car mb-lst)             ; NO MATCH — keep
→ recurse on (cdr mb-lst)            ; try next email
4. FB1: mark (id type mb-lst)
(define (mark id type mb-lst)
(cond
[(null? mb-lst) '()]              ; base case
[(= id (car (car mb-lst)))        ; ID match
(cond
[(equal? type 'flag)
(cons (replace-value 7 #t (car mb-lst))
(cdr mb-lst))]
[(equal? type 'read)
(cons (replace-value 8 #t (car mb-lst))
(cdr mb-lst))]
[else (cons (car mb-lst) (cdr mb-lst))])]
[else
(cons (car mb-lst)
(mark id type (cdr mb-lst)))]))
'flag → replace-value 7 #t → changes Flag (index 7) to #t
'read → replace-value 8 #t → changes Read (index 8) to #t
Inner cond → because 2+ options (flag, read, else). Nested inside the ID-match branch.
= for id → IDs are numbers, = works. equal? for type because 'flag is a symbol.
Pure function → Returns NEW mailbox. Original mb is NEVER changed.
5. FB2: mv-email (id f mb-lst)
(define (mv-email id f mb-lst)
(cond
[(null? mb-lst) '()]
[(= id (car (car mb-lst)))
(cons (replace-value 5 f (car mb-lst))
(cdr mb-lst))]
[else
(cons (car mb-lst)
(mv-email id f (cdr mb-lst)))]))
Changes → Tag (index 5) to folder f using replace-value
vs del-email → SAME pattern. del hardcodes "bin". Yours takes any folder = generalised version.
6. FB3: find-by-date (d mb-lst)
(define (find-by-date d mb-lst)
(filter (lambda (email)
(equal? (list-ref email 3) d))
mb-lst))
filter → Higher-order fn. Keeps elements where lambda returns #t.
lambda → Anonymous one-time function. Tests each email's date against d.
(list-ref email 3) → Gets Date at index 3.
equal? not = → Dates are LISTS like '(3 3 2025). = only works on numbers.
Returns → ALL matching emails. '() if none found.
7. ⭐ FB4: sort-by-to (mb-lst) — 20 MARKS
(define (sort-by-to mb-lst)
(define (insert email sorted-lst)
(cond
[(null? sorted-lst) (list email)]
[(symbol<? (list-ref (car sorted-lst) 2)
(list-ref email 2))
(cons email sorted-lst)]
[else
(cons (car sorted-lst)
(insert email (cdr sorted-lst)))]))
(if (null? mb-lst)
'()
(insert (car mb-lst)
(sort-by-to (cdr mb-lst)))))
Algorithm → Recursive insertion sort
DESCENDING trick → SWAPPED the two arguments in symbol<?
Ascending asks → "is NEW < EXISTING?" → small values first
Your descending asks → "is EXISTING < NEW?" → big values first
To make ascending → Swap the two args: (symbol<? (list-ref email 2) (list-ref (car sorted-lst) 2))
symbol<? → Compares two symbols alphabetically. Works on To field symbols.
insert inside sort-by-to → Local helper. Only used here = better encapsulation.
Why not built-in sort? → Spec explicitly forbids it.
8. FB5: add-stats (bdy)
(define (add-stats bdy)
(let ([p (length bdy)]
[s (if (null? bdy) 0
(apply + (map length bdy)))])
(cons (list 'Stats:
(list "P count:" p)
(list "S count:" s))
bdy)))
p = (length bdy) = count inner lists = PARAGRAPHS
s = (apply + (map length bdy)) = TOTAL SENTENCES
How s works → map length → counts per paragraph → '(2 1 3)
then → apply + → unpacks as args → (+ 2 1 3) → 6
let → Stores p and s as local variables. Calculate once, use in stats.
cons → Puts stats at FRONT of body (not append). Prepends ONE item.
How to calculate p and s (look-up table)
Co

summary: A project role distribution plan for a programming task involving prime number analysis, algorithm optimization, and visualization. Defines responsibilities for implementing algorithms, performance analysis, and documentation.
text:
Group Plan & Role Allocation
Student 1 – Lead Coordinator & Quality Assurance
(Task 5 & Report Integration)
Purpose:
Secure the 20% journal mark and ensure the final submission fully complies with the brief.
Responsibilities:
Set up the MS365 collaboration document.
Track Version History as evidence of engagement.
Perform the final line count check (code must remain under 100 lines).
Verify the output format for $6k ± 1 primes shows only the first 3 and last 3 results.
Compile the final PDF.
Ensure the file naming convention matches the brief exactly.
Support the AI Declaration accuracy (with Student 6).
Student 2 – Sub-Group A: Foundational Logic
(Task 2)
Purpose:
Demonstrate correctness without AI assistance.
Responsibilities:
Implement the Sliding Window using standard index slicing.
Implement Trial Division primality testing (check up to √n).
Store primes in a List (as required in Task 2).
Record runtimes for all 10 test cases.
Expect later Pi cases to exceed 60 seconds (this is useful for analysis).
Student 3 – Sub-Group B: Data Structure Specialist
(Task 3)
Purpose:
Demonstrate performance improvement from O(n) to near O(1) membership checks.
Responsibilities:
Modify Student 2’s solution to use a Set instead of a List.
Explain membership testing differences:
x in list → linear search
x in set → hash table, near constant time
Perform runtime comparison with Student 2’s version.
Document performance improvement clearly.
Student 4 – Sub-Group C: Optimisation Engineer
(Task 4)
Purpose:
Ensure Case 10 runs in under 60 seconds.
Responsibilities:
Implement optimisation strategy:
Prefer Sieve of Eratosthenes (if manageable within constraints).
Alternatively use a highly optimised deterministic is_prime with early exits (6k ± 1 rule).
Do NOT use Miller–Rabin.
Keep implementation concise to remain under the 100-line limit.
Validate performance against Task 2 baseline.
Student 5 – Visualisation & Edge Case Lead
(Task 1 & Task 4 Graphics)
Purpose:
Deliver required visual components and edge-case validation.
Responsibilities:
Task 1:
Create a diagram illustrating the Sliding Window logic.
Draft 5 new test cases (e.g., strings with zeros, no primes, very short strings).
Task 4:
Produce a Line Graph or Bar Chart comparing execution times:
Task 2 (List version)
Task 4 (Optimised version)
Student 6 – Complexity Analyst
(Task 1 & Task 4 Analysis)
Purpose:
Provide formal algorithm analysis required for high-grade justification (80%+ bracket).
Responsibilities:
Write high-level pseudocode for Task 1.
Derive Big-O for the basic version:
O(WindowCount × SubstringsInWindow × √N)
Justify optimised complexity:
Explain how Set reduces lookup cost.
Explain how Sieve / improved primality reduces work per window.
Assist Student 1 in verifying AI Declaration compliance.
