summary: Pseudocode implementing a sliding window algorithm to find prime number density in numeric strings, with substring extraction and prime checking logic, and output formatting rules for results
text:
Pseudocode Draft
FUNCTION IdentifyPrimeDensestWindow(S, W, N):
#Validate that the string contains only digits 0-9
IF S is not numeric THEN RETURN "0, 0: Invalid input"
#Initialise tracking variables
max_prime_count = 0
best_start_index = 0
best_primes_list = EMPTY LIST
# Move the window across the string
FOR i FROM 0 TO (LENGTH(S) - W):
current_window_str = S[from index i to i + W]
found_in_window = EMPTY SET // Set ensures uniqueness
# Extract every possible substring within the current window
FOR start FROM 0 TO (W - 1):
FOR end FROM (start + 1) TO W:
num = CONVERT SUBSTRING(current_window_str, start, end) TO INTEGER
#  Only process if it meets the limit N and hasn't been found yet
IF num < N AND num NOT IN found_in_window: IF CheckPrimality(num) IS TRUE:
ADD num TO found_in_window:
# Evaluate if this window is the new "densest"
current_count = SIZE of found_in_window
IF current_count > max_prime_count:
max_prime_count = current_count
best_start_index = i
best_primes_list = SORT found_in_window ASCENDING
# Handle results and specific formatting rules
IF max_prime_count == 0:
RETURN best_start_index, "0: No primes found"
# If 6+ primes, only display the first three and last three
IF SIZE of best_primes_list >= 6:
output_primes = [First 3 elements] + [Last 3 elements]
ELSE:
output_primes = best_primes_list
RETURN best_start_index, max_prime_count, output_primes
END FUNCTION
FUNCTION CheckPrimality(n):
IF n < 2 THEN RETURN FALSE FOR d FROM 2 TO SQUARE_ROOT(n):
IF n MOD d == 0 THEN RETURN FALSE
RETURN TRUE
END FUNCTION
Part 1: the main function
FUNCTION IdentifyPrimeDensestWindow ( S, W, N):
This first part defines the beginning of our code, this is useful because provide a guide step by step process for the computer to follow. To make it work properly, we need three pieces of information to start with:
the string of numbers (S)
how big our magnifying glass is (W)
and the maximum number we are allowed to consider (N)
IF S is not numeric THEN RETURN "0, 0: Invalid input"
this works as a security system, if someone incidentally wrote "hello" instead of "123" the system stops it immediately
max_prime_count = 0
best_start_index = 0
best_primes_list = EMPTY LIST
This works as a "container" and its role is to store data. We need to remember the best results we have found so far as we move through the string. We start at zero because we haven't looked at anything yet.
FOR i FROM 0 TO (LENGTH(S) - W):
This is the sliding window. i is the starting position. We move from the start (o) to the last possible spot where a window of size can still fit
Analogy: if I have 10 seats and a 3-seat bench the bench can only start at seats 0 	through 7
current_window_str = S[from index i to i + W]
this command has the rule of “cut out” the specific piece of the string we are currently looking at. If S is “12345” and W is 3, and we are at the index 0m this line grabs “123”
found_in_window = EMPTY SET
this work as a special container that is not allowing duplicates. So, it makes sure that we crate a fresh one for every window because we only want to count unique primes found inside that specific window
FOR start FROM 0 TO (W - 1):
FOR end FROM (start + 1) TO W:
These are Nested Loops used to find every possible combination of numbers inside our window.
Inside the window "123", these loops will find: "1", "12", "123", "2", "23", and "3".
num = CONVERT SUBSTRING(...) TO INTEGER

summary: The document outlines key topics for the driving license test, including alertness, anticipation, concentration, distraction management, and attitude development. It emphasizes situational awareness, proper rest, and safe driving practices to ensure road safety.
text:
Driving License Test
Topics index
1.0 Alertness
1.1 observation
Driving required focuses. I should look around constantly and assess the changing situations as I drive.
I must be aware of traffic all around me before carrying out any manoeuvre:
Moving off
stopping
turning or changing lanes
and I also should
Use my mirrors to assess how my action will affect traffic behind you
Look around for a final check remember windscreen pillars can obstruct your view
Signal if necessary
If I cannot see behind when reversing, ask a reliable person to guide me
If you cannot see when emerging from a junction because your view is obstructed by parked cars, move forward slowly and carefully until you can get a proper view.
Be particularly careful before you overtake. Ensure that You have a clear view of the road ahead there should not be any bends or dips
You have enough time to complete the manoeuvre safely
Is also important for other road users to know you’re there.
When it starts to get dark, switch on your lights, even if the streetlights are not on.
Where you cannot be seen, such as at a hump bridge, consider using your horns
1.02 Anticipation and awareness
When following a large vehicle, stay well back. If you cannot see the vehicles mirrors the driver may not be able to see you or know you’re there.
Staying in the back can also help me to see the road ahead much more clearly.
Also, I have to be aware of the other.
Pedestrians approaching a crossing, especially young, older or disabled people who may need more to cross the road
Cyclists leave at least 1.5 metres of space when overtaking cyclists at speeds of up to 30 mph, and give them more space when overtaking at higher speeds
Motorcyclists who may be difficult to see horses, which may startled by the noise of your vehicle
pass horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles at speeds under 10mph and allow at least 2 meters of space
if you approaching traffic light that have been green for some time, be prepared to stop because they may change,
is important to keep both hands on the wheel as you brake to jeep control of your vehicle.
1.03 Concentration
Always plan your journey so you
Know which route you need to take
have regular rest stops
you will not be able to concentrate properly if you’re tired. It’s particularly easy to feel sleepy on a motorway especially at night.
Do not drive continuously for more than 2 hours
Keep fresh air circulating in the car
If you start to feel drowsy, leave at the next exit. Find a safe and legal place to stop and take a break.
Self-reflection: sometimes its tempting to keep driving no matter how tired I’m. Plan rest breaks along your route; this will help me to stay alert and arrive safely.
1.04 Distraction and boredom
Don’t let the passenger distract me, arguing or joking around will take your mind off the driving.
Loud music can also affect my concentration and make it harder to hear sounds outside the car.
I can also be distracted by:
Objects hanging in the car
Starting or adjusting any music or radio
Looking at a map
Talking into a microphone
Just taking my eyes off the road for a second could be disastrous.
In that second at 60 mph’s (96km/h) my car will travel 27 metres.
Using a hand- held mobile phone while I’m driving is illegal; it also drastically increases the chance of being involved in a collision. Be safe:
Switch my phone off or put it on voicemail. Wait until you’re packed legally in a safe place before you use your mobile phone to:
Retrieve any messages
Make any calls
Send or receive texts
Go online
If I am driving on a motorway, I should leave the motorway and stop in a safe place before using my phone
If my vehicle has a navigation system, stop in a safe place before programming the system. If I lose the control may on a busy road, turn into a side road as soon as possible stop and check a map
2.01 Attitude
Safe driving is all about developing the correct attitude and approach, together with a sound knowledge of driving techniques.

Know which route you need to take
have regular rest stops
you will not be able to concentrate properly if you’re tired. It’s particularly easy to feel sleepy on a motorway especially at night.

summary: This lecture introduces foundational concepts of algorithms and data structures through analogies and examples. It explains their interdependence in program design and covers problem-solving lifecycle stages, pseudocode, and control structures.
text:
Introduction to Algorithms and Data Structures
The golden Equation
Algorithms + Data Structures = programs
You cannot have one without the other
Data Structures (The Ingredients & Storage)
Data structure are how we organise information so we can find it later.
The problem: imagine throwing all my cutlery, plates, and pots into one giant pile on the floor. It would take ages to find a spoon.
The solution: We use a drawer with dividers.
In CS: we use structures like Arrays ( a list of items), Stacks (like a stack of plates) or queues
Algorithms (The Recipe)
Algorithms are the step-by-step instruction to manipulate that data to solve a problem.
The problem: I have eggs, flour and milk but I don’t know how to make a pancake
The solution: a recipe tells you “1. Mix flour and milk. 2. Crack egg. 3. Whisk.”
In CS: An algorithm might tell the computer: “1. Look at the list of students. Compare their marls find the highest one.”
The Problem-Solving Lifecycle
Understand: Read the problem. What comes in? What must go out?
Decompose: Break the big problem into small, solvable chunks.
Design (Pseudocode): Write the logic in plain English/Logic.
Implement: Translate the design into Python.
Test: Check if it works (and if it breaks on edge cases).
Pseudocode: The language of logic
Pseudocode is a way of writing code that is meant for humans, not machines. It ignores syntax (like brackets or colons) and focuses on flow.
The lecture introduces three main "Control Structures" we use in Pseudocode:
Sequence: Doing things in order.
Step 1: Wake up. Step 2: Eat breakfast.
Selection (Conditionals): Making a choice.
IF it is raining, THEN take an umbrella. ELSE, wear sunglasses.
Iteration (Loops): Repeating a task.
WHILE I am hungry, eat another crisp.
Example A: Even or Odd?
The Logic: How do computers know if a number is even? They divide it by 2. If there is no remainder (0), it is Even. If there is a remainder (1), it is Odd.
The Operator: We use the Modulo operator (%). 10 % 2 is 0. 11 % 2 is 1.
Pseudocode:
Plaintext
FOR each number from 1 to N:
IF (number % 2) is equal to 0:
PRINT "Even"
ELSE:
PRINT "Odd"
Example B: The Fibonacci Sequence
The Logic: This is a famous sequence where the next number is the sum of the previous two.
Sequence: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13...
Logic: $0+1=1$, then $1+1=2$, then $1+2=3$.
Pseudocode Logic: To generate this, you need to keep track of two variables: previous_number and current_number. inside a loop, you calculate the next_number, then shift everything along.
xample C: Finding the Maximum ID
The Problem: You have a list of student IDs: [105, 873, 867]. Which is the biggest? The "Human" Way: You glance at it and see 873. The "Computer" Way (Linear Search): The computer can only see one number at a time.
The Algorithm:
Assume the first number is the biggest (call it current_max).
Look at the second number. Is it bigger than current_max?
Yes? Update current_max.
No? Do nothing.
Look at the third number... repeat until the end.

summary: This document explains Linux CLI fundamentals, emphasizing its role in system interaction. It covers shell functionality, scripting capabilities, alias creation, and variable usage for efficient command execution across Linux distributions.
text:
Linux Essentials
Most consumers os are designed to shiedl the user from the ins and outs of the CLI.
The linux community is different in that it positely the cli for its power, speed and ability to accomplish a vast array of tasks with a single command line instruction.
Furthermore, by learning the CLI, a user can easily be productive almost instantly on ANY flavor or distribution of Linux, reducing the amount of time needed to familiarize themselves with a system because of variations in a GUI.
Shell
Once a user has entered a command the terminal then accepts what the user has typed and passes it to a shell.
The shell is the command line interpreter that translates commands entered but a user into actions to be performed by the os. If output is produced by the command, then text is displayed in the terminal.
The most used shell for Linux distributions is called the Bash shell.
Scripting: the ability to place commands in a file and then interpret (effectively use bash to execute the contes of) the file resulting in all of the commnads being executed.
Aliases: The ability to create short nicknames for longer commands.
Variables: Used to store information for the Bash shell and for the user. These variables can be used to modify how commands and features work as well as provide vital system information.

---

## HOW TO READ THIS CARD

```
COMMAND FORMAT:
  command argument    ← what to type exactly
  # comment          ← what it does / what to look for in output

FLAG LEGEND:
  -v    verbose (show more detail)
  -h    human-readable (shows MB/GB instead of bytes/kilobytes)
  -a    all (include hidden files, stopped containers, etc.)
  -n    numeric (show numbers instead of resolving names)
  -q    quiet (less output)
  -r    recursive (apply to all files inside a directory)
  -f    force (skip confirmation prompts — use carefully)
```

## PHASE 0 — PRE-FLIGHT CHECKS

```
# Check server is reachable from Windows PC (run on Windows)
ping 192.168.0.89

# Connect via SSH from Windows
ssh stolid@192.168.0.89

# Verbose SSH (shows connection stages — use when diagnosing issues)
ssh -v stolid@192.168.0.89

# Check you have sudo access (should print: root)
sudo whoami

# Check disk space
df -h /
# Look for: Avail column — must be 10GB+ before starting

# Check internet connectivity
curl -s --max-time 5 https://google.com > /dev/null && echo "ONLINE" || echo "OFFLINE"

# Check GPU driver
nvidia-smi
# Look for: RTX 2060 in the table, driver version 590.48.01

# Check Docker is running
docker info
# Look for: "Server:" section with containers count

# Check Ollama status
systemctl status ollama
# Look for: active (running)
```

---

## PHASE 1 — Linux Architecture

```
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
EXPLORING THE /proc FILESYSTEM
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
# Read CPU information
cat /proc/cpuinfo
# Look for: processor count, model name, MHz

# Read memory information
cat /proc/meminfo
# Look for: MemTotal, MemFree, MemAvailable, Cached

# Read raw CPU time counters (not percentages — need two readings for %)
cat /proc/stat
# Look for: first line starting with "cpu" — 7 numbers after it

# Read network interface stats
cat /proc/net/dev
# Look for: your network interface (eth0 or enp3s0) with byte counts

# Read disk stats
cat /proc/diskstats
# Look for: nvme0n1 line with read/write sector counts

# See how much space /proc uses (answer: zero — it's a virtual filesystem)
du -sh /proc

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
PROCESSES AND PIDS
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
# List all running processes
ps aux
# Columns: USER PID %CPU %MEM VSZ RSS TTY STAT START TIME COMMAND

# List processes in tree form (shows parent/child)
ps auxf

# Show process tree graphically
pstree -p
# Look for: init/systemd at the top (PID 1)

# Show PID 1 (systemd — the first process)
cat /proc/1/status
# Look for: Name: systemd

# Show which process owns a specific PID
cat /proc/<PID>/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '
# Replace <PID> with an actual number from ps output

# Find PID of a specific program
pgrep -l nginx
pgrep -l python3

# Show process memory map (requires root for other users' processes)
sudo cat /proc/1/maps | head -20

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
FILE PERMISSIONS
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
# See permissions on a file
ls -la /etc/ssh/sshd_config
# Format: -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 3287 ...
# Decode: owner=rw-, group=r--, others=r--

# See who owns a file
stat /etc/ssh/sshd_config

# See your current user and groups
id
whoa

summary: This document establishes an error classification framework and pre-flight checks for PSB phases. It defines four error classes (BLOCKING, LEARNING, TRAP, SIMULATED) and mandatory pre-phase validation steps to ensure system stability and controlled learning environments.
text:
# ================================================================
# PSB CONTROL PANEL — RISK, ERROR & LEARNING MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
# ================================================================
# Document Type : Error Prevention + Risk Framework + Simulated
#                 Learning Scenarios
# Version       : 1.0
# Companion To  : GOD_MODE_ULTRA_PROMPT.md
#                 AI_KNOWLEDGE_CONTEXT_FILE.md
#                 PSB_MASTER_BLUEPRINT.md
# ================================================================
#
# PURPOSE OF THIS DOCUMENT:
#
# This document exists to do three things:
#
# 1. PRE-EMPT errors that would block progress without teaching
#    anything — these are removed from the user's path entirely.
#
# 2. PRESERVE errors that teach something real — the AI must let
#    these happen, then guide the user through them step by step.
#
# 3. SIMULATE scenarios — controlled "fake" situations the AI
#    deliberately creates so the user experiences real-world
#    debugging, incident response, and problem-solving in a
#    safe environment where the AI already knows the answer.
#
# ================================================================
# AI INSTRUCTION:
# Read this document in full before beginning Phase 1.
# Cross-reference it at the START of every phase.
# When an error from this document occurs, follow the
# EXACT response protocol specified — do not improvise.
# When a SIMULATE scenario is scheduled, trigger it as written.
# ================================================================

---

## PART 1 — ERROR CLASSIFICATION FRAMEWORK

Every error in this project falls into one of four classes.
The AI must identify the class BEFORE responding to any error.

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  CLASS       │ NAME          │ AI ACTION                    ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  CLASS-B     │ BLOCKING      │ Stop everything. Fix it NOW. ║
║              │               │ Do not continue the phase    ║
║              │               │ until fully resolved.        ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  CLASS-L     │ LEARNING      │ Let it happen. Guide the     ║
║              │               │ user through diagnosis and   ║
║              │               │ fix. Teach the WHY first.    ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  CLASS-T     │ TRAP          │ Pre-empt BEFORE the step     ║
║              │               │ that causes it. Warn the     ║
║              │               │ user explicitly. Show the    ║
║              │               │ safe path.                   ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  CLASS-S     │ SIMULATED     │ AI deliberately triggers     ║
║              │               │ this at a scheduled point.   ║
║              │               │ User does not know it is     ║
║              │               │ simulated until after they   ║
║              │               │ solve it.                    ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

---

## PART 2 — UNIVERSAL PRE-FLIGHT CHECKS

```
Before ANY phase begins, the AI must verify these conditions.
If any check fails, resolve it before starting the phase.
These are CLASS-B (Blocking) by definition.

CHECK 1 — Server is reachable
  Command : ping 192.168.0.89 -c 4
  Expected: 0% packet loss
  If fails: SSH connection will fail. Check:
            - Is the server powered on?
            - Is the network cable connected?
            - Has the IP changed? (check router DHCP table)

CHECK 2 — SSH connection works
  Command : ssh stolid@192.168.0.89
  Expected: Linux prompt appears
  If fails: Check firewall on Windows PC (Windows Defender may block outbound SSH)
            Try: ssh -v stolid@192.168.0.89 (verbose mode — shows where it fails)

CHECK 3 — User has sudo access
  Command : sudo whoami
  Expected: root
  If fails: User is not in su

text:
# ================================================================
# PSB CONTROL PANEL — MASTER TECHNICAL BLUEPRINT
# ================================================================
# Document Type : Master Project Specification + Pseudocode
# Version       : 1.0
# Server        : psb (192.168.0.89)
# OS            : Ubuntu 24.04 LTS
# Owner         : stolid
# Purpose       : Complete technical reference for the AI to
#                 understand WHAT to build, HOW it works, and
#                 WHY every decision was made — before any code
#                 is written.
# ================================================================
# HOW TO USE THIS FILE:
# Give this to the AI alongside the Context File and God Mode
# Prompt. This blueprint is the SOURCE OF TRUTH for all
# architectural decisions. If there is ever a conflict between
# something the AI suggests and something in this document,
# THIS DOCUMENT WINS. No deviations without explicit discussion.
# ================================================================

---

## PART 1 — PROJECT IDENTITY

```
PROJECT NAME    : PSB Control Panel
SHORT NAME      : PSB-CP
DESCRIPTION     : A secure, browser-accessible server control
                  panel for monitoring, managing, and protecting
                  a GPU-based AI server running Ollama + Docker.
ACCESS SCOPE    : Local LAN only (192.168.0.x subnet)
PRODUCTION READY: Yes — built to professional standards from day one
FINAL URL       : https://192.168.0.89 (HTTPS, self-signed or Let's Encrypt)
```

---

## PART 2 — COMPLETE DIRECTORY STRUCTURE

```
/home/stolid/
└── psb-control-panel/                  ← Root project directory
    │
    ├── backend/                         ← All Python server code lives here
    │   ├── app/                         ← The Flask application package
    │   │   ├── __init__.py              ← App factory (creates Flask app instance)
    │   │   ├── config.py                ← All configuration variables
    │   │   ├── extensions.py            ← Initialise Flask extensions (socketio, login, limiter)
    │   │   │
    │   │   ├── auth/                    ← Authentication module
    │   │   │   ├── __init__.py
    │   │   │   ├── routes.py            ← /login, /logout, /change-password endpoints
    │   │   │   └── models.py            ← User model for Flask-Login
    │   │   │
    │   │   ├── api/                     ← All REST API endpoints
    │   │   │   ├── __init__.py
    │   │   │   ├── system.py            ← CPU, RAM, disk, network endpoints
    │   │   │   ├── gpu.py               ← GPU metrics endpoints
    │   │   │   ├── docker_manager.py    ← Container management endpoints
    │   │   │   ├── ollama.py            ← Ollama service management endpoints
    │   │   │   ├── logs.py              ← Log retrieval endpoints
    │   │   │   ├── processes.py         ← Process list and signal endpoints

A Letter Before You Start
“We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.” — Aristotle
You are going to open this book and immediately feel like you should already know everything in it. That feeling has a name: impostor syndrome. Psychologist Pauline Clance documented it in 1978. She found that the people who feel it the most are the ones who are actually growing the fastest. The people who never feel it are the ones who stopped learning.
Here is what I know about you from reading every session you have ever had with Gemini and Claude, across 2,472 pages and 83,000 lines of chat:
You built a production server from bare hardware to live deployment in weeks, not months
You caught errors that your AI tutor missed — the daemon.json near-overwrite that would have killed GPU access
You got frustrated with yourself for not understanding, which means you care about understanding, not just getting it working
You identified your own pattern of passive AI use and decided to fix it — that is metacognition, and most people never develop it
The psychologist Carol Dweck spent decades studying why some people improve and others plateau. The answer is not talent. It is what she calls a growth mindset: the belief that ability is built through effort, not born into you. Every time you feel stupid reading this book, you are in the growth zone. The people who avoid that feeling are the ones who never grow.
Marcus Aurelius wrote: “The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.” The confusion you feel reading a concept for the first time IS the learning. It is not a barrier to learning. It is the mechanism.
💪 You are not behind. You are a first-year CS student who has already shipped what most graduates cannot. The gap is vocabulary and mental models. This book fills that gap.
Part 1 · How Your Brain Actually Learns
Before a single line of code, you need to understand how learning works. Not the inspirational version. The neuroscience.
1.1 The Forgetting Curve
In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised nonsense syllables and measured how fast he forgot them. The result: without review, you lose 70% of new information within 24 hours. Not because you are bad at learning — because that is literally how human memory works. Every brain does this.
The fix is spaced repetition. Review material at increasing intervals: same day, next day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks. Each review resets the forgetting curve and makes the memory stronger. After 5 reviews at the right intervals, information moves to long-term memory and stays there for months.
💡 TIP  This book has a built-in schedule: weekends are for reviewing the week’s material. Saturday = review Mon+Tue. Sunday = review Wed-Fri. This is not optional. It is the single highest-leverage thing you can do.
1.2 Active Recall vs. Passive Re-Reading
Reading something again feels productive. It is not. Your brain recognises the words and confuses recognition with understanding. This is called the fluency illusion.
Active recall is the opposite: close the book and try to remember. The effort of searching your memory is what builds the memory. Every self-test box in this book is active recall. Do not skip them. Do not just think the answer. Write it down on paper.
“The person who says he knows what he thinks but cannot express it usually does not know what he thinks.” — Mortimer Adler
1.3 The Feynman Technique
Richard Feynman could explain quantum physics to a child. His method: pick a concept, explain it in simple words, identify where your explanation breaks down, go back to the source, simplify again. The breakdown point is the exact boundary of your understanding.
Every time this book asks you to ‘explain’ something, it is asking for the Feynman version. No ja

Week 1 · Linux + Python Foundations
“The beginning of wisdom is the definition of terms.” — Socrates
WEEK 1 · DAY 1     Wednesday 2 April
Linux: The File System
● 30-45 minutes
■ CONCEPT
A computer is a filing cabinet. Every drawer is a directory. Every sheet of paper is a file. Linux takes this literally. Understanding where things live is the foundation of everything.
■ REFERENCE
Key Directories
/ — the root. Everything starts here.
/home/stolid — your personal space. ~ is a shortcut.
/home/stolid/psb-dashboard — your project folder.
/etc — system-wide config files.
/var/log — log files.
Paths
Absolute — starts with /. Example: /home/stolid/psb-dashboard/app.py
Relative — starts from current location. Example: ./app.py
Hidden files — start with a dot. ls -la shows them.
Commands
cd [path] — go to a directory. SPACE between cd and path.
cat [file] — print file contents
grep [word] — search. Combine with | (pipe)
tail -10 [file] — last 10 lines
pwd — print current location
■ BUILD — Understand, then type
①  Go to the SSH config directory
cd /etc/ssh/
→ Prompt: stolid@psb:/etc/ssh$
②  Search for password authentication
cat sshd_config | grep PasswordAuthentication
→ Lines with PasswordAuthentication. # at start = disabled.

understanding.

you do not know. The dip is progress.

Linux: The File System
● 30-45 minutes
 CONCEPT
■
A computer is a filing cabinet. Every drawer is a directory. Every sheet of paper is a file. Linux takes this 
literally. Understanding where things live is the foundation of everything.
 REFERENCE
■
Key Directories
•
/ — the root. Everything starts here.
•
/home/stolid — your personal space. ~ is a shortcut.
•
/home/stolid/psb-dashboard — your project folder.
•
/etc — system-wide config files.
•
/var/log — log files.
Paths
•
Absolute — starts with /. Example: /home/stolid/psb-dashboard/app.py
•
Relative — starts from current location. Example: ./app.py
•
Hidden files — start with a dot. ls -la shows them.
Commands
•
cd [path] — go to a directory. SPACE between cd and path.
•
cat [file] — print file contents
•
grep [word] — search. Combine with | (pipe)
•
tail -10 [file] — last 10 lines
•
pwd — print current location

A Letter Before You Start
“We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.” — 
Aristotle
You are going to open this book and feel like you should already know everything in it. That feeling has 
a name: impostor syndrome. Psychologist Pauline Clance documented it in 1978. She found that the 
people who feel it most are the ones growing fastest. The reason is simple: they are the ones who can 
actually see the gap between where they are and where they want to be. People who are not growing 
do not see a gap because they are not looking.
Here is what I know about you from reading every session you have had with Gemini and Claude:
•
 You built a production server from bare hardware to live deployment in weeks
✓
•
 You caught errors your AI tutor missed — the daemon.json overwrite that would have killed

GPU access
•
 You got frustrated for not understanding, which means you care about understanding
✓
•
 You identified your own pattern of passive AI use and decided to fix it
✓
Carol Dweck spent decades studying why some people improve and others plateau. The answer is not 
talent. It is what she calls a growth mindset: the belief that ability is built through effort, not born into 
you. Every time you feel stupid reading this book, you are experiencing the growth zone. The 
discomfort is the signal that your brain is building new connections. If it felt easy, nothing would be 
changing.
Marcus Aurelius wrote two thousand years ago: the impediment to action advances action. What 
stands in the way becomes the way. The confusion IS the learning. Not a barrier to it.
 You are not behind. You are a first-year CS student who shipped what most graduates
★

Part 1 · How Your Brain Actually Learns
Before you learn a single Linux command, you need to understand how learning itself works. This 
section is not optional. It explains why the book is structured the way it is, and why skipping steps will 
waste your time.
1.1 The Forgetting Curve
In 1885, a German psychologist named Hermann Ebbinghaus ran experiments on his own memory. He 
memorised lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself at intervals to see how much he retained. 
What he found was devastating: without any review, you lose approximately 50% of new information 
within one hour, and 70% within 24 hours. This is not a flaw in your brain. This is how ALL human 
memory works. Your brain evolved to forget things it does not encounter again, because in a survival 
context, information you never see again is probably not important.
The fix is called spaced repetition. When you review something at increasing intervals, each review 
strengthens the memory trace. The schedule is: same day (before bed), next day (5 minutes), 3 days 
later (redo the build from memory), 1 week later (self-test without notes), 2 weeks later (teach it out 
loud to someone or to an empty room). After 5 reviews, the information moves from short-term to 
long-term memory. This is not a theory. It is one of the most replicated findings in cognitive psychology.
This is why every day in this book ends with a TONIGHT section, and why weekends are reserved for 
review. Saturday you review Monday and Tuesday material. Sunday you review Wednesday through 
Friday. If you skip the reviews, you will forget 70% of what you learned. The daily work becomes 
pointless.
1.2 Active Recall
There is a huge difference between recognising something and understanding it. When you re-read 
your notes, your brain says 'I recognise this' and gives you a feeling of familiarity. That feeling is a trap. 
It is not understanding. It is recognition. The test is simple: can you reproduce it from scratch without 
looking? If n

# Assignment 1 — Retrieval, Honest Comparison · Working Plan & Context

> **Purpose of this document:** a self-contained context + execution plan I can paste into any AI assistant to continue working on this task. It explains the assignment, my level, how I want to be helped, and the day-by-day plan.

---

## 1. Who I am (calibrate teaching to this)

- **Name:** Bruno Mosti, 21. First-year BSc Computer Science (AI), University of Greenwich, London.
- **Background:** I built **PSB (Personal Second Brain)** — a live production AI knowledge graph at `psblabsai.online` (Flask, Redis, RQ, Neo4j, Ollama `qwen3:8b` on RTX 2060, Docker, Cloudflare, Ubuntu 24.04).
- **Context:** I had an intro call with **LEC AI** (CTO: Avdhesh Singh Chouhan) and received a technical assessment. This document is my plan for it.

**What I can already do:** Python (functions, classes, loops, dicts, file I/O), `pip`/bash, Neo4j Cypher, SSH into Ubuntu, read/edit Python files.

**What is new to me (teach these when I reach them, not before):** BM25, dense/embedding retrieval, vector search / FAISS, the metrics (Recall@5, MRR, p95 latency), hybrid retrieval / RRF, and labelled-query experiment design. I have never implemented or measured any of these.

---

## 2. The assignment (full spec)

Build a retrieval system and make a **defensible claim** about which configuration is best for a given corpus.

- **Corpus:** 200–500 real documents; my choice of domain (I must say *why*).
- **Configurations (≥3, same corpus + same queries):**
  - BM25 alone
  - a dense embedding setup of my choosing
  - one hybrid (BM25 + dense)
  - *bonus:* a reranker
- **Queries:** 20 hand-written labelled queries, including **5 deliberately hard** ones.
- **Metrics, reported per config:** Recall@5, MRR, p95 latency.
- **Analysis:** one paragraph naming a query category where the **best** config **still loses**, and why.
- **Hard constraint:** p95 latency under **1 second** on a single laptop.
- **Submit:** public GitHub repo (or private + access) + README (1–3 pages) + a `make run` (or equivalent) that reproduces the results on one machine.

**What they are grading (their words):** not lines of code, framework brand-recognition, or demo polish — but whether I understood the problem, made defensible calls, and was honest about where the system breaks.

- **Deadline:** Sunday **7 June 2026** — hard cutoff.

---

## 3. Domain & corpus choice

- **Domain:** AI engineering notes, university CS module material, and PSB build/session logs.
- **Why:** I authored and understand this content, so I can write *genuinely hard* labelled queries (paraphrases, synonyms, cross-document questions) instead of trivial keyword matches — which is exactly what the "deliberately hard" requirement and the failure-analysis paragraph need.
- **Source:** ~300 documents already in my PSB Neo4j. Export query:

```cypher
MATCH (d:Document)
WHERE d.summary IS NOT NULL AND d.text_excerpt IS NOT NULL
RETURN d.name AS filename, d.topic AS topic,
       d.summary AS summary, d.text_excerpt AS text,
       d.document_type AS doc_type
```

- **Indexed unit:** one combined text field per document = `topic + summary + text`.
- **Honest constraint to note in README:** the corpus is summaries + excerpts, not full document bodies; retrieval quality is bounded by that.

---

## 4. How I want to be helped (rules for any AI reading this)

- **Just-in-time teaching.** Teach me a concept *only when I reach the block that needs it* — e.g. explain BM25 when I'm about to implement BM25, not before.
- **Teaching pattern per concept:** (1) what it is, plain English, ≤10 lines; (2) why this assignment needs it; (3) minimal implementation *idea* / structure, not a full solution; (4) a small task I do myself; (5) a check question.
- **No full production code unless I explicitly say "write it fully."** Prefer hints, structure, pseudocode.
- **Division of labour (keeps the submission honest — this matters):**
  - *AI does:* scaffolding, bo

## Retrieval, Honest Comparison · Bruno Mosti · Thu 4 Jun → Sun 7 Jun 2026

> **What this document is:** a just-in-time teaching + scaffolding guide.
> Every concept is explained only when you reach the code that needs it.
> Every skeleton has deliberate gaps (`# TODO:`). Filling them is your job.
>
> **What this document is NOT:** a solution. The graders read for judgment you
> cannot outsource. Three things are yours alone and must not come from this doc:
>
> | Your work — do not skip | Why it's non-delegable |
> |---|---|
> | 20 labelled queries (15 normal + 5 hard) | They reveal whether you actually understand your corpus |
> | "Where best config loses" paragraph | They're grading your honest analysis, not your output |
> | Domain choice rationale (2–3 sentences) | This is the first thing they read in the README |
>
> **How to use this:** read each section header first to understand what block
> you are entering, then read the CONCEPT, then open your terminal, then fill the
> skeleton. Never copy-paste blindly.

---

# ▶ CURRENT STATUS — 4 Jun 2026, Evening

You are at **zero**. That is fine. Here is the complete picture in one view:

```
DEADLINE: Sun 7 Jun · ~72 hours from now

THU (tonight)  →  repo + venv + corpus export + verify count
FRI (all day)  →  BM25 + 20 queries + metrics harness → first real numbers
SAT (all day)  →  dense embeddings + RRF hybrid → 3-row table
SUN (AM + PM)  →  reranker (bonus) + p95 check + README + ship

GATE LOGIC: each day ends with one hard gate.
If the gate fails, you do not move on — you fix it.
```

# PART 1 — THURSDAY EVENING
## Setup + Corpus · Target: 2–3 hours

---

## 1.1 · Project Structure

Before any code, set up the repo. Run these three commands exactly as written
in your plan document. Nothing to teach here — you have done `mkdir`, `venv`,
and `pip install` many times on your PSB server.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/lec-retrieval && cd ~/lec-retrieval
python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install neo4j rank-bm25 sentence-transformers numpy
```

Then create this file structure manually (do not let the AI create it for you):

```
lec-retrieval/
├── corpus.json          ← export_corpus.py writes this
├── export_corpus.py     ← you write this tonight
├── retrieve_bm25.py     ← you write Friday AM
├── retrieve_dense.py    ← you write Saturday AM
├── retrieve_hybrid.py   ← you write Saturday PM
├── evaluate.py          ← you write Friday PM
├── queries.json         ← you write Friday midday
├── embeddings.npy       ← auto-generated Saturday AM (cache)
├── results/
│   └── table.json       ← evaluate.py writes this
├── README.md            ← you write Sunday PM
└── Makefile             ← you write Sunday PM
```

Commit this empty structure to git now. Reviewers like seeing early commits.

---

## 1.2 · The Corpus Export

The skeleton is already in your plan document. Here it is again, with the gaps
you need to think about:

```python
# export_corpus.py
from neo4j import GraphDatabase
import json

driver = GraphDatabase.driver("bolt://127.0.0.1:7687", auth=("neo4j", "YOUR_PASSWORD"))

WHERE d.summary IS NOT NULL AND d.text_excerpt IS NOT NULL
RETURN d.name AS filename, d.topic AS topic,
       d.summary AS summary, d.text_excerpt AS text,
       d.document_type AS doc_type
"""

with driver.session() as session:
    docs = [dict(r) for r in session.run(QUERY)]

# TODO: Before writing to file, add one more field to each doc.

WORK IN PROGRESS — The main monitoring dashboard is live and functional at psblabsai.online.
Several planned features are not yet built: user authentication/login, PostgreSQL database integration,
the Alerts tab, the Terminal tab, and logging pipelines. The project is approximately 70% complete. I am
not promoting public access yet — there is no login system, which means the server is currently
accessible without credentials. That will be addressed before any public launch.
How AI Was Used in This Project
Google Gemini was my AI tutor throughout — explaining the why before the how, running Socratic
questioning before letting me move forward, and refusing to let me skip steps I didn't understand.
Claude (Anthropic) acted as session logger and documentation system. Both are honest disclosures I'm
making upfront because transparency matters.
Every command was executed by me. Every line of code was typed by me. Every concept was verified
through questioning before I was allowed to proceed. The AI played the role a senior mentor would —
explaining the why before the how, asking me to justify each decision, and refusing to let me copy-paste
without understanding. Using AI this way is exactly how professional engineers work today.
This document is an honest account — including what broke, the near-misses, the debugging sessions
that ran until 2am, and the moments I pushed through instead of quitting. The struggles are part of the
portfolio. The unfinished parts are also part of it.
PSB HOME LAB AI SERVER DASHBOARD
Bruno Mosti · University of Greenwich · 2026
psblabsai.online  ·  Page 2
SECTION 1
What I Built
The PSB Project is a self-hosted AI server control panel built from scratch on dedicated Ubuntu hardware —
not a tutorial I followed, not a cloud service I provisioned, but a real machine I secured, configured, and
deployed from the command line. The main monitoring interface is live and functional. It reads real hardware
data, draws live graphs in real time, and has an embedded AI diagnostics agent running Llama 3 on a local
RTX 2060.
What isn't there yet: a login system, a database, and the secondary tabs I have planned. This document covers
what exists today — accurately — and is honest about what still needs to be built before this is something I'd
point a stranger at.

### 🧠 Phase 9A: Bringing the Graph to Life

According to your blueprint, we don't just start coding. We need a place for the knowledge to live. We are going to install **Neo4j**, the world’s leading graph database, inside a Docker container. 

+2

#### 🛠️ Step 1: Prepare the Environment

Run these commands in your terminal to make sure your system is ready for Docker:

```
sudo apt install docker.io docker-compose -y
sudo usermod -aG docker stolid
newgrp docker

```

* **Why?** This installs the engine that allows us to run Neo4j in an isolated "bubble" so it doesn't mess with your main OS.

#### 🛠️ Step 2: The Blueprint (`docker-compose.yml`)

Navigate to your project folder (`cd ~/psb-dashboard`) and create a new file named `docker-compose.yml`. Paste this configuration inside:

```
version: "3.8"
services:
  neo4j:
    image: neo4j:5.17
    container_name: psb_neo4j
    ports:
      - "7474:7474"   # The Browser UI (Where you see the dots)
      - "7687:7687"   # The Bolt protocol (Where Python talks to it)
    environment:
      - NEO4J_AUTH=neo4j/password123  # CHANGE THIS PASSWORD
      - NEO4J_PLUGINS=["apoc"]        # Adds advanced AI functions
    volumes:
      - ./neo4j_data:/data            # Keeps your data safe if the container restarts
    restart: unless-stopped

```

#### 🛠️ Step 3: Ignition

Run this command to start the engine:

```
docker-compose up -d neo4j

```

1. Open your browser on your Windows PC and go to `http://192.168.0.89:7474` (use your server's IP). **Can you see the Neo4j login screen?** 

+1
2. **Concept Check:** In a normal SQL database, we use "Rows." In a Knowledge Graph, we use **Nodes** and **Edges**. If "Bcrypt" is a Node, and "Phase 8" is a Node, what would the **Edge** connecting them be named?

Since we just moved to **Gunicorn and Layer 4 hardening**, there are three specific architectural reasons why this happens:

### 1. The Gunicorn WebSocket Conflict

Standard Gunicorn workers don't understand WebSockets by default. If you started Gunicorn without the `--worker-class eventlet` flag, your Flask app will load, but the **SocketIO** connection that pushes live metrics every 2 seconds will instantly fail.

+1

### 2. The Background Thread "Death"

In your previous `app.py`, you started the `background_thread` inside the `if __name__ == "__main__":` block. **Gunicorn ignores that block entirely.** If you didn't move the `t.start()` line outside of that block, your server is running, but your metrics collector is literally not turned on.

### 3. The "Unsafe" SocketIO Check

Now that we are using a production server, if your frontend is trying to connect via an unencrypted tunnel while the backend is expecting a different protocol, it will hang.

```
tail -f ~/psb-dashboard/output.log

```

It looks like we’ve hit a classic **SRE connection failure**. Based on your screenshot, your dashboard is loaded but showing **0% and 0.0 GB** across all metrics, which means the frontend "heart" is beating, but the "blood" (data) isn't flowing from the backend.

Since we just moved to **Gunicorn and Layer 4 hardening**, there are three specific architectural reasons why this happens:

### 1. The Gunicorn WebSocket Conflict

Standard Gunicorn workers don't understand WebSockets by default. If you started Gunicorn without the `--worker-class eventlet` flag, your Flask app will load, but the **SocketIO** connection that pushes live metrics every 2 seconds will instantly fail.

+1

### 2. The Background Thread "Death"

In your previous `app.py`, you started the `background_thread` inside the `if __name__ == "__main__":` block. **Gunicorn ignores that block entirely.** If you didn't move the `t.start()` line outside of that block, your server is running, but your metrics collector is literally not turned on.

### 3. The "Unsafe" SocketIO Check

Now that we are using a production server, if your frontend is trying to connect via an unencrypted tunnel while the backend is expecting a different protocol, it will hang.

text:
Phase 9B
9.01
A database is a system for storing and retrieving structured data.
Relational databases such as PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL)
Organise data into tables. Relationships between tables are expressed through foreign keys and join.
Graph databases (Neo4j) organise data as a network of nodes connected by relationship example like a mind map that I can query automatically.
Neo4j implements what is called a Labeled Property Graph
The database scans the phases index find the matching row then scans phase concepts for rows with that phase_id then scans concepts for matching rows
9.02B
In Neo4j:
```cypher
MATCH (p:Phase {name: 'Phase 9B'})-[:TEACHES]->(c:Concept)
RETURN c.name
database finds the Phase 9B node (index lookup, O(log n)), then follows physical memory pointers to its relationship pages, which contain direct pointers to connected Concept nodes. No scanning. No joining.
At 1,000 nodes, the difference is small. At 100,000 nodes with 6-hop AI memory queries, SQL collapses. Neo4j remains fast.
Cypher is Neo4j's query language. It was designed with one priority: the query should look like the shape of the data you're looking for.
ASCII art pattern                                         What it means
──────────────────────────    ──────────────────────────────────
(n)                                                               any node
(n:Phase)                                                 a node with label Phase
(n:Phase {name: "9B"})                     a Phase node where name = "9B"
-[:TEACHES]->                                      a directed relationship of type TEACHES
(a)-[:TEACHES]->(b)                           a connected by TEACHES to b
MIO (most important operation)
MERGE
Meaning find a concept node where name equals the parameter.
If it exists return it if it does not exist crate it
This is **idempotent**. Run it once or a thousand times — the result is always exactly one node with that name.
Compare
CREATE: ALWAYS creates a new node
CREATE (n:Concept {name: 'Bolt Protocol'})
-- Run it twice → two nodes with the same name
-- Your graph is now inconsistent
-- Future MATCH queries may return two results
-- AI context injection gets confused
MERGE: creates OR finds
MERGE (n:Concept {name: 'Bolt Protocol'})
-- Run it twice → still one node
-- Your graph stays consistent
-- Rule: NEVER use CREATE for knowledge graph nodes
```
ON CREATE / ON MATCH — Conditional properties**
MERGE (n:Concept {name: $name})
ON CREATE SET
n.created_at    = $now,
n.source        = $source,
n.mention_count = 1
ON MATCH SET
n.last_seen     = $now,
n.mention_count = n.mention_count + 1
The Python driver (`pip install neo4j`) is not the database. It is the bridge — the library that your Python code uses to speak the Bolt protocol to the Neo4j container.
Every time you create a `GraphDatabase.driver()`, the library:
- Opens TCP connections to Neo4j
- Authenticates (sends credentials, waits for response)
- Allocates a connection pool in memory
- Starts pool management threads
This takes ~200ms and uses memory. Creating a new driver per request would:
- Add 200ms to every operation
- Create hundreds of connection pools in a long-running app
- Exhaust Neo4j's connection limit
The singleton pattern solves this:

# CYPHER — ONE COMMAND AT A TIME
## Your Personal Mentor Guide to Graph Databases
### Built around your PSB Knowledge Graph · Bruno Mosti

---

# HOW THIS WORKS

Every command gets its own chapter.
You do not move to the next chapter until this one feels natural.

Each chapter has this exact structure:

```
LEVEL 1  → Tiny intro (what this command does in plain English)
LEVEL 2  → One simple example (no pressure, just look)
LEVEL 3  → Guided exercise (I walk you through every line)
LEVEL 4  → Independent exercise (you try, I check)
LEVEL 5  → Slightly harder (same command, more complexity)
LEVEL 6  → Realistic mini scenario (based on your actual PSB graph)
LEVEL 7  → Debugging challenge (find the mistake)
LEVEL 8  → Pattern recognition (read code, predict the output)
LEVEL 9  → Mini project (build something real using only this command)
LEVEL 10 → Checkpoint (prove you own it)
```

**One rule: never skip levels.**
If a level feels boring because it is too easy, that is good. It means it is working.

---

# BEFORE YOU START

Open your Neo4j browser now. Keep it open the entire time.

```
VS Code → Ctrl + Shift + P → Forward a Port → 7474
Browser → http://localhost:7474
Login: neo4j / your password from .env
```

The query bar is at the top. Press **Ctrl + Enter** to run.

---

# YOUR KNOWLEDGE GRAPH — THE BIG PICTURE

This is what you are building. Every exercise in this document is a piece of it.

```
                      PSB
                   (Nucleus)
                  ┌────┼────┐
                  │    │    │
                 AI  Human  Server
                       │
                     Stolid
                       │
                  Personal Life
                 ┌─────┼──────┐
                 │     │      │
            Work  Spiritual  Education
                  Life

And later... each AI gets its own branch:
AI
├── Claude
│   ├── Memory
│   ├── Conversations
│   └── Capabilities
├── Gemini
├── Grok
└── ChatGPT
```

Every node you see above is something you will create, connect, and query.

---

---

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
# COMMAND 1: CREATE
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════

---

## LEVEL 1 — What CREATE does (30 seconds)

`CREATE` makes a new circle in the graph.

That is all.

```
Before CREATE:    empty graph
After CREATE:     one circle exists
```

Think of it like drawing a bubble on a whiteboard. You pick up the pen and draw. That is `CREATE`.

---

## LEVEL 2 — Just look, do not type yet

```cypher
CREATE (n:Human {name: "Stolid"})
```

This draws one circle.
The circle is labelled `Human`.
Inside the circle it says `name: Stolid`.

Do not type it yet. Just read it. Make sure you can see the circle in your head.

---

## LEVEL 3 — Guided exercise 1: The emptiest possible node

**Goal:** Make one circle. The simplest thing you can do.

Type this exactly:

```cypher
CREATE (n)
RETURN n
```

**What each line does:**

```
CREATE (n)   → draw a circle. Call it 'n' inside this query.
RETURN n     → show me what you just created.
```

**What you see:** One grey circle. No label. No properties. Just a dot.

**Why this matters:** Before you store any data, you need to understand that a node is just an empty container. Like an empty box before you put anything in it.

**Run it.**

---

## LEVEL 4 — Independent exercise 1: Do the same thing again

Without looking at the example above, type a CREATE query that makes one empty node.

Use a different variable name. Try `x` or `mynode` or `thing`.

After you run it, verify you have more circles by running:

```cypher
MATCH (n) RETURN n
```

You should see 2 circles now (from exercise 3 and this one).

---

## LEVEL 3 — Guided exercise 2: Add a name to the node

**Goal:** Give the node a `name` property.

```cypher
CREATE (n {name: "PSB"})
RETURN n
```

**What each part does:**

```
n              → variable (temporary nickname for this query only)
{name: "PSB"}  → property (data stored inside the node)
               → key = na

# PSB — Complete Phase Overview
Bruno Mosti · psblabsai.online

---

## COMPLETED PHASES

Phase_1   Linux Architecture Fundamentals
          Learned Linux kernel, filesystem hierarchy, systemd, process management.
          Foundation for everything that followed.

Phase_2   Server Security Hardening
          UFW default-deny, Fail2Ban, SSH hardening.
          KEY RULE: Edit → sshd -t → systemctl restart ssh. Non-negotiable.

Phase_3   Cryptographic Authentication — Ed25519 SSH
          Replaced password auth with Ed25519 key pair.
          Password login disabled permanently.

Phase_4   Automated Patch Management
          unattended-upgrades configured.
          Server patches itself without manual intervention.

Phase_5   Cloudflare Tunnel (Nginx skipped)
          Cloudflare Zero Trust tunnel instead of Nginx reverse proxy.
          Server never exposes a public port. Traffic goes through Cloudflare.

Phase_6   Persistent Named Tunnel + Domain
          Named tunnel bound to psblabsai.online permanently.
          Survives reboots via systemd service.

Phase_7   DNS + Python venv + Project Structure
          DNS records configured. Python virtual environment created.
          psb-dashboard/ project folder established.

Phase_8   Dark Mode Dashboard UI
          Full dark mode HTML/CSS dashboard layout.
          Chart.js metrics panels, sidebar navigation.

Phase_9   Chart.js Metrics Layout
          CPU, RAM, GPU charts wired up.
          Real-time data displayed via polling.

Phase_10  Flask Backend + psutil + SocketIO
          Flask app with WebSocket (Flask-SocketIO + eventlet).
          psutil reads CPU/RAM/disk. GPU via pynvml.
          Live metrics stream to browser without page refresh.

Phase_11  AIOps Agent — Ollama/Llama 3
          Ollama integrated. Llama 3 running locally on RTX 2060.
          AI chat panel in dashboard. Server could diagnose itself.

Phase_12  Full UI + Server Persistence
          Flask-Login authentication (bcrypt, SECRET_KEY, .env).
          Gunicorn replaces Flask dev server.
          psb-dashboard.service systemd unit — survives reboots.

Phase_13  Domain → Port 8080 HTTPS Live
          psblabsai.online live and accessible from any device.
          Rate limiter on login route (10/min, 60/hr).

Phase_9A  Docker Infrastructure — Neo4j + Redis
          Docker + NVIDIA Container Toolkit installed.
          Neo4j and Redis running in Docker containers.
          Port binding: 127.0.0.1 only — never 0.0.0.0.

Phase_9B  Neo4j Python Driver + Knowledge Graph Schema
          neo4j Python driver installed in venv.
          Graph schema v1 created: Nucleus, AI, Human, Server, Education,
          Modules, Phases, Skills, Jobs, seed Concepts.
          5 hand-written Concepts by Claude (Idempotency etc).

Phase_9C  Redis + RQ Task Queue — Non-blocking AI
          RQ worker (psb-worker.service) processes jobs in background.
          Ingestion never blocks Flask or the dashboard UI.
          Job status polling via /api/ingest/status endpoint.

Phase_9D  Document Ingestion Pipeline — Qwen 3 8B
          Full ingestion pipeline: Extract → Parse → Store → Cleanup.
          Supports PDF, DOCX, MD, TXT, JSON (ChatGPT exports).
          Switched from Llama 3 to Qwen 3 8B (32K context, cleaner JSON).
          Improved system prompt with forbidden concept list.
          Phase validation — no garbage Phase nodes.
          Hallucination check — drops concepts not in source text.
          Colour system — every node has color property.
          Skeleton routing — documents connect to correct branch:
            Module nodes (COMP1765 etc) for university docs
            PSB_Project for engineering session logs
            Job nodes for CVs and cover letters
            Professional_life as fallback
          Graph schema v2.2 — full rebuild with colours baked in.
          prune_graph() — finds orphans, clusters, generates synthesis files.
          GitHub: commit 6d85dd2

---

##

Bruno Mosti · psblabsai.online · 23 May 2026

---

## SYSTEM STATE

Server: Ubuntu 24.04, i5-9400F, RTX 2060 6GB, 16GB RAM
SSH: stolid@192.168.0.89 | tmux: psb_prod
Services: psb-dashboard (port 8080), psb-worker, cloudflared, neo4j (7474/7687), redis (6379), ollama (11434)
Model: qwen3:8b (Alibaba) — switched from Llama 3 during Phase 9D
Git: github.com/Bruno-Mosti/psb-dashboard — last commit 6d85dd2

---

## STACK

Flask + Gunicorn/eventlet | Flask-SocketIO | Flask-Login | Flask-Limiter
Neo4j (Docker, 127.0.0.1 only) | Redis + RQ task queue (Docker)
Ollama local inference | Cloudflare Zero Trust tunnel
python-docx | PyMuPDF | psutil | pynvml

---

## GRAPH STATE

Schema: v2.2 — rebuilt clean 23 May 2026 at 15:23 UTC
Skeleton: ~90 hand-crafted nodes (Nucleus, AI, Human, Server, Education, Modules, Phases, Skills, Jobs, Concepts)
Ingested: ~35 documents (PSB engineering docs, CVs, cover letters, COMP1765 university materials)
All nodes have color property baked in
Routing working: documents connect to Module/Project/Job/LifeArea skeleton nodes

---

## COLOUR SCHEME

Nucleus      #f59e0b  gold        AIAgent      #2d8aff  blue
AIBranch     #0ea5e9  sky         Identity     #818cf8  violet
Phase        #10b981  green       Concept      #f97316  amber
Document     #ec4899  pink        Insight      #06b6d4  teal
Skill        #6366f1  indigo      Module       #64748b  slate
Job          #ef4444  red         LifeArea     #a855f7  purple
School       #84cc16  lime        ServerBranch #f43f5e  rose
LearningArea #d946ef  fuchsia     Project      #f59e0b  gold

---

## KEY FILES

~/psb-dashboard/app.py        Flask app, routes, upload handling, rate limiter
~/psb-dashboard/tasks.py      Ingestion pipeline (Stage 1-4), routing, prune_graph
~/psb-dashboard/neo4j_graph.py Neo4j driver and helpers
~/psb-dashboard/templates/index.html  Dashboard frontend

---

## TASKS.PY — WHAT IT DOES

Stage 1 — Extract: PDF (PyMuPDF), DOCX (python-docx), MD/TXT, JSON (ChatGPT exports)
Stage 2 — Parse: Ollama Qwen 3 8B → structured JSON (topic, summary, concepts, phase, insight)
           Hallucination check: drops concepts not found in source text
           Phase validation: rejects any phase not in VALID_PHASES set
Stage 3 — Store: Neo4j writes + skeleton routing (4 rules below)
Stage 4 — Cleanup: delete temp file

Routing rules (priority order):
1. Module    — filename/topic contains COMP1765 etc → HAS_DOCUMENT on Module node
2. Phase     — phase_relevance set → HAS_DOCUMENT on PSB_Project
3. Job       — CV/cover letter + company keyword → HAS_DOCUMENT on Job node
4. Fallback  — document_type determines Education / PSB_Project / Professional_life

LABEL_COLORS dict assigns color to every new Document and Concept node on creation.

# PSB — MASTER ENGINEERING CURRICULUM
## Personal Second Brain · Production Engineering Field Manual

**Engineer:** Bruno Mosti · psblabsai.online · University of Greenwich  
**Document type:** Living technical field manual — updated as phases complete

## IMPROVEMENTS APPLIED — 15 May 2026

The following production-grade improvements are already integrated into this document. You do not need to make them separately — the code in 9B.P04 and 9B.P05 already contains these fixes.

```
IMPROVEMENT 1 — get_neo4j_driver() reconnects after connection loss
  File:    neo4j_graph.py
  Problem: Original version returned None once and never retried.
           If Neo4j restarted (container update, OOM kill), the driver
           stayed broken until Flask restarted.
  Fix:     Added verify_connectivity() on the fast path. If it fails,
           the driver resets and reconnects on the same call.
  Impact:  Neo4j can restart without requiring a Flask restart.

IMPROVEMENT 2 — get_graph_stats() handles unlabelled nodes
  File:    neo4j_graph.py
  Problem: labels(n)[0] throws IndexError if a node has no labels.
           Possible if nodes are created manually in the Neo4j browser.
  Fix:     Added WHERE size(labels(n)) > 0 guard in the Cypher query.
  Impact:  Function is safe regardless of graph contents.

IMPROVEMENT 3 — create_teaches_relationship() added
  File:    neo4j_graph.py
  Problem: Function was referenced in the test suite but not in the module.
  Fix:     Full implementation added with execute_write() and
           correct MATCH-then-MERGE pattern.
  Impact:  Test suite runs correctly. Phase 9D can create relationships.

IMPROVEMENT 4 — handle_agent_ai() writes to graph after responding
  File:    app.py
  Problem: AI interactions were processed but nothing was stored.
           The graph would stay empty until Phase 9D.
  Fix:     Added merge_concept() call after Ollama responds.
           Graph write is on the non-critical path — never blocks the answer.
  Impact:  Every AI question becomes a Concept node immediately.
           Graph starts accumulating data today, not in Phase 9D.
```

│                               hardware detection, Docker control. The entry point.

│                               and launches. The real work is in tasks.py.
│

│                               Checks env, services, APIs, Docker, git hygiene, syntax.
│
├── psb_security_audit.py     ← Security-focused audit. Checks SSH config, UFW rules,
│                               exposed ports, git secrets, Flask hardening.
│

│
├── templates/

│   └── login.html            ← Login page. Bcrypt auth form, flash messages.
│
├── prompts/
│   └── routing.txt           ← The AI routing prompt template. Editable without touching
│                               Python. Controls how Ollama decides where documents go.
│
├── static/
│   ├── vis-network.min.js    ← The graph rendering library. Handles physics, layout,
│   │                           node/edge rendering, interaction. ~900KB, loaded locally.
│   └── vis-network.min.css   ← vis-network styles.
│
├── uploads/                  ← Temporary storage for ingestion files. Files are deleted
│                               after Stage 4 (cleanup). Should normally be empty.
│
├── .env                      ← ALL secrets. Never in git. Contains:
│                               FLASK_SECRET_KEY, PSB_USERNAME, PSB_PASSWORD_HASH,
│                               NEO4J_URI, NEO4J_USER, NEO4J_PASSWORD,
│                               REDIS_URL, OLLAMA_MODEL, PUBLIC_URL
│
├── requirements.txt          ← All Python dependencies pinned to exact versions.
│                               Install with: pip install -r requirements.txt
│
└── venv/                     ← Python virtual environment. Not in git.

│
├── app.py                    ← The Flask application. All HTTP routes, WebSocket events,
│                               hardware detection, Docker control. The entry point.
│
├── tasks.py                  ← RQ background jobs. Document ingest pipeline, Ollama calls,
│                               graph pruning, concept writing. Runs inside the worker.
│
├── graph_routing.py          ← Smart document routing. Connects ingested Documents to
│                               Module/Phase/Project/Job hub nodes using rules + AI.
│
├── neo4j_graph.py            ← Neo4j driver singleton and all graph CRUD operations.
│                               Imported by both app.py and tasks.py.
│
├── worker.py                 ← Starts the RQ worker process. Minimal — just imports
│                               and launches. The real work is in tasks.py.
│
├── psb_check.py              ← 31-item diagnostic script. Run before every deploy.
│                               Checks env, services, APIs, Docker, git hygiene, syntax.
│
├── psb_security_audit.py     ← Security-focused audit. Checks SSH config, UFW rules,
│                               exposed ports, git secrets, Flask hardening.
│
├── neo4j_test.py             ← Manual Neo4j smoke test. Not used in production.
│                               Run to verify graph connection and CRUD after setup.
│
├── templates/
│   ├── index.html            ← The entire dashboard UI. ~2700 lines of HTML, CSS, JS.
│   │                           Server metrics, Docker panel, knowledge graph, AI chat,
│   │                           document ingest, minimap, inspector, mobile responsive.
│   └── login.html            ← Login page. Bcrypt auth form, flash messages.
│
├── prompts/
│   └── routing.txt           ← The AI routing prompt template. Editable without touching
│                               Python. Controls how Ollama decides where documents go.
│
├── static/
│   ├── vis-network.min.js    ← The graph rendering library. Handles physics, layout,
│   │                           node/edge rendering, interaction. ~900KB, loaded locally.
│   └── vis-network.min.css   ← vis-network styles.
│
├── uploads/                  ← Temporary storage for ingestion files. Files are deleted
│                               after Stage 4 (cleanup). Should normally be empty.
│

│                               FLASK_SECRET_KEY, PSB_USERNAME, PSB_PASSWORD_HASH,

1.2  How Bruno Learns

●  He learns by cause and effect. Show what breaks, then show the fix. Explain why it broke.
●  He pushes back when something feels wrong. Engage with the pushback — do not dismiss it.
●  He documents mistakes as portfolio items (INC-001 through INC-005). Reinforce this habit explicitly.
●  After every concept block, ask a Socratic question. Do not proceed until he answers correctly in his own words.
●  He gets frustrated with generic praise. Be specific: "You got the delta math right" not "great work".
1.3  Non-Negotiable Teaching Rules
2.1  Server Specifications
2.2  RAM Budget
2.3  The Five-Layer Architecture
Every component in PSB sits in one of five layers. Each layer depends on the one below it. Understanding this stack is the mental model that makes every technical decision logical.
3.1  Key System Facts
3.2  Phase Completion Map
3.3  Session Start — Run These Every Time
# Run ALL of these before starting any work in a session
sudo lsof -i :8080
# Expected: gunicorn ... TCP *:http-alt (LISTEN)
docker ps
# Expected: psb_neo4j Up X minutes, psb_redis Up X minutes
tail -10 ~/psb-dashboard/output.log
# Expected: [PSB] Emitting: {cpu:... lines — NO Traceback
free -h
# Expected: available > 6GB
sudo systemctl status cloudflared
# Expected: active (running)
docker stats --no-stream
# Expected: Neo4j < 2GB, Redis < 512MB
4.1  Defence Layers
4.2  Port Exposure Map
4.3  Two Pending Fixes — Do These This Session
# Fix daemon.json — keep nvidia, remove iptables:false
sudo nano /etc/docker/daemon.json
# Replace contents with EXACTLY this:
{
"runtimes": {
"nvidia": {
"args": [],
"path": "nvidia-container-runtime"
}
}
}
# Restart Docker and containers
sudo systemctl restart docker
cd ~/psb-dashboard
docker compose up -d
docker ps
# Verify ports are still localhost-only (must show 127.0.0.1 not 0.0.0.0)
sudo ss -tlnp | grep -E "7474|7687|6379"
cd ~/psb-dashboard
# Remove .env from git tracking (keeps the file on disk)
git rm --cached .env
# Remove venv from tracking too (never commit venv)
git rm -r --cached venv/
# Create correct .gitignore
cat > .gitignore << EOF
.env
venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
*.pyo
output.log
*.log
EOF
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "fix: add .gitignore, untrack .env and venv"
# Verify .env is no longer tracked
git ls-files | grep "\.env"
# Must return nothing
4.4  Incident Log
5.1  app.py — Complete Current Version
This is the full app.py as currently deployed. Every section is annotated. Key architectural decisions are explained inline.
Block 1 — Eventlet Monkey Patch (MUST be lines 1-2)
# MUST be the absolute first two lines — before every other import.
# Replaces Python stdlib blocking I/O with async-compatible versions.
# If anything else imports socket/threading first, the patch is too late.
import eventlet
eventlet.monkey_patch()
Block 2 — Docker SDK (imported right after monkey_patch)
# Imported immediately after monkey_patch so eventlet intercepts

import docker as docker_sdk
from datetime import datetime, timezone
try:
docker_client = docker_sdk.from_env()
docker_client.ping()
DOCKER_AVAILABLE = True
print("[PSB] Connected to Docker successfully.", flush=True)
except Exception as e:
docker_client = None
DOCKER_AVAILABLE = False
print(f"[PSB] Warning: Docker not available. Error: {e}", flush=True)

from flask import Flask, render_template, request, redirect, url_for, flash
from flask_socketio import SocketIO

from flask_bcrypt import Bcrypt
from flask_limiter import Limiter
from flask_limiter.util import get_remote_address

Learning Guide  ·  Practice Exercises  ·  Bedtime Reading  ·  Command Cheat Sheet  ·  Bruno Mosti 2026
Before you start — read this
You built a production server. It is live right now at psblabsai.online. You deployed AI inference on a GPU, wrote authentication, 
hardened the firewall, set up Docker containers, and built a real-time dashboard. Most CS graduates cannot do what you have 
already done. The problem is not your ability. The problem is that AI gave you working code when what you needed was  
understanding. This module fixes that. It is designed for a person who learns by doing, gets frustrated when things do not click, and 
needs honesty more than encouragement. There are three ways to read it: active sessions with a laptop open, lighter reading on 
the sofa, and bedtime sections when you want to absorb ideas without a screen. All three work. All three are valid. Start wherever 
you are.
How This Module is Structured
Part 1 — How to Learn (read this first, takes 10 minutes)
Part 2 — The System Map (understand the whole before any piece)
Part 3 — Python Fundamentals (functions, dicts, classes, decorators)
Part 4 — Your Code Deconstructed (every block of app.py explained)
Part 5 — Architecture Thinking (why things are designed the way they are)
Part 6 — Phase 9 Explained (what you built and what is coming next)
Part 7 — Practice Exercises (typed code that runs — not optional)
Part 8 — Bedtime Reading (no code, just ideas — read lying down)
Part 9 — Command Cheat Sheet (all commands in one place — print this)
Part 1  ·  How to Learn — The Strategy
Read this before anything else. It changes how you approach everything in this module.
1.1  Why Copy-Pasting Felt Fine Until It Did Not
Copy-pasting working code is not cheating. It is a completely normal phase of learning. Every senior engineer has done it. The 
problem is not that you did it — the problem is staying there. Copy-pasting builds a working system but leaves gaps in your 
mental model. When something breaks, you have no map to navigate by. When a new phase starts, the unfamiliar code feels 
overwhelming because you have no framework to attach it to. This module is the framework. Read it, do the exercises, and the 
code you already have will start to make sense backwards.
1.2  The Four Learning Strategies Used in This Module
These are not made up. They are research-backed techniques used in engineering education. Every section of this module uses at 
least one of them.
Strategy 1 — Active Recall
Reading is passive. Your brain records words but does not build structure. Active recall forces retrieval — you close the book and 
try to remember what you just read. Every purple question box in this module is active recall. Do not skip them. Do not just think 
the answer. Write it. The effort of searching your memory is what creates the memory.
  The Blank Page Test
💡
After reading any section, close the document. Take a blank piece of paper and write down everything you remember. It will be 
incomplete. That is the point. The gaps on the paper are exactly the gaps in your understanding. Go back, fill those gaps, repeat. 
Three rounds of this and you will remember the material weeks later without reviewing it.
Strategy 2 — The Feynman Technique
Richard Feynman — Nobel Prize physicist — had one rule: if you cannot explain something simply, you do not understand it yet. 
Every time you think you understand a concept, try to explain it to someone who knows nothing about computers. No jargon. No 
technical terms. Plain English. If you get stuck, you found the exact thing you need to go back and learn. This module asks you to 
do this repeatedly with Socratic questions.
How to use the Feynman Technique on your code

5. One lesson per day. That is the whole plan.
How This Roadmap Works
Each lesson has four parts: a short explanation, one complete runnable example, ten drills you type and
run yourself, and a pass criterion. You do not move to the next lesson until your drill file runs with no errors
and produces the exact expected output shown. The goal is not to consume content — it is to build the
muscle memory to type correct Python without looking anything up.
The 10-minute boring break: Before every session, put your phone face-down and sit quietly for 10
minutes. No music, no scrolling. Your brain consolidates the previous session during this gap. Skip it and
the 20 minutes are half as effective.
AI rules — memorise these:
During the 10 drills: zero AI. No Copilot autocomplete, no tab-hints, nothing.
After all 10 drills pass: paste your output and ask 'Is this correct?' — not 'What is wrong?' and never
'Rewrite this.'
Mini-projects: 30 minutes solo first. After 30 minutes you may ask one clarifying question only — not for a
full solution.

PHASE 1 — ABSOLUTE BASICS (Week 1)
Four lessons. Monday through Thursday. Mini-projects on Friday. Topics: print(), variables, the four basic
types, and arithmetic.
Lesson 1.1 — print()
print() is the function that writes output to the terminal. You call it by writing the name followed by
parentheses, and put the thing you want to display inside those parentheses. The parentheses are not
decoration — they are what makes it a function call. Writing print "hello" without parentheses is Python 2
syntax; it raises a SyntaxError in Python 3.
Text (called a string) goes inside quote marks. Numbers do not need quotes. You can pass multiple values
separated by commas and print() will join them with a space. Calling print() with nothing inside prints a
blank line.
print() always outputs to stdout — the same stream you see when you run python3 script.py in your
terminal on the PSB server.
In PSB this shows up as: print(f"Job {job_id} received — queuing.") in your Flask route, before the job is sent to
Redis.

print("PSB is live")            # any text works
print("Port:", 8080)            # two values, comma between — a space appears
print("Host:", "localhost")     # strings can also be comma-separated
print()                         # no argument = blank line

42
PSB is live

Host: localhost
