27 March 2026
Talent Acquisition Team
Arm Limited
Budapest Engineering Centre
Re: Software Engineer Summer Intern — Budapest
Dear Arm Recruitment Team,
I am applying for the Software Engineer Summer Intern position at your Budapest office. I am a first-year Computer Science (AI) student at the University of Greenwich — but the work that best represents my engineering capability is not an assignment. It is a production system I built from scratch, running 24 hours a day on dedicated server hardware in my home: an AI inference platform with live hardware telemetry, Docker-orchestrated services, hardened Linux security, and a real-time browser dashboard — all under the constraints of real hardware, real networking, and real failure modes.
Arm sits at the intersection of software and silicon — the space I find most compelling. The Arm architecture underpins the hardware decisions I make every day: when I allocate workloads between my i5 CPU and RTX 2060 GPU, when I tune Docker cgroup memory limits to respect a 16 GB DDR4 budget, when I analyse per-core CPU utilisation to separate AI inference from web-serving work. Understanding the processor makes you a better systems engineer. Working at Arm gives access to that understanding at the deepest possible level — in the people who design the cores, the compilers, and the performance tools. That is exactly where I want to develop.
The project I am most proud of — and which is live at psblabsai.online — is PSB (Personal Second Brain): a self-hosted AI infrastructure platform. Here is what it required:
▸  Hardware-constrained architecture: Llama 3 7B at 4-bit quantisation occupies 4.7 GB of a 6 GB VRAM budget. I designed every layer of the system around this fixed constraint — including a single-inference queue, VRAM-aware model lifecycle management, and CPU-offloaded orchestration.
▸  Linux systems depth: Ubuntu 24.04 headless, managed entirely over SSH. Ed25519 key authentication, UFW default-deny firewall, Fail2Ban intrusion detection, Cloudflare Zero Trust access gateway, and a formal SRE protocol (edit → syntax test → restart) that I developed after two near-miss incidents.
▸  Concurrent systems design: The dashboard uses Flask-SocketIO with an eventlet green thread worker — a concurrency model requiring careful understanding of cooperative scheduling, monkey-patching, and the reason a single Gunicorn worker is a correctness requirement, not a performance choice.
▸  Container infrastructure: Docker with enforced cgroup memory limits, bridge networking, named volume persistence, and restart policies. I understand containers as kernel primitives (namespaces + cgroups), not just abstracted services.
▸  Real-time data pipeline: A background thread collects six hardware metrics every 2 seconds via /proc interfaces and broadcasts them over WebSocket — applying delta mathematics to calculate network and disk throughput rates from cumulative kernel counters.
I bring the instincts of someone who has debugged live infrastructure — not simulated problems. I document my mistakes (five incidents, each with root cause analysis and formalised corrective protocols). I read the kernel documentation, not just the stack overflow answer. And I build things that continue running after I close the laptop.
I am fully prepared to relocate to Budapest for the placement. As an Italian national (EU citizen) I have the right to work in Hungary without restriction. I am genuinely excited by the possibility of contributing to engineering work at Arm — and I am ready to learn from engineers who build the foundation that every device in the world runs on.
My live system is publicly accessible at psblabsai.online if you would like to see the dashboard in operation. My CV and GitHub (github.com/brunomosti) provide further technical detail.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to discussing this opportun

The project I am most proud of — and which is live at psblabsai.online — is PSB (Personal Second Brain): a self-hosted AI infrastructure platform. Here is what it required:
▸  Hardware-constrained architecture: Llama 3 7B at 4-bit quantisation occupies 4.7 GB of a 6 GB VRAM budget. I designed every layer of the system around this fixed constraint — including a single-inference queue, VRAM-aware model lifecycle management, and CPU-offloaded orchestration.
▸  Linux systems depth: Ubuntu 24.04 headless, managed entirely over SSH. Ed25519 key authentication, UFW default-deny firewall, Fail2Ban intrusion detection, Cloudflare Zero Trust access gateway, and a formal SRE protocol (edit → syntax test → restart) that I developed after two near-miss incidents.
▸  Concurrent systems design: The dashboard uses Flask-SocketIO with an eventlet green thread worker — a concurrency model requiring careful understanding of cooperative scheduling, monkey-patching, and the reason a single Gunicorn worker is a correctness requirement, not a performance choice.
▸  Container infrastructure: Docker with enforced cgroup memory limits, bridge networking, named volume persistence, and restart policies. I understand containers as kernel primitives (namespaces + cgroups), not just abstracted services.
▸  Real-time data pipeline: A background thread collects six hardware metrics every 2 seconds via /proc interfaces and broadcasts them over WebSocket — applying delta mathematics to calculate network and disk throughput rates from cumulative kernel counters.
I bring the instincts of someone who has debugged live infrastructure — not simulated problems. I document my mistakes (five incidents, each with root cause analysis and formalised corrective protocols). I read the kernel documentation, not just the stack overflow answer. And I build things that continue running after I close the laptop.
I am fully prepared to relocate to Budapest for the placement. As an Italian national (EU citizen) I have the right to work in Hungary without restriction. I am genuinely excited by the possibility of contributing to engineering work at Arm — and I am ready to learn from engineers who build the foundation that every device in the world runs on.
My live system is publicly accessible at psblabsai.online if you would like to see the dashboard in operation. My CV and GitHub (github.com/brunomosti) provide further technical detail.

text:
Bruno Mosti
brunomosti.24@gmail.com  |  07401 055101  |  London, UK
March 2026
Hiring Team
G-Research — AI Engineering Intern
I am writing to apply for the AI Engineering Intern role within G-Research’s Core AI team. The description of building the infrastructure that lets researchers deploy AI solutions safely and at speed is exactly the kind of work I have been teaching myself to do — not in a classroom, but on real hardware.
Over the past months I have built a private AI server from scratch on a machine I reassembled myself: an i5-9400F with an RTX 2060, running Ubuntu Server 24.04 headless. I configured the full security stack — UFW with a default-deny policy, Fail2Ban watching auth.log in real time, Ed25519 SSH key authentication with password auth disabled entirely — and deployed Ollama to run local LLM inference directly on the GPU. I then set up a Cloudflare Tunnel to expose the server securely to the public internet without touching the home router, and acquired and wired a domain through Cloudflare’s Zero Trust platform. Every layer was chosen deliberately, and I can explain why each piece exists.
What excites me about G-Research’s Core AI team specifically is the scope: GPU clusters, LLM orchestration, RAG pipelines, and platform services that the rest of the firm depends on. I do not have production experience with LangGraph or Pydantic yet, and I am honest about that. But I understand the infrastructure layer those tools sit on: containerisation, service isolation, network security, and how to keep a service alive under load. I am actively learning FastAPI and I am comfortable in Python. C# is new to me, but picking up a language has never been what separates people in this field — understanding systems has.
Outside the server project I am studying Computer Science at the University of Greenwich, and I previously worked as an Assistant Digital Marketing Coordinator tracking engagement metrics and as a Court Hearing Assistant, where precision and calm under pressure were not optional.
I am available for both the March and June start dates and can work fully on-site in London. I would welcome the opportunity to talk through the role in more detail.
Yours sincerely,
Bruno Mosti

summary: A tutorial detailing code audits, critical bug fixes, and improvements for Bruno's Flask-SocketIO dashboard, focusing on port configuration, async_mode settings, and XSS prevention.
text: PSB Dashboard — Phase 7 Gemini Teaching Brief: Code Audit, Bug Fixes & Step-by-Step Guide March 2026 | Prepared by Claude | For: Gemini AI Tutor 1. What Bruno Has Built Bruno independently produced a working two-file Flask-SocketIO dashboard. The architecture is correct and the overall approach is sound. The code was written by Gemini guiding Bruno step by step, and Bruno typed it himself. File structure ~/psb-dashboard/ app.py <- Flask + SocketIO backend templates/index.html <- Frontend: Chart.js + Socket.IO venv/ <- Python quarantine zone 2. Bugs Found — Audit Results Five bugs were identified. Two are critical (the app will not work without fixing them). Three are moderate. BUG 1 — CRITICAL: Port mismatch Location — app.py, last line The backend runs on port 5000. The Cloudflare tunnel is wired to port 8080. These two numbers must match or the site returns a connection error to every visitor. # WRONG socketio.run(app, host='0.0.0.0', port=5000, allow_unsafe_werkzeug=True) # CORRECT socketio.run(app, host='0.0.0.0', port=8080, allow_unsafe_werkzeug=True) BUG 2 — CRITICAL: SocketIO async_mode not set Location — app.py, SocketIO initialisation Without async_mode="threading", the background thread and the web server fight over the same event loop, causing random freezes and dropped WebSocket connections. # WRONG socketio = SocketIO(app, cors_allowed_origins="*") # CORRECT socketio = SocketIO(app, cors_allowed_origins="*", async_mode="threading") BUG 3 — MODERATE: Temperature sensor is fragile Location — app.py, background_thread(), temperature block The original code grabs the very first sensor family. On some Ubuntu configurations this returns the wrong sensor or crashes with IndexError. The fix tries coretemp first (Intel), falls back gracefully. # WRONG — grabs first sensor blindly temp_val = round(list(temps.values())[0][0].current) # CORRECT — checks sensor families by name for name in ('coretemp', 'k10temp', 'acpitz'): if name in sensors and sensors[name]: temp_val = round(sensors[name][0].current); break BUG 4 — MODERATE: Chart.js CDN source Location — index.html, The original HTML loads Chart.js from cdn.jsdelivr.net. Cloudflare's Content Security Policy can block jsdelivr. The fixed version uses cdnjs.cloudflare.com which is always permitted. BUG 5 — MODERATE: XSS vulnerability in AI chat Location — index.html, askAI() function The original code injects user input directly into innerHTML. If a user types into the chat box it executes. The fix sanitises input through a temporary DOM element. // WRONG chatBox.innerHTML += `You: ${question}`; // CORRECT function sanitize(str) { const d = document.createElement("div"); d.innerText = str; return d.innerHTML; } chatBox.innerHTML += `You: ${sanitize(question)}`; 3. Improvements Added Beyond Bug Fixes • Collapsible sidebar — CSS --sb-width variable + body.collapsed class. Smooth 0.2s transition. • Metric cards switch the graph — clicking any of the 6 cards changes label, y-axis scale, and tracked data. • animation: false on Chart.js — no visible "jump" on every 2-second update. • Socket connect/disconnect events logged to console — visible in browser DevTools. • Chart history kept at 30 points instead of 20 — smoother curve. • Enter key uses keydown instead of deprecated keypress. 4. How to Teach the Fixed Code to Bruno Bruno has said explicitly: "I want to write the code, not copy-paste." He does not learn from reading complete files. He learns by understanding each line and typing it himself. Session opening — ask these two questions first, do not skip "The Cloudflare tunnel points to port 8080. Your app.py ran on port 5000. What do you think happened when a visitor typed psblabsai.onlin

summary: A teaching guide for Bruno to rebuild a Flask-based AI server from scratch, emphasizing understanding over copy-pasting. Focuses on app.py and index.html implementation with strict knowledge verification.
text:
PSB Dashboard — Phase 7
Gemini Teaching Brief: Guide Bruno to Re-Build This From Scratch
Prepared by Claude · March 2026 · Confidential Teaching Document
This document exists for one purpose: you must understand this codebase so completely that you can
guide Bruno to write every line himself tomorrow, without pasting complete files at him. Read every section
before the session starts.
I Session Goal
By the end of tomorrow's session, Bruno should have typed every line of
app.py and index.html himself, understand what each line does, and be
able to explain it back without prompting. He does NOT learn from
copy-pasting. He learns from writing and understanding.
1 · Who Bruno Is — Read This Before You Say Anything
Bruno is a fast learner with zero prior programming experience beyond this project. He built this server
from hardware up. He shuts down completely when asked to apply knowledge he was never given. His
single biggest trigger for disengagement is being asked to fill in blanks he was never taught.
What he knows (confirmed, tested):
 Flask routing: @app.route, render_template, what import means
 Python venv: why isolation matters, how to activate, pip install inside venv
 Linux kernel basics: /proc filesystem, UFW, SSH hardening, systemctl
 HTML structure: h1-h6, p tags, that HTML is a skeleton not a language
 Jinja2: the {{ }} bridge between Python and HTML templates
 Cloudflare tunnel: the full chain from browser to Flask on port 8080
 psutil basics: he has seen cpu_percent and virtual_memory in action
 Docker: the container isolation concept
 systemctl: start, stop, restart, status
What he does NOT know (never introduce without teaching first):
 JavaScript — has written zero lines before this project
 WebSockets — never explained before Phase 7
 Threading in Python — never used, never taught
 CSS Grid in depth — knows colours and fonts, not layout systems
 Chart.js — never touched
 HTTP POST requests in code (requests library)
 JSON serialisation — what it is and why it happens automatically
 XSS attacks — never heard of it before the audit
 async_mode and why it matters for Flask-SocketIO
2 · Complete Code Breakdown — Understand Every Line
app.py — The Python Backend
Block 1: Imports (lines 1-7)
These six imports are the tools the file needs. Never skip explaining them — Bruno needs to know why
each one is there before writing it.
from flask import Flask, render_template
Flask creates the web app. render_template serves HTML from the templates/ folder.
from flask_socketio import SocketIO
Adds WebSocket support. Without this, there is no real-time. Only polling, which is inefficient.
import psutil
Reads CPU, RAM, disk, network from the Linux kernel. The interface to /proc.
import time
time.sleep(2) pauses the background loop. Without it, the CPU would spike to 100%.
import threading
Runs the background collector in parallel with Flask. Without it, Flask would be blocked.
import requests
Sends HTTP POST to Ollama at localhost:11434. The HTTP client library.
Block 2: App Initialisation (lines 9-11)
app = Flask(__name__)
socketio = SocketIO(app, cors_allowed_origins="*", async_mode="threading")
latest_metrics = {}
Flask(__name__) creates the app. __name__ is a Python magic variable that resolves to the file's module
name, telling Flask where to find templates/. cors_allowed_origins="*" allows connections from any
domain — necessary because Cloudflare serves the page from psblabsai.online but the WebSocket
connects to the server directly. async_mode="threading" is critical: it tells SocketIO to use Python threads,
so the background collector and Flask web server can run simultaneously.
II Bug #2 was
here
The original code had no async_mode set. Result: random WebSocket
drops and freezes as the background thread and Flask competed for the
GIL.
Block 3: The Route (lines 13-15)
@app.route('/')
def index():
    return render_template('index.html')
@app.route("/") registers the function as the handler for GET re

summary: A learning module explaining four research-backed strategies for mastering technical concepts: active recall, Feynman technique, spaced repetition, and interleaving. Contains exercises and troubleshooting guidance for overcoming learning barriers.
text:
PSB
Personal Second Brain
Complete Learning Module
Learning Guide  ·  Practice Exercises  ·  Bedtime Reading  ·  Command Cheat Sheet  ·  Bruno Mosti 2026
1.1  Why Copy-Pasting Felt Fine Until It Did Not
Copy-pasting working code is not cheating. It is a completely normal phase of learning. Every senior engineer has done it. The problem is not that you did it — the problem is staying there. Copy-pasting builds a working system but leaves gaps in your mental model. When something breaks, you have no map to navigate by. When a new phase starts, the unfamiliar code feels overwhelming because you have no framework to attach it to. This module is the framework. Read it, do the exercises, and the code you already have will start to make sense backwards.
1.2  The Four Learning Strategies Used in This Module
These are not made up. They are research-backed techniques used in engineering education. Every section of this module uses at least one of them.
Strategy 1 — Active Recall
Reading is passive. Your brain records words but does not build structure. Active recall forces retrieval — you close the book and try to remember what you just read. Every purple question box in this module is active recall. Do not skip them. Do not just think the answer. Write it. The effort of searching your memory is what creates the memory.
Strategy 2 — The Feynman Technique
Richard Feynman — Nobel Prize physicist — had one rule: if you cannot explain something simply, you do not understand it yet. Every time you think you understand a concept, try to explain it to someone who knows nothing about computers. No jargon. No technical terms. Plain English. If you get stuck, you found the exact thing you need to go back and learn. This module asks you to do this repeatedly with Socratic questions.
Strategy 3 — Spaced Repetition
Your brain forgets things on a predictable schedule. Reviewing material right before you forget it is the most efficient use of study time. The schedule: review new material the same day you learn it, then after 1 day, then after 3 days, then after 1 week, then after 2 weeks. After 2 weeks of spaced repetition, the material is in long-term memory. Do not try to learn everything in one session. Learn a chapter, sleep on it, review it briefly the next morning, move on.
Strategy 4 — Interleaving
Do not study one topic until it is perfect before moving to the next. Mix them. Study Python classes, then do a Docker exercise, then come back to Python. This feels less efficient because each switch is harder. It is actually more efficient because the difficulty of switching builds stronger memory traces. The practice exercises at the end of this module are intentionally mixed — they do not map neatly to the chapters. That is by design.
1.3  What to Do When You Hit a Wall
You will hit walls in this module. Some concepts will not click on the first read. This is not a sign you are doing it wrong. It is a sign you are doing it right — you are encountering genuinely new ideas. Here is the protocol when you feel stuck or frustrated:
▸  Step 1: Stop reading. Close the document.
▸  Step 2: Write down, in plain words, what you understood before the wall. Not what you read — what you actually got.
▸  Step 3: Write down exactly where it stopped making sense. One specific sentence or line of code.
▸  Step 4: Take 10 minutes away. Walk, get water, look outside. Not a phone — physical movement.
▸  Step 5: Come back and read just the paragraph before the wall again. Often the wall dissolves.
▸  Step 6: If still stuck — go to the Bedtime Reading section for that topic. The plain English version often unlocks the technical version.
2.1  Your System in Plain English
You have a computer in your room that runs 24 hours a day. It has a web server on it. When you visit psblabsai.online, your browser asks that server for a webpage. The server sends back your dashboard. Then the dashboard opens a permanent live connection back to the server — like a phone call that stay

summary: Explains building a self-updating second brain using Neo4j, Ollama/Llama 3, and D3.js visualization. Focuses on four layered architecture for knowledge graph ingestion, processing, storage, and querying.
text:
PSB Knowledge Graph
Building a Self-Updating Second Brain on Your Home Server
Bruno Mosti  ·  PSB Phase 9+  ·  March 2026  ·  Architecture by Claude  ·  For Gemini
What you saw in that screenshot is a knowledge graph — a database that stores not just data, but the relationships between data. Every dot is a node (a concept, a conversation, a file, a project, a person). Every line is an edge (a relationship: "RELATES_TO", "LEARNED_FROM", "PART_OF", "CAUSED_BY"). The AI agent can traverse this graph — moving from node to node — to answer complex questions, find connections you did not know existed, and update itself as new information arrives.
Your PSB server can run this. The technology stack is: Neo4j (the graph database, runs in Docker), Python (ingestion and query API), Ollama/Llama 3 (processing and categorisation), and a D3.js or Neovis.js visualisation in your dashboard. This document teaches you every layer.
The simplest possible explanation
A normal database stores facts in rows and columns. "Username: Bruno, CPU: i5-9400F." That is a table. It answers questions like "what is Bruno's CPU?" but it cannot answer questions like "what concepts is Bruno working on that connect to his security knowledge and his AI project?"
A knowledge graph stores three things: Nodes (things that exist), Properties (facts about those things), and Edges (how things relate to each other). The power is in the edges. They turn isolated facts into a web of meaning that an AI can reason over.
Graph DB vs SQL vs NoSQL — when to use each
Your PSB system needs four clean layers. Each layer has one job. They communicate through defined interfaces. This prevents the system from turning into spaghetti as it grows.
LAYER 1 — INGESTION LAYER
What it does
Receives raw information — chat logs from Claude/ChatGPT, your own notes, server logs, code comments, learning sessions. Normalises them into a standard format before anything else touches them.
# Standard ingestion format — every source converts to this
{
"source":    "claude_conversation",   # claude | chatgpt | manual | server_log
"timestamp": "2026-03-24T14:30:00Z",
"raw_text":  "Full raw content...",
"metadata":  { "session_id": "abc123", "tags": ["security", "flask"] }
}
LAYER 2 — PROCESSING LAYER (AI BOUNCER)
What it does
Takes raw ingestion objects and runs them through Ollama. The AI extracts concepts, relationships, and categories. Removes noise. Outputs structured JSON. This layer runs asynchronously in a background queue — it never blocks Flask.
# Prompt sent to Ollama for every ingestion object
EXTRACTION_PROMPT = """
You are a knowledge extraction engine.
Read the following text and extract:
1. Key concepts (nouns, technologies, ideas)
2. Relationships between concepts
3. Category: Technology | Mindset | Security | Project | Learning
Respond ONLY in this exact JSON format:
{
"concepts": ["Flask", "WebSocket", "real-time"],
"relationships": [
{"from": "Flask", "to": "WebSocket", "type": "USES"},
{"from": "WebSocket", "to": "real-time", "type": "ENABLES"}
],
"category": "Technology",
"summary": "One sentence summary"
}
Text: {raw_text}
"""
LAYER 3 — STORAGE LAYER (NEO4J)
What it does
Receives the structured JSON from the processing layer. Creates or merges nodes and edges in the graph database. MERGE is critical — it prevents duplicate nodes when the same concept appears in multiple ingestion sources.
# Cypher query — the query language for Neo4j
# MERGE = "create if not exists, otherwise find the existing one"
MERGE (a:Concept {name: $from_concept, category: $category})
MERGE (b:Concept {name: $to_concept})
MERGE (a)-[r:RELATES_TO {type: $relation_type}]->(b)
SET r.last_seen = datetime()
SET r.count = coalesce(r.count, 0) + 1
RETURN a, r, b
The count property on edges is important. If "Flask" → "USES" → "WebSocket" appears 47 times across your conversations, the edge weight grows to 47. This tells the AI which connections are strong in your knowledge base vs which are weak.
LAYER 4 — QUERY AND

version: "3.8"
# PSB Dashboard — Phase 9A Docker Infrastructure
# Neo4j (Knowledge Graph) + Redis (Task Queue)

services:

image: neo4j:5.17
container_name: psb_neo4j
ports:

- neo4j_logs:/logs

command: redis-server --maxmemory 512mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru --save 60 1
ports:
- "6379:6379"
volumes:
- redis_data:/data
restart: unless-stopped
mem_limit: 512m
memswap_limit: 512m
volumes:
neo4j_data:
neo4j_logs:

text:
PSB Dashboard
Phase 7 Complete — Personal Study Guide
Bruno Mosti · University of Greenwich · March 2026
What this document is
You just built a real-time AI server dashboard from scratch. Flask, WebSockets, Python threading, Chart.js,
Ollama — all of it running live at psblabsai.online. This guide exists so you can truly understand every
decision that was made, not just the fact that it works. Read this before you open the IDE next time. The goal
is simple: one day you sit down with a blank file and build this from memory.
I Your Learning Objective
By the time you finish this document you should be able to: (1) draw the full data flow from the
Linux kernel to the browser graph on paper, (2) explain every import and every function in your
own words, (3) describe the three bugs that were found and why they broke things, and (4) explain
the CSS scroll fix and why it works. If you can do all four, you have genuinely mastered Phase 7.
Contents
1
The Big Picture — Architecture, layers, and the complete data flow
2
Python Backend Deep Dive — Every line of app.py explained
3
Frontend Deep Dive — HTML, CSS Grid, animations, JavaScript, Chart.js
4
The CSS Scroll Fix — Why min-height: 0 matters and how Flexbox really works
5
Security Concepts — XSS, ports, sanitisation, and why they matter
6
Concept Reference Cards — Quick lookup for every major idea
7
The 3 Bugs That Were Fixed — What broke, why, and what you learned
8
How to Memorise This — Science-backed study schedule and techniques
9
Study Materials — Where to go next
1 · The Big Picture
Architecture, layers, and the complete data flow
Before a single line of code makes sense, you need the map. This section gives you the full picture of
what you built and how all the pieces connect. Read this first, every time.
The Four-Layer Stack
Layer
Technology
Lives on
What it does
Linux Kernel
/proc filesystem psutil
library
Ubuntu 24.04 (psb
server)

temperature sensors, network counters
Python Backend
Flask + Flask-SocketIO
psutil + GPUtil + requests

Reads kernel data every 2s, pushes it
to browsers via WebSocket
Browser Frontend
HTML + CSS + JavaScript
Chart.js + Socket.IO client
Your browser (any
device)
Receives live data, updates numbers,
draws the animated graph
AI Brain
Ollama + Llama 3 RTX
2060 (6 GB VRAM)
psb server port
11434
Reads the question + live metrics,
generates a human-readable answer
The Complete Data Flow — Trace Every Packet
This is the single most important thing to memorise. A CPU reading travels this exact path from silicon to
your screen:
1
Kernel writes ticks
/proc/stat is updated by the Linux kernel every few milliseconds. Each CPU core writes how many
ticks it has spent in user mode, system mode, and idle mode since boot.
2
psutil reads and calculates
psutil.cpu_percent(interval=None) reads /proc/stat twice with a gap and computes the percentage of
non-idle ticks. It abstracts all the raw kernel maths.
3
background_thread packages it
Every 2 seconds, the Python background thread collects CPU + RAM + GPU + Temp + Net + Disk
into a dict called payload.
4
socketio.emit broadcasts
socketio.emit("metrics_update", payload) converts the Python dict to JSON and pushes it over
WebSocket to every connected browser simultaneously.
5
socket.on receives it
The browser JavaScript function socket.on("metrics_update", ...) fires the moment the data arrives.
No refresh needed — the connection is always open.
6
DOM updates
JavaScript writes the new values into the HTML elements:
document.getElementById("ui-cpu").innerText = data.cpu + "%"
7
Chart.js draws the point
The new value is pushed into the chart dataset. chart.update() redraws the line with a smooth 400ms
ease animation.
The AI Path (parallel to the above)
1
User types in chat and presses Enter
JavaScript emits an agent_ai event over WebSocket: socket.emit("agent_ai", { question: q })
2
Python catches it
@socketio.on("agent_ai") fires. Python reads the question and the late

This is the single most important thing to memorise. A CPU reading travels this exact path from silicon to

Kernel writes ticks
/proc/stat is updated by the Linux kernel every few milliseconds. Each CPU core writes how many
ticks it has spent in user mode, system mode, and idle mode since boot.

psutil reads and calculates
psutil.cpu_percent(interval=None) reads /proc/stat twice with a gap and computes the percentage of
non-idle ticks. It abstracts all the raw kernel maths.

I How AI Was Used in This Project
Google Gemini served as my AI tutor throughout this project. Claude (Anthropic) acted as session
logger and documentation system. Both are honest disclosures I make upfront because
transparency matters. Every command was executed by me. Every line of code was typed by me.
Every concept was verified through Socratic questioning before I was allowed to proceed. The AI
played the role a senior mentor would — explaining the why before the how, asking me to justify
each decision, and refusing to let me copy-paste without understanding. Using AI assistance this
way is exactly how professional engineers work today.
This document is a honest account of the project — including the parts that broke, the near-misses, the
debugging sessions that ran until 2am, and the moments where I pushed through instead of quitting. The
struggles are documented because they are where the real learning happened.
SECTION 1
What I Built
The PSB Project is a self-hosted AI server control panel built from scratch on dedicated Ubuntu hardware
— not a tutorial I followed, not a cloud service I provisioned, but a real machine I secured, configured, and
deployed from the command line. The final product is a live, globally accessible dashboard at
psblabsai.online with real-time hardware monitoring and an AI diagnostics agent running Llama 3 locally
on an NVIDIA RTX 2060.
The project spans 13 phases over multiple weeks, covering Linux systems administration, network
security, cryptography, Python web development, WebSocket architecture, CSS layout engineering, and
local LLM deployment. Every phase was verified — I could not advance until I explained each concept
back correctly.

↓ Any device, any network, worldwide
↓ HTTPS — TLS at Cloudflare edge, automatic certificate management
Cloudflare Edge — DDoS protection, bot management, global CDN
↓ Named Tunnel — encrypted outbound connection, no open router ports

Flask + Flask-SocketIO — Python backend, WebSocket engine
Browser — Chart.js graphs, 6 metric cards, AI chat panel
Ollama — Llama 3, NVIDIA RTX 2060 VRAM, local inference
SECTION 2
The 13 Phases
Every phase follows the same format: Concept → Deep Dive → Command/Code → Line-by-Line
Breakdown → Recap → Socratic Questions → Gate Checkpoint. Nothing was implemented until I could
explain it. Phases are listed with the real deliverable and the skills they required.
1
Linux Architecture Fundamentals
Built foundational mental model of how Linux works at kernel level before touching any configuration.
SSH flow · /proc filesystem · CPU delta math · PIDs · boot sequence · file permissions

Server Security Hardening
Deployed UFW firewall (default-deny) and Fail2Ban intrusion prevention. Two near-miss incidents in this
phase created the safety protocol used for every subsequent change.
UFW · Fail2Ban · default-deny posture · auth log monitoring · strong credential management
3
Cryptographic Authentication
Replaced password SSH with Ed25519 key pair and fully disabled password authentication over the
network.
Asymmetric cryptography · Ed25519 · authorized_keys · sshd_config hardening
4
Automated Patch Management
Set up unattended-upgrades to apply

summary: Comprehensive teaching guide for PSB Dashboard Phase 8 codebase covering app.py, index.html, and login.html. Explains every code block's purpose, connects concepts to system architecture, and uses Socratic method for instruction.
text:
PSB Dashboard — Complete Teaching Document
app.py · index.html · login.html — Every Block, Every Concept, Every Why
Bruno Mosti  ·  PSB Phase 8 Complete  ·  March 2026  ·  Prepared by Claude for Gemini
GEMINI — READ THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE
This document is the master teaching reference for the PSB Dashboard Phase 8 codebase. It covers every block of code across three files — what each line does, why it exists, what concept it teaches, and how it connects to everything else. Your job is to teach Bruno each block using the Socratic method: explain the concept, ask him to predict the answer, then confirm or correct.
app.py is the brain of the entire dashboard. It sits on the Ubuntu server, runs 24/7, reads hardware metrics from the Linux kernel, broadcasts them to browsers via WebSocket, handles login/logout authentication, and routes AI queries to Ollama. Nothing the user sees happens without app.py making it happen first.
BLOCK 1 — IMPORTS
What imports are and why they exist
Python does not load everything at once. You choose what tools you need. An import statement is you telling Python: "Go find this library, load it into memory, and make it available under this name." This keeps programs small and fast — you only pay for what you use.
from flask import Flask, render_template
from flask_socketio import SocketIO
import psutil
import time
import threading
import requests
from flask_login import LoginManager, UserMixin, login_user,
login_required, logout_user, current_user
from flask_bcrypt import Bcrypt
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
Line-by-line breakdown
flask → Flask — The web framework. Flask is the engine that listens for HTTP requests (GET /login, POST /login, GET /) and decides what to do with them. Without Flask, there is no web server — just a Python script.
flask → render_template — Flask's function for loading .html files from the templates/ folder and sending them to the browser. Flask uses Jinja2 to process {{ }} and {% %} placeholders before sending.
flask_socketio → SocketIO — Extends Flask with WebSocket support. Normal HTTP is one request → one response → connection closes. WebSocket is a persistent bidirectional pipe — the server can push data to the browser at any time without being asked. This is what makes the live graphs work.
psutil — Python System Utility. Reads live hardware data from /proc/stat, /proc/meminfo, /proc/net/dev and other kernel interfaces. The abstraction layer between your Python code and the Linux kernel.
time — Python standard library. Used for time.sleep(2) — pauses the background thread for 2 seconds between each metric emission cycle.
threading — Python standard library. Allows multiple functions to run at the same time. Flask's web server and the background metric collector run as separate threads — without this, the server would freeze while collecting metrics.
requests — HTTP client library. Used to send POST requests from Python to Ollama's local API on localhost:11434. The same library you'd use to call any external API.
flask_login → LoginManager — The session manager. Tracks who is logged in across requests using encrypted cookies. Without this, every page load would be as if the user had never logged in.
flask_login → UserMixin — A helper class that gives your User class all the methods Flask-Login requires (is_authenticated, is_active, get_id, etc.). Inherit from it so you do not have to write them yourself.
flask_login → login_user / logout_user / current_user / login_required — Four tools: login_user() creates the session cookie, logout_user() destroys it, current_user gives you the logged-in user object inside templates, @login_required redirects unauthenticated users to the login page.
flask_bcrypt → Bcrypt — Password hashing library. Takes a plain text password and runs it through the bcrypt algorithm — a one-way mathematical scramble that is computationally expensive to reverse. Stores the hash, never the password.
os — Python standard library for Operating

summary: This guide explains Bruno's self-hosted AI server architecture, including WebSocket communication, Docker containers (Neo4j/Redis), Ollama integration, and five layered system design. It covers hardware-software interactions and phase-specific infrastructure setup.
text:
PSB
From Copy-Paster to Engineer
The Complete Self-Teaching Guide — Updated Edition
Python  ·  Architecture  ·  Your Actual Code  ·  Phase 9  ·  Practice Exercises  ·  Bedtime Reading
1.1  Your System in Plain English
You have a computer in your room that runs 24 hours a day. It has a web server on it. When you visit psblabsai.online, your browser asks that server for a webpage. The server sends back your dashboard. Then the dashboard opens a permanent live connection back to the server — like a phone call that stays open — so the server can push CPU readings, RAM usage, GPU load, and temperature to your browser every 2 seconds without you having to refresh.
At the same time, the server is running a loop in the background. Every 2 seconds it reads the hardware sensors from the Linux kernel, packages the numbers, and broadcasts them to every open browser. Your dashboard receives those numbers and updates the chart and cards.
There is also an AI assistant. When you type a question, the browser sends it to the server over the same live connection. The server forwards it to Ollama — a local AI program using your GPU — which generates an answer. Your GPU does the thinking. No cloud. No cost. No data leaving your home.
There are also two database containers running in Docker. Neo4j is a graph database. Redis is a task queue. They are running but not yet connected to the main app — they are the infrastructure waiting for phases 9B through 9D.
1.2  Two Ways Browsers Talk to Servers
When you first visit psblabsai.online, that is an HTTP request — browser asks, server sends the HTML page, done. Then the JavaScript inside that page immediately opens a WebSocket connection that stays open for your entire session. Every metric update, every AI response, every Docker status travels over this one persistent connection.
1.3  The Five Layers — Why Nothing Is Random
Every decision in this project — every config file, every function, every security measure — exists to serve one of five layers. Once you see the layers, nothing will feel random again.
Layer 5  —  Browser  — index.html (templates/)
The page you see. HTML + CSS + JavaScript. Knows nothing about Linux or Docker. Its only job: show data nicely, let you click things, talk to the server over WebSocket.
Layer 4  —  Web Server  — app.py (Flask + Gunicorn)
The Python program on Ubuntu. Receives browser connections. Serves the HTML. Manages WebSocket events. Collects metrics. Calls Ollama. Talks to Docker. The brain.
Layer 3  —  Containers  — docker-compose.yml
Isolated programs in Docker. Neo4j (knowledge graph) and Redis (task queue). Running but not yet connected to the main app. Infrastructure for future phases.
Layer 2  —  Operating System  — Ubuntu 24.04, UFW, Fail2Ban, SSH
Linux manages the hardware. Controls who can connect (firewall). Blocks attackers (Fail2Ban). Provides the data that psutil reads from the /proc filesystem.
Layer 1  —  Hardware  — i5-9400F, RTX 2060, 16GB RAM
The physical machine. CPU handles orchestration. GPU handles AI inference. Every architectural decision respects these fixed limits.
2.1  Variables and Types
A variable is a named box that holds a value. The type of value determines what you can do with it. In Python you do not declare the type — Python figures it out from what you assign.
# These are variables:
cpu_usage    = 12.5       # float (decimal number)
ram_gb       = 4.2        # float
is_running   = True       # bool (True or False)
container    = "neo4j"    # string (text)
port_number  = 7687       # int (whole number)
# You can change them at any time:
cpu_usage = 15.1          # box now holds 15.1
# Types matter:
print(cpu_usage + 1)      # 16.1  ← works
print(container + "_db")  # "neo4j_db"  ← works
print(cpu_usage + container)  # ERROR — cannot add float to string
In your app.py, DOCKER_AVAILABLE is a bool. latest_metrics is a dict (see below). thread is either None or a background task object. Understanding the TYPE of a variable tells you w

summary: This SRS document outlines functional and non-functional requirements for a cross-platform malware detection system using Sysmon/Auditd telemetry, ML-based classification, and rule-based heuristics. It emphasizes explainable AI, local storage, and collaborative development for a student portfolio project.
text:
Software Requirements Specification (SRS) 
Project: Intelligent Malware Detection & System Protection 
 Platform: Windows & Linux (user-space) 
 Team: 4+ students (expandable) 
 
Introduction 
This document defines the functional and non-functional requirements for an 
intelligent malware detection and system protection system. The system is designed 
to work on Windows and Linux, monitoring system behaviour, running ML-based 
detection, and providing explainable output to the user. Its purpose is to provide a 
portfolio-grade project for a student team while demonstrating practical skills in 
cybersecurity, machine learning, software engineering, and secure system design. 
The system does not operate in the kernel, making it safe, legally compliant, and 
suitable for beginner-to-intermediate developers. It leverages existing telemetry 
frameworks such as Sysmon for Windows and Auditd for Linux, combined with a 
modular ML-based decision engine, a rule-based heuristics engine, and a simple 
user interface for alerts and reports. 
 
Project Purpose 
The goal is to create a cross-platform, intelligent malware detection tool that 
provides: 
• Real-time monitoring and logging of system events 
• Behavioural anomaly detection 
• Machine-learning–powered risk scoring 
• File isolation and quarantine 
• Explainable output so the user understands why a file or process was flagged 
This project is intended to demonstrate technical skills in a real-world context, 
producing a professional, portfolio-ready prototype. It highlights collaboration, 
planning, secure software engineering, and technical documentation. 
 
System Overview 
The system consists of the following modules: 
1. Telemetry Collectors – Collect system events from Windows and Linux 
using Sysmon and Auditd. 
2. Data Normalisation & Feature Extraction – Convert logs into a unified 
internal format suitable for ML processing. 
3. Machine Learning Engine – Classifies files/processes as benign or 
suspicious based on extracted features. 
4. Rule-Based Heuristics Engine – Adds additional logic to combine known 
safe/unsafe patterns with ML output. 
5. Explainability Module – Provides human-readable reasoning for detections 
and quarantine actions. 
6. Local Storage – SQLite/PostgreSQL database to store events, detections, 
and explanations. 
7. User Interface – Dashboard or CLI showing alerts, logs, quarantined files, 
and analysis details. 
 
Functional Requirements (FR) 
FR1: Collect and monitor system events from Windows and Linux. 
 FR2: Normalise logs into a unified schema. 
 FR3: Extract ML features from events (API calls, process behaviour, registry 
changes, etc.). 
 FR4: Run ML classification locally to determine risk. 
 FR5: Combine ML output with rule-based heuristics for final scoring. 
 FR6: Isolate suspicious files into a quarantine folder. 
 FR7: Provide human-readable explanations for each detection. 
 FR8: Display alerts, logs, and quarantine info in the UI. 
 FR9: Store events, detections, and explanations in a local database. 
 FR10: Run entirely offline, with no external network dependency. 
 FR11: Support cross-platform operation (Windows and Linux). 
 FR12: Allow multiple developers to work collaboratively without conflicts. 
 
Non-Functional Requirements (NFR) 
NFR1: Lightweight – Average CPU usage ≤5% during monitoring. 
 NFR2: Privacy – All data remains local; no cloud transmission. 
 NFR3: Security – Quarantine protection, file permissions enforced. 
 NFR4: Maintainability – Modular code for easy updates by a student team. 
 NFR5: Portability – Single codebase runs on both Windows and Linux. 
 NFR6: Explainability – Every detection must include clear reasoning. 
 NFR7: Reliability – Continuous 24/7 monitoring without crashes. 
 NFR8: Scalability – Easy to add new detection modules or update ML models. 
 
Constraints 
• Small team of 4 students (expandable to 6–7 in the future). 
• 1-year project timeline. 
• Limited hardware (consumer-grade PCs). 
•

summary: This document outlines a project combining AI and cybersecurity to create an advanced threat detection system. It emphasizes explainable AI, cross-platform compatibility, and hybrid architecture to address modern security challenges beyond traditional antivirus limitations.
text:
security system optimised with artificial intelligence 
Content 
• Why the project exists? 
This project is designed to demonstrate our capacity to lead ambitious initiatives 
within the modern IT sector. Its primary objective is to validate the high-level skills 
required to position us as top-tier talent. By fostering autonomy and technical 
independence, this project culminates in a digital portfolio that serves as tangible 
proof of expertise for future employers. 
 
• Target users? 
The target audience for this project includes AI industry professionals, software 
engineers, and corporate stakeholders. Unlike a commercial product designed for 
revenue generation, this initiative is strictly non-commercial. Its primary function is to 
serve as a vehicle for professional branding, establishing our technical competence 
and readiness for the industry. 
• Value for cybersecurity and ML 
Core Value: Addressing Modern Security Challenges 
Our system provides significant value by filling the gaps left by traditional security 
measures. 
The Problem: Most traditional Antivirus (AV) products rely heavily on static 
methodsspecifically signature databases, pattern matching, and rigid rule-based 
systems. Consequently, modern threats and modified malware can easily bypass 
these defenses. 
Our Solution: By integrating Behavioral Analysis and Machine Learning, our system 
looks at what the file does, not just what it looks like. 
The Result: This approach allows us to detect new malware variants, obfuscated 
files, and "zero-day-like" behaviors that traditional tools miss. effectively elevating 
our project to the standard of professional Endpoint Detection & Response (EDR) 
systems. 
Explainable isolation increases trust 
What does this mean for our antivirus? It means it won't tell us generic information 
but like: 
• "This file could cause problems" 
 
 
 
 
 
• "This file is dangerous" 
 
• "This file has been quarantined" 
 
But it will explain why. 
For example: 
  
"High entropy suggests obfuscated code." 
  
"Suspicious API calls: CreateRemoteThread." 
  
"Executable packed with UPX-like patterns." 
  
And everything will have the most user-friendly explanation possible. 
  
Explainability improves: 
•  user understanding 
•  transparency 
•  decision-making 
•  educational value 
•  Cybersecurity companies love this approach. 
Cross-platform coverage is rare for students 
Most student projects target only Windows. 
You target: 
• Windows 
• Linux 
This demonstrates: 
• broader system knowledge 
• wider applicability 
• professional relevance 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Advanced Machine Learning Implementation 
This project distinguishes itself by applying Machine Learning to a hostile, high-
stakes domain rather than standard academic problems. 
Application to Real-World Security Data 
 While many portfolios rely on basic datasets (e.g., sentiment analysis or image 
classification), this system tackles binary analysis and anomaly detection. We 
address the complexities of non-standardized data, moving beyond "textbook ML" 
into the messy reality of cybersecurity. 
Advanced Feature Engineering  
We demonstrate rare entry-level skills by extracting complex features from raw 
binaries, including: 
• Entropy Calculations: To detect packed or encrypted malware. 
• N-gram Analysis & Embedded Strings: To identify malicious patterns in code. 
• API-Call Sequence Modeling: To understand the intent of a program. 
Engineering for Efficiency  
Companies prioritize models that are resource-efficient. We demonstrate an 
understanding of practical constraints by building a system that is lightweight, cross-
platform, and fast—proving we can engineer solutions that run on real hardware 
without unnecessary overhead. 
Industry-Standard Hybrid Architecture  
Modern security engines (like those from CrowdStrike or Microsoft Defender) rarely 
use ML alone. Our system mirrors industry standards by utilizing a Hybrid AI 
approach: combining the predictive pow

summary: Evaluates feasibility of building a cross-platform malware detection platform using modular, non-kernel architecture. Analyzes technical viability, team collaboration strategies, and resource requirements for beginner developers.
text:
Feasibility Report 
 
Intelligent Malware Detection & System Protection Platform 
(Cross-platform, non-kernel, multi-developer architecture — Beginner-friendly) 
 
Executive Summary 
FEASIBILITY REPORT 
Intelligent Malware Detection & System Protection Platform 
(Cross-platform, non-kernel, multi-developer architecture — Beginner-friendly) 
 
1. Executive Summary 
This feasibility report evaluates whether a team of three beginner developers can 
successfully build an intelligent malware-analysis and system-protection platform 
using a modular, non-kernel approach. The project blends cybersecurity telemetry, 
machine learning–based detection, behavioural monitoring, an analysis engine, and 
a simple user interface. 
The analysis demonstrates that: 
• the system is technically feasible using user-space monitoring (Sysmon / 
Auditd), 
• development can be realistically divided between three students, 
• cost and resource requirements are extremely low, 
• risk can be controlled with proper planning, 
• and the final result will significantly strengthen each participant’s technical 
portfolio. 
The project is challenging but achievable, and provides strong career value in 
cybersecurity, machine learning, and software engineering. 
 
2. Project Overview 
2.1 Project Purpose 
The project aims to build an intelligent, cross-platform malware-detection prototype 
capable of analysing system behaviour and identifying potentially malicious activity in 
real time. The platform does not rely on kernel-level operations (no drivers, no 
rootkits), making it safe, legal, and beginner-friendly. 
2.2 Key Features 
• Real-time log ingestion (Windows Sysmon, Linux Auditd). 
• Behaviour-based anomaly detection. 
• Machine-learning model trained on clean vs malicious samples. 
• Signature-independent scoring engine. 
• Dashboard/API for alerts and system status. 
• Modular design supporting multi-developer collaboration. 
2.3 Target Use Case 
• Students building a portfolio. 
• Cybersecurity analysts showcasing capability. 
• A research prototype for behavioural malware detection. 
 
 
 
 
3. Stakeholder Analysis

4. Project Planning Strategies Considered 
4.1 Waterfall Model 
Useful for documentation, research, and structured planning. 
 But too rigid for experimentation. 
4.2 Agile (Scrum/Kanban) 
Better for this project because: 
• Small team 
• Frequent iteration 
• Experimental ML component 
• Multiple rapid prototypes 
4.3 Hybrid Model (Recommended) 
Use Waterfall for: 
• Requirements 
• Architecture 
• Research 
• Documentation 
Use Agile for: 
• Telemetry agent development 
• Machine-learning pipeline 
• Dashboard 
• Integration 
This hybrid model keeps structure while allowing flexibility. 
 
5. Technical Feasibility 
5.1 Architecture Feasibility 
The system uses a modular user-space architecture: 
1. Telemetry Collectors 
a. Sysmon (Windows) 
b. Auditd (Linux) 
c. Output normalised into a unified format (JSON/SQLite) 
2. Feature Extraction Layer 
a. Converts raw logs → numerical ML features 
b. Event frequency, entropy, DLL usage, registry modifications, process 
graph structure 
3. ML Engine 
a. Random Forest or LightGBM 
b. Lightweight and safe 
4. Analysis Core 
a. Combines ML probability + rule-based heuristics 
b. Produces risk score 
5. User Interface 
a. Local dashboard or CLI output 
b. Visualisation of alerts and logs 
Conclusion: 
 All components can be implemented without kernel drivers → fully feasible.

Explainability Specification 
Project: Intelligent Malware Detection & System Protection 
 Module: Explainability Engine & User Communication 
 Platform: Windows & Linux (User-space) 
Introduction 
This document defines the functional and architectural specifications for the 
Explainability Module. In this system, explainability refers to the capability to translate 
complex technical detection data (machine learning probabilities and heuristic signals) 
into clear, human-readable reasoning. 
The primary goal is to ensure the system is not a "black box." By providing transparent 
justifications for every alert, the project demonstrates a professional standard of trust 
and user education, elevating it above a typical student portfolio. 
 
Purpose and Objectives 
The Explainability Module serves four critical functions: 
1. Demystification: Translate raw binary features (e.g., entropy levels, API calls) 
into understandable risk factors. 
2. Transparency: Justify system decisions by clearly distinguishing between ML 
predictions and deterministic rule-based results. 
3. Actionability: Recommend user actions (e.g., "Quarantine immediately" or 
"Monitor process") instead of issuing generic alerts. 
4. Traceability: Link every alert to a unique Event ID in the local database for 
auditing and debugging. 
 
Components of Explainability 
The system uses a hybrid detection model. The Explainability Module synthesises 
outputs from two engines into a coherent message. 
3.1 Machine Learning Interpretation 
• ML Engine outputs a probability score (0.0–1.0). 
• The module maps this to a qualitative risk label and provides context based on 
the most influential features (e.g., SHAP values, feature importance). 
Output: Risk Level (Low, Moderate, High, Critical) 
 Example Explanation: "Statistical analysis of the file structure indicates a 92% 
resemblance to known ransomware variants." 
3.2 Heuristic Context 
• Rule-Based Engine flags deterministic behaviours. 
• Explanations must cite the specific rule triggered. 
Trigger: VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory 
 Explanation: "The process attempted to inject code into another running application, 
typical behaviour of malware attempting to hide itself." 
3.3 Technical Indicator Translation 
• Translate technical jargon for end-users: 
Raw: "High Entropy (>7.2)" 
 Explained: "The file code is heavily obfuscated or packed, suggesting an attempt to 
evade analysis." 
 
Functional Requirements (EX) 
Aligned with the SRS: 
EX-01: Comprehensive Alert Structure 
 Each alert must include: 
• Trigger: Behaviour or file characteristic causing the flag 
• Confidence: ML probability or rule certainty 
• Logic: Plain-English description of why it’s dangerous 
• Recommendation: Suggested user action (Quarantine, Delete, Whitelist) 
EX-02: Database Traceability 
 Explanations must be serialized and stored in the local database (SQLite/PostgreSQL) 
linked to Event IDs, ensuring historical logs remain interpretable. 
EX-03: Export Capability 
 Users can export explanations in JSON (technical analysis) or PDF (reporting) formats. 
EX-04: Cross-Platform Consistency 
 Explanation logic must be uniform across Windows and Linux, normalizing OS-specific 
terminology (e.g., Registry vs Config Files). 
 
User Interface Presentation 
The UI (dashboard or CLI) must present explanations hierarchically to avoid 
overwhelming the user. 
Example Dashboard Card: 
  THREAT DETECTED: Critical Risk 
• File: update_installer.exe 
• Reasoning: 
o Heuristic: Process attempted to modify system startup keys (Registry 
persistence) 
o Analysis: High file entropy suggests code is packed/encrypted to hide 
content 
o ML Score: 94% probability of malicious intent based on API call sequence 
• Recommendation: The file has been automatically quarantined. No further 
action is required. 
 
Implementation Strategy 
• Integration: Positioned between the Decision Engine and UI. Receives raw data, 
outputs formatted strings/JSON. 
• Perform

summary: Bruno outlines his final revision strategy for three key subjects, emphasizing structured study sessions with theory, practice, and exam simulation. The plan integrates active recall, spaced repetition, and real-world applications to prepare for university exams.
text:
I’m entering my final revision phase before my university exams in early November.

You are my AI Study Tutor. I want you to guide me through a complete and intensive revision program for the following subjects:

1. **COMP1811 – Paradigms of Programming**  
   Focus: Python fundamentals, control flow, functions, arrays/lists, debugging, small projects.

2. **MATH1179 – Mathematics for Computer Science**  
   Focus: Logic, sets, functions, algebraic manipulation, and problem-solving techniques.

3. **COMP1821 – Principles of Software Engineering**  
   Focus: Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), UML diagrams, testing, documentation.

---

### 🔍 What I want you to do:
1. Build a **step-by-step revision framework** that consolidates theory, practice, and exam preparation for each subject.  
2. For each session:
   - Give a **concise theory recap** (simple but technical explanation).  
   - Provide **practice questions** or **mini coding/math challenges**.  
   - Include **exam-style questions** or small scenarios to simulate real assessments.  
3. At the end of each revision block:
   - Give me a **self-assessment test** (10–15 questions).  
   - Provide **feedback and explanations** for any incorrect answers.  
4. Always connect examples to **real-world computing or AI contexts** when relevant.  
5. Keep the tone academic, structured, and clear — as if preparing me for first-year Computer Science exams.

---

### 🧩 Revision Strategy
- Use **active recall** and **spaced repetition** to help me remember key definitions and concepts.  
- Alternate between **theory → application → reflection** phases.  
- Focus more deeply on my weaker areas: **Programming and Mathematics**.  
- Include **short reflection prompts** (e.g., “Explain this concept aloud in your own words”).

---

### 🕒 Structure each session like this:
1. **Topic Overview** – 10 min theory summary  
2. **Guided Practice** – 30 min of exercises or code  
3. **Challenge Mode** – 15 min timed quiz or mini-project  
4. **Summary & Self-Reflection** – Key takeaways + what to review again later

---

At the end of the final revision week, create a **Comprehensive Exam Simulation** combining all subjects, with mixed theoretical and practical questions.

Make the revision experience engaging, adaptive, and academically rigorous.

Maths
Sets
A set is formally defined as a collection of objects (should be consider as an empty box)
That satisfies a clear criterion of membership, allowing one to unambiguously decide if something belongs to it or not. Sets are typically denoted using capital letters and their contents are enclosed in curly brackets {}
Main characteristics of sets include:
No duplicates: only different elements are counted
Order Unimportant: The elements can be in any arrangement without changing the set.
Number
The number system expands systematically to allow closure under more mathematical operations.
Clouse is the property ensuring that an operation on members of a set always result in a number that set till within that (e.g., adding two natural numbers always yields a natural number.)
Number systems validation
1.2 Operations and Properties
The order of operations (often remembered using the BIDMAS/BODMAS mnemonic) dictates the sequence in which calculations must be performed: brackets, indices/Orders, division and Multiplication (from left to right), Addition and subtraction (from left to right).
2.1 Factors, Multiples, and Primes
Factors are whole numbers that divide another number exactly
Multiples are numbers obtained by multiplying a base number by an integer.
A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that has exactly two distinct natural divisors’ 1 and itself. Prime numbers are fundamental, sometimes considered the "building blocks" of all natural numbers. In computing, prime numbers are essential for cryptography algorithms (e.g., RSA encryption)

Algebra uses letters )variables=to represent unknown quantities or value that may change, allowing us t express complex relationships concisely. Simplifying Involves reducing an expression by combining like terms, while expanding uses the distributive law to remove brackets. Welcome to MATH1179 Mathematics for Computer Science. The module is a 15-credit 
course that runs in  term 1.  
 
This module aims to ensure students have fundamental mathematics knowledge, of a similar 
level to the non-calculus and non-statistics content of A’ level mathematics and above 
 
This handbook provides essential information about this module including the aims and 
learning outcomes, the schedule of teaching and learning activities, assessment tasks, 
resource recommendations and, if applicable, any additional resources that you will need. 
Please read it at the start of term so you are aware of key details and important dates.

3. Module details and learning outcomes 
 
Host faculty: Faculty of Engineering and Science  
Host school: School of Computing and Mathematical Sciences 
Number of credits: 15 
Term(s) of delivery: Term 1  
Site(s) of delivery: Greenwich 
Pre-requisite modules: GCSE Mathematics or equivalent. 
 
Aims 
This module aims to provide computer science and computing students with the knowledge 
and understanding of mathematical methods and statistical techniques required to solve 
problems and analyse data throughout their undergraduate studies as well as in their further 
studies of computer science or in the work place. Along with its Term 2 counterpart, 
Advanced Mathematics for Computer Science, it also aims to prepare computer science 
students with sufficient mathematics tools and techniques for the level 5 Computer Science 
mathematics modules associated with these programmes and possible level 6 mathematics 
modules. Overall, this module aims to ensure students have fundamental mathematics 
knowledge, of a similar level to the non-calculus and non-statistics content of A’ level 
mathematics and above. 
 
Learning Outcomes 
On successful completion of this module a student will be able to:  
1. Demonstrate an understanding of sets, logic, graph theory and discrete mathematics 
algorithms and their applications in computing.  
2. Understand vectors and matrices and apply them to a range of problems and apply 
arithmetic and algebraic expressions in a range of number types and bases.  
3. Apply basic principles of statistics and probability and use software for data analysis and 
data visualisation and be able to interpret results. 
 
 
6

• 
A pre-requisite module is one that must have been completed successfully before 
taking this module.  
• 
A co-requisite module is one that must be taken alongside this module.  
• 
A learning outcome is a subject-specific statement that defines the learning to be 
achieved through completing this module.

This module develops cognitive skills by exposing you to a wide range of problem solving 
approaches so you can successfully tackle challenging problems whose solutions require 
creativity, great attention to detail, and/or the ability to combine knowledge and skills from 
different areas of the mathematical sciences and apply them to data science problems.

summary: Course notes outlining Mathematics for Computer Science topics like sets, number theory, and linear algebra. Emphasizes lecture attendance, tutorial participation, and workbook exercises for understanding. Includes assessment details and recommended resources.
text:
MATH1179  
Mathematics for 
Computer Science 
Part 1 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Dr Yvonne Fryer 
September 2021 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
MATH1179 
Mathematics for Computer Science 
 i 
Mathematics for Computer Science 
This handbook contains the basic material you will need for the first half of the module. Worked 
examples and further explanations will be given in the lectures and tutorials so it is very important 
that you attend lectures and tutorials and work through these notes. Only the most basic information 
about each topic is contained in this handbook. Accompanying these notes will also be a workbook 
with corresponding questions on a particular topic that are to be completed during the tutorials. Bring 
the workbook to the tutorials.  
 
What is this course about? 
We will look at some of the fundamental ideas of mathematics that are useful and applied in aa 
computing setting. You will gain far more from this course if you engage fully, work hard, contribute, 
and have fun! 
 
Course topics 
A variety of topics will be introduced. Some may be familiar to you, others possibly less so. You will 
be encouraged to read around and find out more about the topics. 
Topics will include sets, number theory, linear algebra, calculus, graph theory… and more! 
 
How will the course run? 
There is a two-hour lecture, that includes recorded and live sessions, plus there is a tutorial session 
each week for the module.  
 
Tutorials 
The tutorials allow you the opportunity to really make use of the tutors help and guidance. The tutors 
will be monitoring your completion of the tutorial exercises in the workbook. 
There will be tutorial exercises accompanying every week of lectures - you must try to complete these 
exercises - the most important reason is to develop your understanding. If you cannot do an exercise 
then ask for help! 
Working together on tutorial exercises is encouraged and strongly recommended – you can learn from 
each other! 
You should work through a selection of exercises and ask for help on ones you don’t understand how 
to do. 
Solutions will appear on Moodle a little while after the tutorial, after you have had time to try all the 
exercises for yourself. 
 
Attendance  
It is expected that you attend all lectures and tutorials. Records of attendance are kept. There is always 
a very strong correlation between attendance and marks. 
MATH1179 
ii 
Term 1 
If you cannot make a class, make sure you notify your absence online, let your personal tutor know 
there is a long term problem. 
Assessment 
This course is assessed by two tests each worth 50% of the marks available for the module. There 
will be formative assessment prior to the summative tests. This formative assessment will be used as 
a practice for you. More information will be given on this in the lectures. 
 
Books 
We do not “lecture from a book” and are therefore not expecting you to go out and buy a book. 
There are some books and sites listed that may be useful for you, but it is not compulsory to buy 
anything. 
If you find any really good books or sites, let me know, so that I can recommend them to other 
students! 
www.mathcentre.ac.uk has useful resources and practice material, often referred to on the course. 
 
Finally … 
Finally, we want you to enjoy this course! We want to get you thinking in different ways. 
Put the work in and contribute to lectures, and you will learn more and hopefully enjoy it while you 
are doing it! 
And ask me anything you want to ask! 
 
 
 
 
MATH1179 
Mathematics for Computer Science 
iii

Page No.

1.1 Subsets ................................................ 2 
1.2 Venn diagrams .................................... 3 
1.3 Laws of Operations of Sets ................ 6 
Product Set .......................................... 7 
2: Numbers.................................................... 9 
2.1 Numeric systems ........................

summary: Course notes covering foundational math topics for computer science, including vectors, matrices, graph theory, and algorithms. Emphasizes active engagement, tutorial exercises, and assessment structure.
text:
MATH1179  
Mathematics for 
Computer Science 
Part 2 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Notes 2 
 
 
Dr Yvonne Fryer 
September 2021 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
MATH1179 
Mathematics for Computer Science 
 i 
Mathematics for Computer Science 
This handbook contains the basic material you will need for the first half of the module. Worked 
examples and further explanations will be given in the lectures and tutorials so it is very important 
that you attend lectures and tutorials and bring these notes with you. Only the most basic information 
about each topic is contained in this handbook. Accompanying there notes will also be a workbook 
with corresponding questions on a particular topic that are to be completed during the tutorials.   
 
What is this course about? 
We will look at some of the fundamental ideas of mathematics that are useful and applied in aa 
computing setting. You will gain far more from this course if you engage fully, work hard, contribute, 
and have fun! 
 
Course topics 
A variety of topics will be introduced. Some may be familiar to you, others possibly less so. You will 
be encouraged to read around and find out more about the topics. 
Topics will include sets, number theory, linear algebra, calculus, graph theory… and more! 
 
How will the course run? 
There is a two hour lecture and a two hour tutorial session each week for the module.  
 
Tutorials 
The tutorials allow you the opportunity to really make use of the tutors help and guidance. The tutors 
will be monitoring your completion of the tutorial exercises in the workbook. 
There will be tutorial exercises accompanying every week of lectures - you must try to complete these 
exercises - the most important reason is to develop your understanding. If you cannot do an exercise 
then ask for help! 
Working together on tutorial exercises is encouraged and strongly recommended – you can learn from 
each other! 
You should work through a selection of exercises and ask for help on ones you don’t understand how 
to do. 
Solutions will appear on Moodle a little while after the tutorial, after you have had time to try all the 
exercises for yourself. 
 
Attendance  
It is expected that you attend all lectures and tutorials. Records of attendance are kept. There is always 
a very strong correlation between attendance and marks. 
If you cannot make a class, make sure you notify your absence online, let your personal tutor know 
there is a long term problem. 
MATH1179 
ii 
Term 1 
Assessment 
This course is assessed by two tests each worth 50% of the marks available for the module. There 
will be formative assessment prior to the summative tests. This formative assessment will be used as 
a practice for you. More information will be given on this in the lectures. 
 
Books 
We do not “lecture from a book” and are therefore not expecting you to go out and buy a book. 
There are some books and sites listed that may be useful for you, but it is not compulsory to buy 
anything. 
If you find any really good books or sites, let me know, so that I can recommend them to other 
students! 
www.mathcentre.ac.uk has useful resources and practice material, often referred to on the course. 
 
Finally … 
Finally, we want you to enjoy this course! We want to get you thinking in different ways. 
Put the work in and contribute to lectures, and you will learn more and hopefully enjoy it while you 
are doing it! 
And ask me anything you want to ask!

Mathematics for Computer Science
